div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. At the meeting of this society on Sunday, the chair. was occupied by Mr. Healey, who delivered an address in which he showed hew other lives were influenced by ours, and pointed out the importance of making our influence a good one. Mr. W. Light delivered a thought- ful address in which he defended the Bible against some recent attacks which had been made. In referring to the criticism that the Bible was not adapted to the requirements and wants of the 20th century he said the Bible contained truths calculated to make this world what it ought to be, and was able to lead poor weak humanity to the imperial strength of a living God.— Miss Walsh was the soloist and very effectively sang two solos entitled "There is a green hill" and "The Gate of Mercy." The service was also taken part in by Mr. S. Rowlands, Mr. Smiley, and Mr. B. Farrar. Mr. Farrar announced that four new members had been enrolled, making the membership 536.

div.head: Transcendent Choice of Moses.
div.p: The Transcendent Choice of Moses.

This was the subject of a special sermon to young men and women by the Rev.. John Yonge at Wycliffe Congregational Church, on Sunday evening. He based his discourse onthe 11th chapfer of Hebrews, 24th and 2 following verses. He pointed out that even in this twentieth century there was a good deal to be learnt from Moses. He presented one of the noblest examples of true manhood and he did so because of the great choice he made when he was come to years. The preacher discoursed on the choice of Moses in which he elected to suffer affliction with the people of God, rather than enjoy the pleasures of an Egyptian prince, and appealed to his -young hearers to make the choice of faith at whatever cost.

div.head: St. Paul's Church.
div.p: St. Paul's Church.

At this church on Sunday the harvest festival services were continued the preacher in the morning being the Rev. Morley Stevenson. In the afternoon a children's service was addressed by the Rev. T. W. Barber, and in the evening the Vicar of the parish, the Rev. W. Bracecamp preached. There was a record attendance in the evening. The church was crowded long before the service commenced and quite 200 persons had to stand in the side aisles and chancel. Special hymns were sung, and the choir rendered an anthem. Mr. Wilkes was at the organ. The collections for the whole of the services amounted to £35 17s. 11 . The number of coins received was 1,388.

SUCKING CORDITE TO PRODUCE INTOXICATION.

Quite an original species, of narcotic intoxication was discovered by Major Jennings, D.S.O.,during the recent operations in South Africa. It consists in the eating of cordite, with which the Lee-Metford cartridges are charged, and which is made up of 58 parts of nitro- glycerine, 37 parts guncatton, and 5 parts mineral jelly. The effects, according to the "British Medical Journal," are so unpleasant that it is difficult to understand how the habit should gain any hold on individuals. After sucking a strand of cordite for two minutes, Major Jennings found that it caused the most mcking,splitting headache he had ever felt in his life, which lasted quite 36 hours, and was accompanied by hammering and ring- ing noisos in the ears. The taste was sweet, pleasant and pungent. When dissolved in tea, the narcotic pro- duces an exhilarating effect, "inciting to almost demoniacal actions."

LIFE SAVED BY A SWALLOWED BUTTON. 1 In the "Medical World," Dr. Moses describes a novel method of removing a fish-bone crosswise from the throat. The bone was too low to be reached by any forceps at hand, and the author recalled a method of procedure told him by an old doctor who had been taught it by a boy, namely, to tie a string in the eye of a smooth button, and let the patient swallow the button edgewise of course, and draw the button back by the string. This was done, and the bone , was promptly dislodged.

A woman's skeleton, with a full set of gold teeth well arranged on a plate is stated to have been uncovered in digging for a cellar in a house in Rozella-street, Rome. It is asserted by some that the woman most have lived in the time of the ancient Romans.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

A good deal of the criticism directed against the doings of fashionable society is much exaggerated, but there is one matter for which the well-to-do classes are greatly to blame, and that is the countenance and encouragement they have given to clairvoyants, spiritualists, and other quacks. For want of something better to do they have turned for amusement to these people, who pretend to possess all sorts of mysterious powers,but who really live in luxury upon nothing more than the old common tricks of vagabond association. It would he too much to hope that these quacks will be put to silence by the terrible tragedy of Miss Hickman's death. Nearly the whole community of clairvoyants i were engaged n the case, and many had every , facility they asked for, to aid them in revealing the unknown, They described all sorts of possible though irreconcili- able scenes, and yet not one of them was so near the truth as any policeman would have been by the exercise of his ordinary abilities and judgment. An old Divining Custom.—Many were the customs and practices in olden times for divining the future, but they were mostly of an entertaining and harmless nature. One commonly indulged in by rustic young women during the first week in Advent, was designed to dis- cover the name and disposition of the desired husband. For this purpose she placed onions in the chimney corner,—one for each possible and eligible young man, —and the first to sprout, was supposed to represent the husband. Having settled this point, she had then to pluck a stick from a faggot, and if straight, he would be gentle and good natured, but if crooked and knotty, he would prove a churlish husband. The Broom in Folk-lore.—Another old custom amongst the poorer classes, that of "putting a broom out of a window," was recently referred to in a court of law, but judge and counsel were alike ignorant of its mean- ing. In olden times, it was a device of the grass- widower and was taken to mean that as he was lonely he would be glad to entertain his friends if they would look in and join him in a convivial glass. Another ver- sion is, that when a broom was thrust out of the window by the housewife, it meant that she had got the better of a quarrel with her lord and master. The broom in that case was a sign of triumph, and we know it was used in this sense by the Dutch Admiral Van Tromp, who sailed the seas with a broom always displayed at the masthead.

The Game of Golf—There have lately been numer- ous complaints in the newspapers from women who have a grievance against the game of golf. Their husbands, they say, not only neglect their business to spend their days on the golf course, but in the evenings, they 15ore them with the small talk of the hobby, instead of being the agreeable companions they once were. That is the general burden of the complaint, though to this, some add that their husbands have greatly deteriorated in temper, since they succumbed to the golf mania. Many stories might be quoted illustrating this. There was,for instance, the golfer who, having had a bad day and lost several balls, came home and broke up his clubs. Any- body else, he said, would have Jost their temper. The moral of it all seems to be that golf, like everything else, is bad when indulged in to excess, but apart from this objection, the complaints brought against it are not to be seriously entertained. It is a health-giving game, and good health must mean brighter spirits, and more- over it is a game which above all others, shows the loss and folly of losing one's temper over great things, orin small.

The Walking Mania.—The walking craze has died down on this side of the Channel, but last Sunday was a great day for the Paris shop girls, who took part in a huge walking competition. Nearly three thousand girls entered for the race, the distance being about 8 miles, and for weeks previously many trained for the ordeal by taking long walks in shortened skirts and light clothing. To preveht too much heart burning or disappointment 800 prizes were distributed, the first ones being of very handsome value. Similar competitions have been held by shop girls in London, but the walking craze seems to have been wound up in this country by the children's competitions, which were organised by the niggers at all of the seaside resorts during the holiday season. Women's Greater Burden.—As a rule the women of Germany are more disposed than we aee to study dress from a hygienic point of view, but a doctor residing in that country declares that women's clothes weigh on the average about one third more than those of men. If that is the case in Germany, it is presumably the same in this country. Women with less strength, and a smaller frame, carry the heavier burden of clothing. But it is not only the weight, but also the style of dress that puts a heavier strain upon them. Men com- monly overlook this fact when walking or cycling with a woman, and in going against a strong head wind it would be safe to say that a woman cyclist does almost twice as much work as a man, on account of thd greater resistance her clothing offers to the elements. Irish Dolls.—ln a comparatively brief time, we shall be seriously contemplating Christmas gifts, indeed some ." previous " people have already commenced operations in this direction. The new dolls—of Irish manufacture, will most certainly appeal to all in search of presents for the little folks. The material employed for the faces stands the roughest usage, yet is as natural an attractive as wax, while the bodies and limbs are stronger and very much better finished, than those sent us from Germany. These Irish dolls—often fashioned in the likeness of celebrated personages—may be had, or ordered, at all the largest shops, and are most mod- erate in price. An Old-fashioned Trimming.—Punched embroidery which was the rage some three or four decades ago, is once more fashionable, the only difference being in the fact, that whereas it was in the olden days executed upon white lawn, it is. now being done upon coloured cambric, and linen. For trimming morning shirts, for vests, collars,and cuffs, this old world form of orna- mentation is delightful, and opens up wide possibilities to the home worker.

A Convenient Mode.—The removable basque will come as a boon and a blessing to those women who either cannot or will not wear the long coat, so modish just now, and who consider the coatee which reaches only to the waist, insufficient protection during the cold weather. The basque can be either short, or quite long, as may best suit the wearer. The edges are, for the most part scalloped and bound with a narrow hem- ming of fur, which should match that employed on, or for the coatee.

A Stupid Craze.—The fashion of being tattoed has been revived in America, but it is too silly a craze, one may hope, to be taken up over here. There may be no particular harm in having a pictorial representation of a flight of birds across one's arms, but once tattoed, always tattoed, and before long those orho suffer this disfigurement will be in the position of the fox, who having lost his tail, tried to persuade his brethren to cut off their's. It will not be only a disfigurement, but the hall mark of a particularly weak-minded and silly person.
MADGE.

lANOTHER GERMAN ELECTRIC EXPRESS RECORD.— ' The electric motor carriage of the General Electrical j Company on Wednesday attained a speed of 131 miles , an hour over the experimental line between Berlin and Zossen. This is the highest railway speed as yet attained It is an increase of three miles an hour over the record ! reported from Berlin on Friday last, and it is six miles an hour better than the speed attained at a test on the ; 6th inst.

div.head: Examiner Saturday, October 31, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, October 31, 1903.

div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
Sleeves form an ever-varying part of the dress scheme which cannot at the present time be overlooked, for they form one of the

most pronounced features of the very smartest toilettes. It is very easy for most of us—and particularly to those whose dress allowance is but a small one—to smarten up an old dress or costume by the introduction of new and ornamental sleeves, which, in order to meet the requirements of the pre- vailing modes, should be quaint and pic- turesque, fashioned very much after the style of an inverted gigot, and 'caught in at the

div.head: SMART COAT.
div.p: A SMART COAT.

wrists by deep gauntlet cuffs. The new sleeves do not by any manner follow the lines of the natural arm after the elbow is reached, but on the under-side swell downwards _ to the wrist, where the fulness is caught into a band. Variety, however, is apparently everything in the realms of dress, hence this introduction of many varieties of sleeve, which at least can claim novelty as their own, if there is something a little lacking beauty. It seems that to be . fashionable one's sleeves should be (below the elbow) as enormous as possible. One of, perhaps, the newest varieties which is often employed on elegant tea-gowns has a series of kilted frills starting from the close-fitting upper arm- piece mounted on the usual full under sleeve. which in turn is caught into a pointed tight. fitting cuff. The smart coat depicted displays a new style of sleeve which is particularly well suited for any garment for outdoor wear. There is nothing, perhaps, 4. very remark- able about the sleeve proper: which is only loose and easy-fitting; but the cuff is ecr. tainly out of the common and very chic In this case it is made of black cloth de.coupe

on to bright red velvet, the collar and revers being en suite. Nearly every coat sleeve boasts a gauntlet cuff in one form or another, while a very favourite device for blouses shows in place of the stiff cuff a wide plisse frill of muslin or lace, which falls right over the hand.

The fashion for hemming or bordering one material with another in the embellishment of collars, revers, and cuffs is very marked of late, and very strange and striking are the contrasts thus brought about. Silk is bor- dered with cloth or velvet, or vice versa, the former mode, however, having the greater vogue at present, as cloth bordered with silk cannot offer any claims to novelty. Heavy velvet and chenille fringes are also much en evidence on cloth gowns, as likewise are circular bands or ruchings in velvet. The becoming, hat sketched is of the picture order, and boasts a couple of hand- some ostrich feathers which curl over the brim at the back. • There is plenty of variety this season as regards millinery, and there is certainly a marked tendency towards a revival of higher crowns. A pretty style of hat which I saw recently was expressed in red straw, with one brim rolled up very high at the side, rather narrow and long in shape, projecting over the face in front, and fitting

div.head: [NG BODICE
div.p: [NG BODICE

closely to the head at the back. The crown in this instance was rather high, and the hat was trimmed with magpie - coloured- feathers. For wear with plain tailor-made costumes there are some very dainty toques, which are smaller and neater than those of 'a few months ago, and so more suited for the comfortable adjustment of a veil. The correct veils, by the way, are worn loosely disposed from the brim of the hat ; and it must be confessed are not very easy ,to adjust nor comfortable to wear on a windy day. The loose floating veil has already been accepted by the Parisiennes and Americans and are often of lace with a deep embroidered border. Others, again, are of gauze with large coloured or black chenile spots. The evening bodice illustrated is of pale pink chiffon drawn and finished with some handsome chenille fringe. It is in quit: the latest mode.. Evening toilettes are. once again clamouring foe notice, and there are already many pretty styles to be seen. The. bodice, however, no longer offers a contrast to the skirt, but must harmonise with it in even" the smallest details. Silks and moussolines are lavishly trimmed with ribbons' and lace, and are much ruched and. frilled. Many bodices are draped across the figure and round the waist in the cross-over style, or are long and sharply-pointed in a correct imitation of the modes of 1830. Shot taffetas are also much employed for evening dresses, .and when made in a picturesque fashion with numerous frills of embroidery, muslin, or fine lace, look very charming. The rich brocades and velvets and pompadour silks trimmed with Lace are suited for dinner or theatre wear.

div.head: TWO LADS AND A LASS.
div.p: TWO LADS AND A LASS.
BY AARON WATSON,
Author of "Sep Sowerby's Success," "Brown Studies," "Waifs and Strays," "For Lust of Gold," &o.

Cockney Jim was explaining those meteorological theories on which he had spent most of the leisure of a vaguely reflective life. His accent sounded, amid the broad Scotch of his interrupters and interrogators, like that of some ancient people, of whom only one representative had survived into a new era.

For Jim lived in a little fishing village on the east coast of Scotland, and spoke the dialect of Stepney as it may have been spoken at a time more than sixty years gone by. He was little more than a lad when a tempestuous sea cast him ashore at Braemouth. Unconscious, and more than half-drowned, he still clasped one of his shipmates under his arm; but the shipmate's face had been smashed out of recognition on the rocks, and it was only a torn and disfigured corpse that Cockney Jim, with a tenacity which insensi- bility did not relax, bore to the feet of the fisher- men who had been helplessly looking out at the storm. _ _

And Jim never again faced the sea. He settled down where he had been thrown by the god of storms; and mended sails, and made crab-pots, and married, and buried his wife and his children, and retained his Cockney ideas and his Cockney idiom, and became a curious old withered phenomenon, with one grandson—a dark, heavy- browed, fierce-looking fisher-boy—to remind him of those who had come and gone since the sea, in one of its strange humours, had cast him forth, as a man for whose life it had no present hunger. "It's just this way, yer see," Jim was saying. "It was a cold, hard, bitter winter, wasn't it, now? Well, there! And it's a bright, warm, cheerful summer, and there ain't been any bad weather to speak of for this many a month agone. And whit I says to you is: What's the cause of this here?' an' you says you doesn't know, as, of course, you doesn't; and I says I've thought abaht these things for these, ever so many years past. See? I've thought of 'em all night. and all day mostly, and I've thought of 'em as I mended the sails and made the crab-pots, and what I says is this: We drifts awajr to the North Pole, and we drifts away from the North Pole. We're here, and the North Pole's there, and we drifts away from it, and we drifts away to it. It's like this here. The Pole is that crab-pot. See? And the airth is this stone, on which lam sittin'. See? I drifts towards the crab-pot an' I gets colder, an' I drifts away from the crab-pot, an' I gets warmer. Stand's to reason. 'Tis a warm summer now 'cos we have drifted far away from the North Pole, and the further away we drifts the hotter we gets. Stands to reason, as I said." _

This was a speech much interrupted in its pro- gress. It would doubtless have been subjected to rude and contemptuous criticism; but just then there was a shout from the harbour, which lay round a bend of the cliffs about a hundred yards away; and it was the kind of shout which told experienced ears, familiar with all the terrors of a fearful coast, and all the moving tragedies of fisher- life, that somebody was struggling in the water, and in danger of drowning. There was a rapid movement harbourwards ; but far ahead of all the other folk there pelted a lithely-built lass of about fifteen years of age, her bare legs glancing red in the sunlight beneath her short, quilted skirts, her hair flying wild about her shoulders, and her eyes full of a straining terror.

"There's a creel for ye, Angus," she shouted, as she' ran along the pier and leaped on board a fishing lugger. From the deck of this small vessel the grandson of Cockney Jim was prodding with an oar at a struggling figure in the water. The girl's eyes had taken in the situation at once.. It was a water-frolic, and not a case in which drowning was at all possible. For Angus Anderson could swim like a cork, but always as he made for the side of the lugger David Sherlock, as Scotch as the rest, in spite of his Cockney forbears, gave him a thrust with the oar, and, with a laugh, sent him down into the deep water again. "Ye awfu' villain," cried the girl, springing on young Sherlock as soon as she had thrown the creel to his playmate, "ye wad ,have drooned him, ye wad!" And, knocking the oar from his hands, she drove her teeth savagely into the brown, bare roundness of his arm.

Five years had passed away, and the summer fishing had come to an end. The people of Braemouth, ordinarily dour, silent, solemn as if with apprehension of coming evil, were indulging in a brief season of festivity. Some of them had gone on a trip as far as Glasgow; some had made the shorter journey to Edinburgh. Several of the younger men, most of them being such as lacked sweethearts, and had lost character, therefore, had been spending much of their time at the little public-house at the top of "the brae," imbibing potations to the frequent tune of: "We are na fou, we are na fou ; but jist a wee drap in oor e'e." There was a general unloosing of all rules, a tem- porary casting of all fixed habits, in Braemouth just now. Conduct which would have been subject to severe condemnation at any other season of the year was now passed over as the natural effervescence of "sattling-up time." Everybody had money in his pocket—an unusual experience—and part of it was to be spent by each on his own manner of breaking away for a day or two from the ' hard world and the deadly- Monotony of life in a fishing village. Tam and Jock will make " awfu' fules of thersels, " as their elders say, but, their brief spell of dissipa- tion at an end, they will sit for a whole day in the darkest corner of the cottage, doing nothing, and feeling too ashamed to complain of a racking headache, which, nevertheless, proclaims itself in all their looks. Then, when the next morning dawns, they will go rummat ng about in a dark room upstairs, and in due course they will bring down the haddock lines, and gravely and industriously, and in an earnest spirit of repentance, set to work to prepare for the winter's fishing in "the muckle boats.

But as yet the tide of enjoyment was at its height. The rollicking choruses were being sung in the little inn above the brae. The village itself —wedged between the cliffs and the sea, with a narrow beach of shingle sloping down to jagged rocks that were covered with the brown and green of dense seaweed—was almost wholly deserted of its inhabitants. Only Cockney Jim kept watch and ward, seated on a stool by the door of his cottage, a knitted red cap on his head, his feeble hands busy with woman's work, the baiting of a basket of lines.

Oh, and there were two others who had neither gone to Glasgow, nor to Edinburgh, nor to other far away scenes of enjoyment, nor even to "the public" at the top of the brae. They were strolling away along the narrow beach in the direction of Gull Rock, which stood, a tall, red, conical pillar, near the cliffs from which it had been severed, about half a mile from the village. • Cockney Jim looked at them now and again with eyes that still seemed to have the keenness and the brightness of youth. "It seems a beastly bad job for that lad of mine," he reflected. "There ain't no chance for him there, as I reckon; and he's as fond of that lass as I was of his grandmother—how long is it ? why, nearly sixty years ago, no less. And yet," he went on, "it does look to me as how they ought to come together, them there two, Euphy Mulock and our David. Stands to reason they should. She stuck her teeth in his arm. That should a'most make 'em one flesh, as it were. But there's really no tellin' how these kittlish things will turn out. There's really no tellin'." And yet any other spectator might have told easily enough. Angus Anderson and EtiphY Mulock walked on in happy unconsciousness alike of the old man's watchfulness and of the subject of his meditations. They spoke little. There seemed no need for speech. They were too illimitably happy to put their feelings into words. And this was the stay of fisher lovers. There were no embraces; no declarations. The time for kisses would come later on. They simply "walked out" together, and felt each other's meanings, and knew each other's soul.

"I maun be trippin' up the brae," said Euphy to Angus, as the shadows of the cliffs began to lengthen at their feet. "The fowk will a' be haine from Embro' ere long, and I maun hae the hoose and the bit supper ready an' they come." "I will gae wi' ye so far," said Angus. And so, again, in blissful silence, they walked up the steep. winding road which had been cut out of the

Me of the brae, the cottage of the lYlulocks stand- ing about half-way up, on a flat projection of rock by the roadside. There was some lingering at the gate of the small garden, and many silent, happy looks; and then Euphy said "Weel, Angus, an' I wish ye a fair guid nicht." "It has been a joyfu' day to me, Euphy," said Angus sending a tender message straight into the beloved eyes. "An' to me as weel, Angus," said Euphy; "but guid nicht again, Angus; guid nicht. I maun mak' mysel' gey busy agen they come." Angus paused a moment, loth to part, and then said: "Weel, guid nicht, Euphy. I will look oot for ye doon in the harbour the morn," and with these words he began to descend the brae, Euphy watch- ing him till a bend of the precipitous road carried him wholly out of sight. Then, as she was lifting the latch of the door, she paused to listen to an approaching voice. It was a husky voice, striving to be musical.

"We are nae fou, We are nae fou; But jist a wee drap in oor e'e," ran the hoarse accents, gaining distinctness as they became near. "Why, it's Davie Sherlock, of aw fulish folk!" exclaimed Euphy under her breath, astonished at what was to her a new manifestation of Andrew's character and tastes. "Is that yersel', Euphy ? " said David, lurch- ing into the now dim light. "Euphy, I was coming to find ye. I have something to say to ye. I was coming doon to yer hoose, an' here I am." "I see ye are here, wed l enough," said Euphy; "but, eh man, ye're a sair sicht for freettly e'en. fe may sing ye are nae fou, Davie Sherlock, but hoo does that mend it? Ye're jist as fou as ever ye can be." "I'm fu' o' love for ye, Euphy; that's just what's the maitter wi' me. That, and naething else. An' I cam' to tell ye so," said David, reaching over the gate and grasping Euphy's arm. "Let gae, Davie Sherlock; let gae! " said the girl, "ere I call Angus Anderson, wha's only a wee bit doon the brae. Wad ye quarrel wi' Angus again, and ye workin' in the same boat together ? " With the sweeping, theatrical gesture of a drunken man, David threw from him the hand he had seized upon. "We may quarrel again, Euphy," he said; "but the next time we quarrel, be will droon."
M.

The fishermen had been pacing along the wall of the harbour all the afternoon, and looking at the sky, and dropping casual words to each other, and pulling hard at their pipes, and looking again in glum silence at the sky. It was one of those days which threaten, and may yet prove kind. "Will the boats gae oot the nicht, think ye, Euphy ?" said an anxious-looking woman, leaning out of the door of her cottage as Euphy passed. "Wha kens ?" said Euphy. And, in fact, not one of the fishermen knew. Each was waiting on the decision of the other, reluctant to come to any conclusion of his own. At length, Anty Martin, one of the older and more weather-beaten and more trusted men, turned homewards in silence, and shortly afterwards emerged from his cottage in his seaboots and oil- skins, with a basket of lines on his shoulders, his son following him similarly laden. Then there was a general movement from the pier to the cottages, and from the cottages to the boats. Anty's example had settled the question that had disturbed all minds in Braemouth that afternoon. If Ant y went out, so would all the rest. Anty was weather-wise with the weather-wisdom of sixty years. Euphy sat on an upturned creel, the grey water of the harbour plashing within a yard of her feet. She was quite happy, though she knew there was peril of a storm. "My laddies always come back safe hams," she said to herself. And her laddies were Angus Anderson and David Sherlock, rivals, but comrades ; •working in the same boat, loving the same woman, but only one of them aware of the other's ' love.

They waded into the water in their tall sea. booth, these two; leaped on board their boat, The Two Brothers, half-hoisted the sail, and then turned towards Euphy with the same instinct and in the same instant, each waving an arm as a signal of good-bye. Then the sail was hoisted almost to the masthead, and the boat was scudding eastwards into a grey mist, in which the sails of some of the other boats were now only distinguishable as pale shadows.

A chill wind surged in, and Euphy shuddered. "The Lord bless an' guide them baith, and may they never fall oot," she said, as the happy look faded from her face, and she recollected what David Sherlock had said to her before the widiter fishing commenced, not more than a week Ifgo. " 'Twas ill on him sayin' that," she murmured. " 'Twas ill on him. The next time we quarrel, he will droon.' "

And the words haunted her as she went up the brae to her snug little home; and she turned back to look at the sea; but not a fishing-boat was in sight, for the mist had thickened, and crept further inshore, and there was hardly any visible distinction between sea and land.

On the morning that followed, the sea could be seen far out; but it was a waste of white, tumultuous water, and huge waves rolled to the shore like squadrons of cavalary in attack. Euphy grew very pale as she looked out of the little window of her bedroom, for the boats should uow be coming home. "Eh, the twa laddies!" she said. "The twa laddies—and Angus, Angus, maist of aw " The folk remaining in the village were eagerly looking out to sea when she had hurriedly dressed herself and run down to the foot of the brae— the old men, anxiously levelling their glasses at the horizon, the wives, the daughters, the widows made by many a previous storm. Occasional sails might be seen for an instant between the harbour and the horizon—square patches of brown, thrust up out of the sea, as it seemed, and then immediately dipping out of sight. "They're all makin' for Bridlingham," said Cockney Jim, his keen eyesight enabling him to see to the horizon's length without the aid of a "spy-glass." "They're all making off together, clear as can be. There'll be no boats at Braemouth this mornin', ye'll see." "The Lord be thankit," said a stout fishwife; "yet I'll e'en gang hame an' get some warm things ready for my man. One never kens." An old fisherman lowered his glass and rubbed the eye-piece then raised it again, peered out to sea, and handed it to another veteran, who stood close to ,his side.

"What mak' ye o' that?" he inquired. "Why, guid Lord, she's stannin' in!" said the old fisherman, with dismay in his voice. "It's fair murder," said the man with the glass. "There's nae possibeelity o' landin' here, and nae boat could live in sic' a sea, even if there was men to handle her. Fair murder it is! "he repeated. Cockney Jim, gazing out seawards, staggered towards a pent-house roof to support himself against the wind. Then a wet mist came over the eyes that discerned distant things so clearly. "It's the Two Brothers," he said, in an awe- struck voice.

"Aye, its's the Twa Brithers," said one of the old fishermen, "and not a man on board of her can e'er hope tae reach the village alive." But the boat was nobly sailed, as every straining eye could see. It dipped out of sight, and then bounded over the crest of a wave and dipped out of sight again; but it was always making clear and straight for the harbour. It Was almost a matter of seconds now. Should the boat survive five minutes longer it would be riding safe within the sheltered water behind the pier. "The Lord guide us an' save us!" There was a general cry from the women—a cry of agony and %error and pain. The boat had been lifted up on the crest of a huge; combing wave, and then cast down on a reef, with such terrible force that the !,)und of the impact cOuld be heard above the 'Paring of the storm. The boat which had been bounding shorewards :hit a moment bPfore was now a chaos of scattered planks, and seven men were struggling with the water for their lives.

Euphy had fainted away at the sound of the truel contact between the boat and the reef, and knew nothing more until, on opening her eyes, she caw David Sherlock kneeling before her, and chafing her hands.
"They're carryin' him hame, Euphy," he said. *He's -nne the waur. Only a wee bit dinged, ye ken." Euphy looked at him without understanding the meaning of his words.

"I biought him in to ye alive, Euphy. Ha wad surely have drooned but for me. Winnat ye love tne'a Wee bit, now that I brought him in alive? Pin fell fond of ye, Euphy. And, Euphy, it's God s truth that I tell ye; Angus wad hae drooned but for me."
The girl was now awake to all that she had witnessed. and to David's uresent meaning..

_ mair. Livin' or deed, it's- Angus—Angus---'ingus and that's the tune that ever sings itsel' in my heart. Eh, ma puir,. Oavie, an' I'm sorry for ye —real sorry I am, siilrye.love me so. Ye said he should droon, and ye have brought him in to me alive. Davie, what can I do, what can I do? I shall pray for ye as long's I leeve." And David rose from her feet with a black look on his face; and, tottering from his efforts in the storm and the work of rescue he had just accomplished, went home to his grandfather's chill cottage a dour man.

There was a wedding in Braemouth, and it was the great event of the year. Without exception, the fisherfolk took holiday, and most of them walked all the way to the parish church of the neighbouring town of Marwick to see Angus Ander- son and Euphy Mulock made man and wife. Now, there survived in Braemouth a quaint custom from olden times. The creel was the mark of the woman' s• calling and subjection; but often enough an unmarried man had to bind the creel on his own shoulders and go off seeking for bait, or to sit by the door of his lonely cottage baiting lines. So, when one of the fisher lads got married it was the way of the folk to bind a creel on his back, and compel him to make a tour of the village, and of all the neighbouring houses for a mile or more. Then, the bridegroom, returning to the cottage he had just fitted up as a home of his own, the bride would step from the doorway and cut the creel loose with her scissors, this signifying to all whom it might concern that henceforth she relieved her new-made husband—her "man "—of all the mean drudgeries of life. When the wedding party came back from Marwick Angus Anderson must set off through the village with the creel on his back, and then ascend the brae, to let the neighbour-folk witness the last act before his emancipation. It was a pilgrimage of mingled joyousness and humiliation, for the shamefaced bridegroom was welcomed, wherever he came, by a mixture of congratulations and jeers. "I'm gey weel pleased to be gettin' past it aw," said Angus to himself, as he rounded the walls of a farmhouse above the cliffs, and looked down towards the village, which was some half-a-mile away. He had come in sight of the folk as he left behind him the farmhouse wall. They made a gay group together at that end of the pier. Euphy waved some piece of colour as he came in sight, and all the others joined in a friendly shout, which reached him in faint reverberations as it smote against the cliffs. He commenced to run, that he might kiss Euphy all the sooner ;'but just then a shout from someone near at hand arrested his footsteps. He turned quickly round, and beheld David Sherlock coming towards him. What was said, nobody knows to this day. What the people saw was the two men coming to grips with each other, and swaying this way and that, and ever getting nearer to the edge of the cliffs. One or two of the younger men started to run up the brae, hardly knowing to what purpose, but with some indefinite idea of help. "Come in ben, lass," said Euphy's. mother, leading the now terrified wife towards the door of the small, neat, newly-whitewashed cottage. "I mann see it through, mother; I maun see it through!" "Oh, my puir lassie, my only bairn!" said the mother, "come ben. 'Tis only a wee bit joke, maybe. Angus will be here aw richt the noo." Euphy looked again to the cliff-tops, and fell with a heart-breaking scream into her mother's arms.

"Eh, poor lass, it's a sair, sair thing for her," was the immediate tearful comment of the women. "Wife and widow in ae day." The two struggling men, in that instant in which Euphy had looked round, had fallen headlong over the cliffs, clasped in each other's arms. "An' it was my own lad David as did it," said Cockney Jim, grown immeasurably older at one sudden stroke. "Help me to get out a boat, you men; I cannot row, it'ts so very long -since I have been on the sea. Yet I must go and seek my lad, my daughter's lad. We've drifted away. There's none of all of us left but me. And David did it —.my own daughter's lad! And there's none of us left but me. "
UNE END. 1

ST. MARY'S MISSION.—A meeting was held in the Infants' schoolroom on Monday night last, to consider the formation of a social organization to be called St. Mary's Mission Institute. Mr. John Hill was voted in the chair, and gave a short outline of the proposed scheme, which will no doubt be of great benefit to the younger portion of the village. A committee was selected to look after arrangements, and a general meet- ing of all interested is dated for Monday next. Various projects for the working of the society were projected and discussed, and will no doubt be fully gone into at the forthcoming Meeting. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.—The first meeting of the session of the above Society was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Wednesday night last. The meeting took the form of a sort of feception of the members by the president, Mr. Thomas Gandy. Mr. Gandy remarked that this was the 21st year of the Society's existence, and he read a long letter from Mr. Parker, who was unable to be present. Mr. Parker was one of original promoters of the Society, and gave an interesting resume of the intervening sessions. A most interesting series of papers have been arranged for, and many schemes were suggested for making the session attractive and profitable. Refreshments were partaken of at the invitation of the president, and the following contributed to the programme. Song "The promise of Life," Miss Connie Atherton' song "Distant yet," Miss F. Woods; song "The sea is England's glory," Mr. 11. Plumpton. Mrs. Parker gave a pianoforte solo, and also accompanied the singers during the evening. THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—The usual monthly " Open Sunday," promoted by the Men's Bible Class was held in the above chapel on Sunday afternoon last. There was a large attendance, as every effort is made to make the meetings RS brigh+, and attractive as possible. Mr. C. E. Parker presided, and addressed the meeting and Councillor Brough, also gave a characteristic address. Master M. Pearce contributed several well executed selections on the organ and also accompanied the solo- ists, and hymns. Solos were cleverly rendered by Miss M. B. Wilkinson and Mr. Hannan. Suitable hymns were sung

div.p: THE CATTLE MAIMER.

r The Birmingham solicitor, George Ernest Thompson Eda.lji, was on Friday last sent- enced to seven years' penal servitude for the cattle palming outrages at the little village of Grait Wyrley, Staffordshire, where his father was vicar. The actual crime for which Edalji was con- victed was the mutilation of a pony belonging to the Great Wyrley Colliery Company on the night of August 17 ; but there can be little doubt that he was the perpe- trator of the seven similar outrages. I n connection with the anonymous letters that were a feature of the
case, it is er- missible to say, GEORGE EDALJI, WHO HAS now that Edalji BEEN SENTENCED TO SEVEN is convicted, YEARS' PENAL SERVITUDE, that his name has for the last
twelve years

been connected with anonymous letters of a similar charac- ter. Edalji has also gained for himself the reputicion of being a lover of mystery—an Oriental trait, and one that goes far to ex- plain the anonymous letters. Love of mys- tery rather than blood-lust was, according to the Crown, the predisposing motive. The story of the Edaljis and their connection with the little village of Great Wyrley is somewhat interesting. Many years ago the Rev. S. Edalji, a Parsee, came to the village as cura,te. He fell in love with the daughter of his vicar (who had the gift of the living) and married her. The vicar died after transferring the living to his son-in-law, and that is how the Great Wyrley church came into the hands of a Parsee. George Edalji was the eldest son of the marriage. He was sent to Rugeley Grammar School, where he met young Green, who confessed to the mutilation of his own horse at Great Wyrley on September 21. About this tithe—which would be nine years ago—strange things began to happen at Wyr- ley; and the centre of them was the vicarage. Mysterious letters were scattered about the district. Most of them purported to come from the Rev. S. Edalji, and they were signed by his name. One day a most devout vicar who had been paying a visit to the church received a letter at his home in the North of England to the following effect: "Dear Sir, —I beg to state that you are a d—d thief. Last Sunday when you visited my church you stole a prayer-book. It you do not return the same at once and apologise, an action will be commenced against you.—Yours, &c., ( REV. ) S. EDALJ r." These letters were hoaxes and forgeries, and the pain and annoy- ance and trouble they gave to Mr. and Mrs. Edalji can easily be imagined.

div.head: NEWEST IN RAILWAYS.
div.p: THE NEWEST IN RAILWAYS.

New York, which is usually the pioneer nowadays in all forms of locomotion, is once more about to show the way with an entirely new type of railway. It is to be a railway without trains or st(ippages, to take the place of the ordinary underground methods. It is, in a word, to be worked on a system of moving platforms which will never stop. Beside the stationary platform at which you enter or get off will run another platform at the rate of three miles an hour; beyond it will be another moving at six miles an hour; and beyond that yet another, provided with com- fortable seats, moving at nine miles an hour. Thus by this graduated process it will be easy for any passenger to step from one plat- form to another without difficulty or fear of falling, getting on or alighting at whatever point suits best. The platforms will run with-
0 To`a.
THE NEW AMERICAN MOVING PLATFORM RAILWAY.

out stopping for twelve hours, and will be capable of carrying 70,000 persons in the hour and 840,000 in the day. The cars are joined in such a way as to present a continu- ous line of flooring without any intervening space. The great advantage is that passen- gers need not waste a second in waiting for a train to come in, but can get on at once and get off as soon as their destination is reached. Mr. Cornelius Vanderbilt is keenly interested financially in the scheme, which will involve the outlay of two millions. If it is a success, we are certain to have it over here ere long.

div.head: LADY ELECTIONEERER,
div.p: THE LADY ELECTIONEERER,

The first batch of the " fiscal " elections have passed off without any disaster to the Government, though in some cases the majorities have been reduced. Whether this is directly due to the fiscal question or not is a moot point, and is being hotly argued by partisans on both sides. In politics it is always easy enough to produce pros and cons, according to the views of the indi- vidual, and the only fact Which is important for general purposes is that Mr. Lyttelton, a pronounced follower of Mr. Chamberlain, almost in the Chamberlain country, and Mr. Arnold Foster, the new Secretary of State for War, have been re-elected, while Lord
TO WHOSE EFFORTS HE LARGELY
OWES HIS RE-ELECTION

Stanley, the' new Postmaster-General, was un- opposed in the Westhoughton division. • In the two former cases both the candidate: were unfortunately ill, and had to fight mainly by proxy. Mr. Arnold-Foster wa: unable to make any appearance at all in West Belfast, and is only now able to be about again in a quiet way, owing to an accident incurred whilst riding, which was not ,so much dangerous as extremely painful. At Leamington Mr. Alfred ryttelton was able to make one or two speeches, but was for the main part confined to his room, and the fighting of the election devolved upon his clever and plucky wife. She did her part nobly, and the new Colonial Secretary must feel that he has to thank her for a great deal. ,Mrs. Alfred Lyttelton, who is a cousin of 'the present ' Premier, while her husband is a relative of the late Mr. Gladstone, on his mother's side, has won a great name for her- self throughout the .country by her election- eering fight, and will, in future, be classed with the beautiful Duchess of Gordon i who raised the Gordon Highlanders, the beautiful Duchess of Devonshire; who bribed with
kisses, and the late Mrs. Brand, who died this year under such sad circumstances, who " sang " her husband into Parliament.
IRON FROM SAND.

The latest marvel in the way of inventions is the new process of extracting iron from sand, which, if as successful as it promises to be, will entirely revolutionise the iron trade, and divert a great deal of it to the colonies. The inventor of the process is a Mr. Rouse, and he is now experimenting at Messrs. Martin's Foundry in Lambeth. The idea is simplicity itself. A certain kind of sand, found chielly in the colonies, contains iron, and this Mr. Rouse proposes to sepa- rate by the use of a magnet. In his machine the sand is first emptied into the hopper A, which passes into the separator B, which
THE MAGN
TILE INVENTOR, MR. ROUSE.

contains a magnetic arrangement which separates and catches the particles of iron. Then the quartz sand is blown out at the opening C by a strong current of air which is forced through by the fan D, the iron falling out at the flue E by its own weight. Then it is placed in the mixer F and treated with binding fluid till it is a stiff paste, after which it is moulded into briquettes. These are either dried for smelting into pig- iron or passed direct into a blast furnace and melted at once. It is calculated by this means and process to save from fifteen to twenty shillings a ton.

div.head: FAVOURITE OF IRELAND.
div.p: A FAVOURITE OF IRELAND.

By the death of Mr. W. H. Lecky Ireland bSCS the most eminent of her literary children, 3.nd one whom, perhaps, in her heart of hearts she most respected and admired. His was a varied career--rather more strenuous, perhaps, than most people are wont to be- lieve. Born near Dublin onMarch z6th, 1838, of ln old landed fa mily, he passed from Chelten- aam to Trinity ::.ollege, Dublin, where he gradu- ited. His bril- liant intellect leveloped early —he had writ- ten "The Rise Ind Influence of Rationalism in Europe" before he was thirty, a masterly work, ut scarcely with the ele- ments of dura- 3ilit y. The 'History of European Mor- ils from Augustus to Charlemagne" followed. Under curious circumstances it was quoted in the House of Commons by Mr. Samuel Smith, when the author was a member. Then came his great work, "History of England in the Eighteenth Century" (1878- 9o), and his "Democracy and Liberty" (both works which will probobly stand the test of time). As a historian, especially as an Irish historian, Mr. Lecky is above all praise, in that he was scrupulously accurate and just. It should ever be recollected that all parties ift Ireland spoke of his historical work with praise—surely a marvellous tribute. The closing years of his life brought him full into the public gaze, for he entered Parliament in 1895, easily defeating a Con- servative lawyer who stood against him. Probably his resolute anti-Home Rule atti- tude since 1886 won him his seat, till failing health drove him to retire early this year.

div.head: FIRELESS STEAK ENGINE.
div.p: A FIRELESS STEAK ENGINE.

A locomotive that goes by steam and yet has no fire has been made and is working successfully. The engine, of which a sketch is here presented, has just been completed at the Hohenzollern works at Dusseldorf, and is designed for shunting in explosive' factories. Instead of carrying fire in its own boiler it is filled with steam from stationary/ . _ _ _
boilers, and when so charged is capable Of several hours' work. The first warming up occupies half an hour, and subsequent re- charging can be done in a quarter of an hour.

The apparatus is so simple that an unskilled workman is able to look after it. The ab- sence of fire in a place where dynamite or gunpowder is being handled is the reason for the invention of this type of engine, which is known to engineers- as the Lamm Franc system, but it is, nevertheless, difficult to understand why an electric or cable rail- way should not have been decided upon. Perhaps the reason is that the new fireless steam engine is inexpensive to work. It is said it costs just half, as much to work it %s an ordinary steam locomotive.
THE NEW GERMAN STEAM ENGINE, WHICH HAS NO FIRE.

div.head: LATEST MOTOR RECORD.
div.p: THE LATEST MOTOR RECORD.

Motor records come and go, but soon it seems that the rock bottom must be reached. However, in Germany on the new electric railway they have touched the terrific speed of 140 miles an hour; and it is possible that the foolhardy motorist will try eventually to emulate this achievement on the road, despite the fact that it is reported to have been a most uncomfortable and unpleasant sensation. The new motor record, which' was only over a kilometre, quite pales beside the others as it was just under 85 miles an hour—first enough in all conscience, and too fast ever to be practicable on the open road. This remarkable time was set up by the Hon. Os S. Rolls at Welbeck, where he covered the

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
THE COUNTY CHAMPIONSHIP.
LANCASHIRE v. CHESHIRE

This engagement, the second under the new twelve- aside rules, took place at Broughton on Wednesday. The weather was beautifully fine, but the attendance did not exceed 3,000. The visitors had to take the field with rather a mixed team, no fewer than three of the originally chosen backs being unable to play, viz., Houghton ( who has retired), Jones, and Moran all of Runcorn. The first-named's place was taken by Harri- son, and the other vacancies (both at wing three- quarters) by Dutton and Davies. On the Lancashire side the only change was the inclusion of W. James at half back in the place of Lomas. Butterworth'started for the visitors, who were immediately- forced back. The Lancashire three-Quarters were quickly in posses- sion' and Wilson kicked well out towards touch, where Fish was in waiting, and tricking both Dutton and. Harrison, scored a try. The same player made an abor- tive attempt at goal. Further success followed to the home men, who were playing a fine game, and a com- bined passing run between Wilson and Hogg resulted in the first named scoring Lancashire's second try. James failed with the place kick. Then the Cheshire forwards dribbled down and Walker kicked across to Davies, and, the latter scored a 'fortunate try, which Molynenx im- proved by placing a goal. Succeeding play enabled i Lancashire to attack. Fish ran and dodged n clever 'fashion before kicking across the front of the posts, andßaxter completed a try,James again failing at goal. Another try came before the interval, Wilson turning a bad pass into good account by dribbling over the line. Fer,gusson took the kick at goal, but was unsuccessful. Half-time :—Lancashire, four tries (12 points) ;Cheshire, one goal and one try (five points). On resuming the visitors were again compelled to de- fend, and Fish, after beating 4half a dozen i men punted across to the other wing, and Wilson registered his third try. No goal resulted from the attempt made by Fergusson. Lancashire again attacked. A magni- ficent try, the best of the day, followed, for Wilson and Hogg by a brilliant piece of combination ran through the Cheshire defence and the last named scored. Fish placed a goal, and followed by running in a clever try single handed, whilst Hogg also broke through the de- moralised defenders. Fish failed in each instance to place a goal from the place kick, and theugh in the last few minutes Cheshire reached the Lancashire line through a fine run by Richardson, Baxter relieved, and a one-sided game ended—Lancashire, one goal and eight tries (26 points); Cheshire, one goal and one try (five points). The teams were : Lancashire: D. Smith (Salford), full back; J. Fish (Warrington), R. Wilson, and A. Hogg (Broughton Rangers), threequarter backs; W. James (Broughton Rangers) and .T. Baxter (Rochdale Hornets), half backs; P. Tunny, J. Rhapps,and G. Heath (Salford), J. Fergus- son and G. Frater (Oldham), and G. Boardman (Leigh), forwards.

Cheshire: E. Harrison (Runcorn), full back ; J. Dutton and J. Butterworth (Runcorn), and T. Davies (Birkenkead), threequarter backs; J. Richardson (Run- corn) and J. lVfolyneux (Leigh), half backs; S. Walker, W. Woods, A. Moulton, and A. Richardson (Runcorn), and J. W. Davies and J. Belton, (Birkenhead), forwards. Referee: Mr. W. Robinson (Manningham), Touch judges Messrs. J. Love (Birkenhead) and J. H. Hough- ton (St. Helens.)
YORKSHIRE v. DURHAM AND NORTHUMBER-
LAND.

This championship match took place at Wakefield on Wednesday and was played under the twelve-aside rule. There were several changes in the teams previously an- nounced. Early on Llewellyn scored a point for York- shire, but Ritson immediately equalised. In quick suc- cession Hector placed a goal, which gave the visitors the lead. Following some give-and take play Sinton scored a try, while one was allowed the visitors for ob- struction. Ritson then scored a splendid try, which Hector converted, and the visitors led at the interval by five points.—The second half was of a very scrambl- ing kind, and the Opinion on the twelve-aside rule was distinctly unfavourable. Davies kicked a penalty goal for Yorkshire, after which Fletcher scored, Davies placing Yorkshire ahead by the goal. Dick and Llewellyn scored, Davies converting. Starks also scored. Result: —Yorkshire, five goals and five tries (25 points) ; Dur- ham and Northumberland, two goals and three tries (13 points).

div.head: FIRST DIVISION.
div.p: FIRST DIVISION.
WARRINGTON V. SWINTON.

The Swinton team were the visitors to Warrington on Saturday, and a good crowd turned up in the expecta- tion of seeing the tables turned on the famous" Blues," which have been successful at Wilderspool rather too often for the liking of the homesters. Warrington were at full strength for the first time this season, Harris having recovered from his injuries' and Bate having settled his difference with the club. Swinton as the result of accidents and in view of their poor record this season, made several changes. Dixon went full back,and Lewis and Taylor came into the three-quarter line. Teams :

Warring to n—Hallam,back"; Fi sh, Isherwood,Dickenson, and Harris, three-quarter backs; B. Bate and Davies, half backs ; Boardman, Morrison, Swift, Edmondson, Harmer, Thomas, Naylor, and Lunt, forwards. Swinton—Dixon, back; Lewis, Valentine,Taylor, and Hampson, three-quarter backs; Morgan and Ryan, half backs; Evans, Preston, Simister, Cheetham, Pomfret, Tickle, Burrows and Coletrap, forwards. Referee, Mr. W. McCutcheon, Oldham. Touch judges, Messrs. W. Hancock, Runcorn, and R. Yates, Salford. D:ckenson kicked off, and Lewis knocked on, .giving Warrington the advantage of the side. Davies quietly got away and passed to Isherwood. Eventually Harris got the ball, bat missed his kick, and Hampson easily stopped further progress. Bate charged a kick and almost got over. Dickenson all but broke through the next minute. Swinton up to now had never reached the half-way line. A long kick by Di ton, however, at length put them on the Warrington portion of the field for the first time, but only for a few seconds, and they were defending once more. Fish made a fine mark andf Thomas smartly supplemented, with the result that Et scrimmage was formed under the Swinton post. A score seemed certain when Vernon Hainpson intercepted, and covering half the length of the field a score would certlinly have followed but his pass was knocked on. Warrington again sent the Swintonians back, and Harris, fielding the ball well at half-way, kicked over the line. Morrisson followed up smartly and scored, for Fish to kick a goal. Scarcely had the game restarted when Dickenson in- tercepted a pass, and was only brought down by Dixon when only a few yards from the line. Quiet play followed fo: a long time. Fish just missed a penalty goal. War- rington had a great amount of the play, and Fish on one occasion almost wriggled through. Some good p .ssing between Isherwood, Harris, and Dickenson almost ended in a score. A change came over the game whenlHampson got the ball from Valentile over half- way. He transferred to Taylor, who gave back to Hampson, and the latter got over just as he was tackled by Hallam. Half-time arrived .soon after, Warrington leading by 1 goal 1 try (5 points) to 1 try (3 points). The second half was also in favour of the homesters, but Swinton gave a better display and some end to end play was witnessed. Warrington were slow in scoring, but after Davies and Bate had been pulled up near the line, Bate initiated a passing movement from which Isherwood scored cleverly, Fish making a fine bid for goal.. Swinton resorted to purely defensive tactics, and Warrington were always masters of the situation. In the last minute of the game Dixon obstructed, Davies and the penalty which followed culminated in Dickenson adding the goal. Result :--Warrington 2 goals and 2 tries (10 points), Swinton 1 try (3 points).

div.head: RUNCORN v. HALIFAX.
div.p: RUNCORN v. HALIFAX.

The play during the first half of this contest at Run- corn was always interesting, the Cheshire club being responsible for the only score of the first half in the shape of a goal. Halifax tried bard to respond, but their efforts were unavailing. Restarting, the Halifax forwards dribbled to the Runcorn quarter flag, and Harrison did some fine defensi ye work. Faulkner kicked into touch, and reaching the quarter flag Butterworth scored it try, the same player kicking a goal. Halifax, by strong forward play, attacked, but Rigg kicked too hard, and the advantage was lost. The Runcorn for- wards now played up and reached the Halifax line, and Butterworth misfielding the ball Williams fell just out- side the post and missed what appeared a certain try. Result :—Runcorn, two goals and one try (sevenpoints); Halifax, nothing.

div.head: BATLEY v. WIDNES.
div.p: BATLEY v. WIDNES.

Widnes visited Batley to fulfil their engagement with the Yorkshire club. The first portion of the contest provided some interesting play,both sides working very hard and displaying excellent combination. A try was the only score throughout the first half, Widnes holding the advantage of a three points lead at the change of ends. The visitors attacked strongly in the second portion, and scored repeatedly, whilst the Yorkshiremen, were only once able to get through their rivals' lines, the final scores being :—Widnes, two goals and two tries (ten points); Batley, one try (three points).

div.head: HULL v. BROUGHTON RANGEkS.
div.p: HULL v. BROUGHTON RANGEkS.

This match was played at Hull, before about 8,000 spectators. A spendidly contested game took place, which ended in a win for Hull by seven points, but this result was never anticipated, as Hull had shown very poor form this season.—Hull, two, goals and one try (seven points); Broughton Rangers, nothing.

div.head: WIGAN v. BRADFORD.
div.p: WIGAN v. BRADFORD.

An even and interesting game, played in the presence of about 8,000 people at Wigan, ended in a victory for the home side by one -try (three points) to one goal (two points). Anderson scored a capital try for Wigan in the first half. LEEDS v. HUDDERSFIELD.

Sutcliffe commenced for the visitors in this match at Headingley, Larard surprising the home team by scoring in the first five minutes, Walton failing at the place kick. This roused the Leeds men, who quickly equalised through Jenkins, Ward also scoring, and Littlewood converting. Result :—Leeds, one goal and six tries (20 points); Huddersfield, one goal and two tries (eight points).

div.head: KEIGHLEY v. HUNSLET.
div.p: KEIGHLEY v. HUNSLET.

Admirably matched teams representing these clubs faced each other at Keighley. Both sides attacked in turn during the opening half, but the defence was very sound, and when the change of ends arrived there was no score. Result :—Keighley, two goals and one try (seven points); Hunslet, one goal and one try (five points).

div.head: SALFORD v. OLDHAM.
div.p: SALFORD v. OLDHAM.

There was a large crowd of people on the Salford ground to see the match between these clubs. Salford turned out as selected but- on the Oldham side S. Lees, jun., took the place of A. Lees at half back. An inter- esting game was played, which ultimately resulted in Salford being defeated for the first time this season. At half-time Oldham led by five points to nothing. D. Smith dropped a goal which reduced Oldham's lead to three points. Phil Thomas scored another try for Old- ham, which Ferguson failed to improve. Oldham attacked till the finish, and won by One goal and two tries (eight points) to Salford one goal (two points.)

div.head: LEIGH v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.
div.p: LEIGH v. HULL KINGSTON ROVERS.

At Leigh, before 3,000 spectator. Ganley supdrse- ded Neville at wing three-quarters for Leigh. The Rovers won the toss, and Leigh started against a strong wind. The visitors wheeled the scrummages in excel- lent styleand made a series of fine rushes, but Pearson proved a great stumbling-block. Eventually the Hull forwards beat Leigh for possession, and after clever passing by Barry, Gordon, and Sleep, West scored a try, no goal resulting. Leigh made ineffectual efforts to transfer play to the other end, but by long kicks the Rovers regained their lost ground, and splendiii play by Barry ended in West scoring his second try Gordon again failing at goal. Eventually, about tenminutes from the close, a round of passing ended in Bennett making an opening for Johnson, who scored, Molyneux failin at goal. The Rovers afterwards kept Leigh at bay. Result :—Hull Kingston Rovers, two tries; Leigh one try.

div.head: SWINTON "A" v. "WARRINGTON "A."
div.p: SWINTON "A" v. "WARRINGTON "A."

At Swinton, before a capital gate. The visitors had the most of the opening play, but the heavy nature of the ground prevented anything approaching accurate play. Knight essayed a long shot at goal without success. Eventually, the home team took up an attack- ing position, and as the result of neat passing Barnett scored, the point being improved upon by Preston. During the second half Swinton added another try, and won by eight points.

div.head: Parish Church Sale of Work.
div.p: The Parish Church Sale of Work.

This sale: was concluded on Saturday, the total amount realized on behalf of the Church Restoration Fund being £214 16s. 11d., from which a few expenses must be deducted,including a reduction of £lO for the ladies of the weekly sewing meeting to procure materials for the coming year. The sum of £146 13s. 11d, was taken the first two days, and about £6B the last day. £250 still remain to be raised. The ladies who assisted at the stalls were as follows : Parochial stall, Mesdames, Craik, Dexvhurst, Peter Rylands, W. Price, Farrall, D. THE MURDER OF A BARMAID AT SWINDON SEN- TENCE OF DEATH.-At the Wilts Assizes at Devizes on Wednesday Edward Richard Palmer was found guilty of the murder of Esther Swinford, a barmaid, at Swindon, and sentenced to death. The prisoner had promised to marry the girl, but failed to keep his promise and went away from Swindon, saying he was going to Canada. He returned, however, and on September 18 shot the young woman dead in the bar at which she was serving.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW STREET. ANOTHER TOWN COUNCIL DISCUSSION. Councillor Lord's Amendment Defeated.
div.p: THE PROPOSED NEW STREET. ANOTHER TOWN COUNCIL DIS- CUSSION. Councillor Lord's Amendment Defeated.

The proposed new street from Sankey street to Rylands street was again the subject of discussion at the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tues- day evening. Councillor Lord moved the following amendment :—That the resolution of the General Pur- poses Committee as passeg on October 6th, 1903, "That the proposal contained in the following resolution of the Street Improvement Committee be approved. 'A proposal from Mr. R. E. Garnett to add 20 feet in width co-extensive with his premises to the proposed passage behind the new premises in Bridge street, and to give the scheduled property belonging to him, containing an area of 316 square yards, in exchange for land in the Eagle and Child Yard,,lcontaininglis3l square yards " be rescinded. The town generally, he contended, was against the scheme ; as was shown by the Parr Hall meeting, and the resolution of the Property Owners' Association. The street was not required for traffic on account of its close proximity to Bridge-street. The Corporation shouldlget on with the improvements in Bridge-streetiand the other main arteries of the town, and let side streets alone. Provision had been made fnr the widening of Bridge-street to sixty feet, but he would suggest that the width at Market Gate should be 80 feet. The proposed new street would be practically nothing but an outlet for the back premises of Bridge-street. Why they wanted to make a new street with front property facing back property he could not see. The street, he also contended, would be a breach of the bye-laws as it would form a cul-de-sac. Six months ago Alderman Sutton strongly objected to a new street being made from Latchford to Wilderspool on the ground that it would be a cul-de-sac. __

Alderman Surrox : Not at all. Councillor LORD: I think Alderman Sutton's objec- tion was that the street was a breach of the bye-laws. Alderman SUTTON: It was because there was a big axe to grind on the part of Councillor Pemberton. Councillor LORD: Councillor Pemberton did not come into this case. I object to that. It was not mentionedat all. ‘Continuing,he said the street at Latchford would have been made and handed over to the Corporation. In the present case the Corporation were asked to make and pave the street, and he said that they ought to throw out the scheme because it was against the bye-laws. Mr. Garnett's offer was a very good offer on one side only. It was not a good offer to the Cor- poration and the ratepayers. Mr. Garnett, he contended, would get an undue benefit in the transaction as he would receive nearly two hundred yards more from the Corporation than he was giving. Councillor Lord instanced how Messrs. Skeltons recently had to pay £2OO for betterment, and if they had to pay that amount for about 15 yards Mr. Garnett ought, considering the froutage,..to pay £2,000 or £3,000. . _ _

secondea because he considered the street unnecessary. Councillor PEMBERTON supported and pointed out that the Corporation had not only to pave the street but they had also to give the land. He disclaimed the insinuation of Alderman Sutton that he had anything to do w:th the proposedistreet fsom Latchford to Waders- pool. He had no interest in the land that it was intended to utilize for that street. The whole of the land on that (side belonged It Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company. In regard to the present scheme he con- sidered that the money might very well be spent on Bridge-street. Alderman SUTTON said that at the time the suggested L atchford improvement was mentioned Councillor Pemberton had a great deal to say about members of the Council having axes to grind. (Hear, hear.) On that occasion he (Alderman Sutton) opposed, on his (Councillor Pemberton's) own bringing forward, a resolution that the Council should take over a road in which Councillor Pemberton and his partner were interested.

Councillor PEMBERTON rose to a point of order. Alderman SUTTON: 'didn't intend to say any more, but I will say tlaislmuch. It was one of the biggest axes that ever any member of this Council— Councillor PEMBERTON: I didn't bring it before the Council. The MAYOR called Alderman Sutton to order.

Councillor DODDS (to Alderman Sutton) : You made an insinlation against •Councillor Pemberton in regard to the land. You did it before. If thereis any man in the Council who ought not to make insinuations in regard to axe-grinding you are the man. Alderman SurroN: That is your opinion. We will take it for what it is worth. Continuing Alderman Sutton pointed out that the matter had been fully dis- cussed by the Council and the result was the recommend- ation of the committee. Yet, Councillor Lord and a few others with their superior wisdom and with the determination, which had been characteristic of their conduct throughout,to obstruct and oppose anything and everything which the various committees might con- descend to bring forward—however beneficial it might be in the interests of the borough—persisted in trying their best on all occasions to rescind resolutions which had been so often discussed and approved of. The new scheme would enable them to construct a , street 40 feet wide at a smaller cost than a 15 or 20 , feet passage originally proposed. He asked thesensible ' members of the Council if their decisions after due and careful thought and deliberation were to be over- looked and upset by a party of men who systematically objected to everything for their own purposes, and then crowed over them for having been such simple- tons? He asked them not to be so cowardly as to shirk their duties for fear they would not have the Non-Traders' support at the elections, but let them manfully and without fear or favour do what their con sciences believed to be best for the benefit of those whom they represented. He could respbct anyone who honestly opposed any scheme or resolution which he considered was derogatory to the interests of the borough, and acted in a straightforward and upright way. But when, in order to get his object, he descended to the use of deliberate falsehoods to injure his neigh- bour, then he was•unworthy of being held in the slightest respect. In order to hhow the vindictiveness of some men, he must tell them that it had come to his knowledge that a certain member of the Council had been informed bya party outside, who must know better that he (Alderman Sutton) was to receive compensation to ft very large amount. He believed it was stated that the amount to be paid to him by iMr. Garnett was £2,000. All he would say was that he had never spoken to Mr. Garnett on the subject—in fact he did not know whether if ho met him in the street he cvouldj knowhim. During the long time he had been a member of the Council, instead of reaping any benefit from it, it had cost him a very considerable amount of time and it had also meant a considerable amount out of his pocket. He thought that when statements of that kind were thrown broadcast throughout the town to the injury of one who had always been determined to do his best in the interests of the town for so long a period he ought to be really deserving of something better than that. If gentlemen could not carry their objects without des- cending to such accusations as these, not only the few good members—the cream of the Council—who had already retired, but every member should retire if he was to be accused, villified and scandalised in that manner.

Councillor PEACOCK supported the motion on the ground that the street was not necessary. Councillor JAMES EVANS spoke at considerable length in support of the scheme. Until the question was settled, he said, the Bridge-street improvements could not proceed. In regard to the statement that Mr. Garnett was getting the best of the bargain, Councillor Lord had omitted to mention that Mr. Garnett had three rights of road over the land, aNd also possessed the rights of light all round the land. That, of course. materially enhanced the value of the lanzl. He had never heard a single member of the Street Improve- ment Committee suggest that the street should be taken through to Sankey-street. _ _ _
Councillor PEMBERTON: Councillor Wilkinson said so at the last Council_ meeting. _ . .

Continuing Councillor EVAtiS said he had never had that proposal in his mind. He contended it was in the interests of the town that a new street shduld be con- structed at a smaller cost than a passage 20 feet wide. He understood that Mr. Garnett wished to utilize the land h would acquire for the purpose of extending his works. Would not this be in the interests of the ratepayers?

Councillor PE.MBERTON said Mr. Garnett would ex- tend the works at a cost to the town of £15,000 for purchasing Mr. Benson's shop, Sr.c. Councillor JAM ES EVANS : As long as I am a mem- ber of the Council, I shall oppose the buying of Mr. Benson's shop. Councillor PEMBERTON : You won't stop it. Continuing; Councillor EVANS said the new street was part of the plan of a great improvement.
COMICIIIOr BURTON : Councillor EVANS: Where Councillor Bu,rton has considered this for Ave minutes I have conAdered it for hours.

Councillor BURTON: You are looking at it through rosy glasses. Councillor EVANS : I will throw out a challenge to Councillor Burton, I am prepared to debate the question anywhere he likes if he can show me from a financial point of view that the passage is cheaper than the street. lam looking through the glasses of common sense and not through the glasses of prejudice. Con- tinuingthe said that if Mr. Garnett did not extend his works the Corporation could not make the land profitable Having regard to the cost of paving the passage and connecting it with the existing entry he considered that the new street would be of more benefit to the town. Councillor DODDS contended that there was no necessity for hurrying in the matter. Mr. Garnett might make them a better offer. Councillor BURTON said that if the committee were advocating a street worthy of being called a street he would not object but as it was, they proposed to con- struct a street only 40 feet wide in the heart of the town. He could see that the scheme was going to cost the town between £20,000 and £30,000. , Councillor TINNION pointed out that the scheme

would help ...vet Improvement Committee if they- decided to make Bridge-street 80 feet wide as instead of having a2O feet passage at the rear there would be a a feet street. If the scheme did not pass that night the present Bridge-street scheme would go through. Councillor LORD having inquired as to what it was proposed to do in refereace to Mr. Benson's shop, Councillor WILKINSON said he did not state that the Committee intended to purchase it, but he was of the opinion that they ought to do so. Councillor LORD said it would cost something like £20,000 to £30,000 to open out the street. Councillor WILKINSON: Do you know what £20,080 is? (Laughter).
