WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE FEDERATION. Rev. J. F. Matthews and the Compensation Question. The second of the series of public meetings promoted by the Warrington Temperance Federation was held in Ebenezer Church, Buttermarket-street, on Wednesday evening, Mr. T. Dale presiding over a fair attendance. In his address the Chairman ,laid stress upon the fact that the working classes were responsible to a great extent for the infliction upon themselves of much of the poverty that they were enduring. He referred to the need of active temperance work in Warrington and expressed regret at the action of the magistrates in granting the transfer of the "Green Dragon" licence to Lovely-lane and allowing old houses to be rebuilt. In regard to the Compensation Question, he hoped the Prime Minister's statement would come to nothing. It behoved the temperance organizations of the country to assert themselves and to show that the public ani not the trade must receive first consideration. Mrs. MOORES then delivered a short address.

The Rev. J. F.MATTHews spoke on the compensation question which he said was a difficult and delicate sub- ject to deal with. At the same time it was a question which not only temperance and social reformers gener- ally, but the whole body of English ratepayers would have to face seriously. The brewers demanded a measure of compensation if possible out of the public funds. Temperance workers had to face that problem and they had to settle it, or the brewers would settle it in favour of themselves. It was argued that when a man spent £5,000 or £6,000 on a house it was exceedingly hard lines for the licence to be taken from him. On the face of it, it looked monstrous and unjust. They must, how- ever, bear in mind that when a man paid such an ex- orbitant sum for a licensed house he did so with his eyes open. If he did not, he was a born fool. He bought the house knowing that there were risks attached to the house which were not attached to any other business. He was practically purchasing the right—for twelve months only—to sell intoxicating liquors; and he had to face the possibility that the licence would not. be renewed. That was one of the reasons why they ob- jected to compensation out of the public funds when a licence was allowed to lapse. There was no moral reason under the sun why compensation should be granted. The drink traffic was legalized but it was a grossly immoral traffic. They had the evidence of judges, peers of the realm, princes, barristers, solicitors, ministers and all sorts and con- ditions of the great army of social benefactors who told them that a great deal of the crime committed in the country was directly traceable to the influence of strong drink. They felt from a social and moral standpoint, having regard to the welfare of the public, that there was no reason on moral grounds why compensation should be allowed. The rev. gentleman advanced as a third argument against compeniation that the drink trade was essentially a monopoly. He alluded to the influentially signed manifesto on the ques- tion which had been published in the Press. Assuming for the molpent that the Legislature would have to deal with tlie compensation question, there were certain things that must be safeguarded. In any measure of compensation-introduced in the House of Commons there must inevitably be provision made for not only a large but an immediate reduction in licences. The present unrestricted power of the magistrates to reduce licences at their pleasure must be preserved, and some measure of effective public control in every llocality must be granted. The manifesto, Mr. Matthews continued, brought them to the parting of the ways. Men whose names carried com- &Sanding weight, by signing it directly admitted that they thought the legislature should take in hand not only the question of temperance reform but the • question of compensation. They did net say that the ! legislature should compensate the publicans ; out of public funds but that they should create a body of commissioners, something like the Irish Church commissioners, who themselves shouldact by, and through and on behalf of the drink trade at large and any system of compensation should be levied from ' those who were left in the trade after the licences not wanted were allowed to lapse. He (Mr. Matthews)did not believe in the legislature touching the question of ' compensation at all. if the brewers wanted compens- ation let them have mutual insurance or create a compensation measure and make it corn pulsory among themselves. (Applause.) He hoped with all his heart that there would be no split in the temperance party over that inoppor- tune document. It had not received the benediction of the great temperance societies of the country but he understood that an important authorised manifesto was 6hortl3 to be issued. If a compensation bill were in- troduced it must not in any way trench upon public funds and accompanying it there must be a very large attempt made to reduce licences. (Applause). 1 Mr. R. WYLLIE also addressed the meeting. Solos were rendered by Miss Littlewood and Mrs. Moores.

it is with keen regret that we record the death this week of Mr. Joseph Shaw Green, who was prior to April, an alderman of the Borough. War, rington has been fortunate in possessing many public men who have whole-heartedly given their services to the town, and among these men the late Mr. Shaw Green ranked highly. During the fifteen years he was in the Town Council he per- formed an altogether uncommon amount of diffi- cult and valuable work. Early in his municipal career he took a prorninen6 part in the purchase of the Water Works uLdertaking, and ever after he was closely associated with the financial affairs of the Corpoiation—an association which we do not hesitate to say beneficially affected the interests of the ratepayers. He was our local Chancellor of the Exchequer, and the town never had a better man in this posi- tion. The gap his retirement caused was most difficult to fill, and we can give personal testi- mony to the sense; of loss which every member of the Council felt on that occasion. That feeling I will be all the more poignant now that death has claimed the late Alderman. He has not been so '1 long out ,of public life as to be forgotten, and among his many Corporation, Wes;eyan and Liberal friends, the tidings of his death will indeed be sad tidings. We are sure the sympathy of all will be extended towards the late gentleman's sorely bereaved family.

The last meeting of the Town Council for the closing municipal year was held on Tuesday even- ing, when occasion was taken to pass a resolution of thanks to Mr. J. C. Parr, Mayor, whose second year of office expires in the course of another ten days. Mr. Parr has had a difficult task—in fact, we do not think any Mayor of Warrington ever took office under such discouraging conditions. He came to preside over the Council when that body was rent by the Non-Trading agitation, and doubt- less he hoped that, as an outsider, he might be instrumental in restoring peace. In that he has failed, but the fault is not Mr. Parr's. There has been no prospect of peace during the period which has elapsed since he was first elected,, and there is only a faint prospect even now. The Non-Traders themselves will have to make the first move in the desired direction, and they are not ready to do so. Mr. Parr has, however, acquitted himself with credit, for he has not only been impartial, but he has been industrious and painstaking to an un- common degree. His has been no half-hearted Mayoralty, and we think the town, as well as,the Council, owes him gratitude for having taken the helm and steered so straight a course during troublous times.

It is unfortunate that Mr. Parrs last Council meeting should be distinguished by incidents of the most disagreeable character. The revelations by Councillor Lord in regard to recent slack con- tracts were of the most unsavoury kind, and they culminated in a motion for the dismissal of the Water Engineer, which was only negatived by a majority of two votes. We are glad that the motion was defeated—for it is impossible to en- tirely eliminate sentiment from such a matter— and by the Committee's recommendations Mr. Peas gets a chance to 'quit him like a man. He has three months in which to regain the lost con- fidence of the Council and of the town, and we shall be pleased indeed if he merits the trust again reposed in him. The whole history of the slack contracts, as recently revealed, fills a page in the municipal histor, of the town which all will be glad to see turned over.

Another feature of the meeting, in pleasant contrast to the one above alluded to, was the granting of an honorarium to Mr. John Fairhurst, the Borough Treasurer, on the satisfactory term- ination of his negotiations with the Count! authorities regarding the financial adjustment between County and Borough necessitated 1)7 Warrington's promotion in the scale of large towns. The Council has recorded its appreciation of Mr. Fairhurst's valuable services and m Ide him a present of £5O. We are p9rsonally acquainted with with the labour thrown on Mr. Fairhurst s shoulders by the arduous and protracted nature of the work he has been engaged in, and for that alone he is deserving of recompense. But the ability he has brought to bear on the task, and the advantageous result of his efforts, are even more important and worthy of recognition. In less capable hands the adjustment might have cost the ratepayers many more thousands of pounds, and the remark of Councillor Pemberton that Mr. Fairhurst was" paid for it was so ungracious as to earn general condemnation. It is not by treat- ing them in so carping and cavalier a spirit that we are to get the best service from our officials. We are delighted to have the opportunity of adding our congratulations to those the Borough Treasurer has already received.

There have been interesting developments in re- gard to the inquiry deadlock since our Idst issue. The Town Council, at its meeting on Tuesday, de- cided that the Commissioners be asked to con- tinue the inquiry and deal with the question of reporting in their own way. Since Mr.H.Roberts J.P., has created a mild sensation by issuing a placard containing the copy of a letter he had addressed to the Mayor, enclosing a cheque for £250 towards the cost of reporting the:proceedings 'of the Commissioners on condition that the Non Traders contributed a similar sum. The Mayor, in reply, has very properly, we think, returned the cheque and declined to interfere pointing out that "the matter of the inquiry has been left in the hands of the six commissioners". In a further letter to the Mayor, Mr. Roberts says: "Your suggestion that I hould forward my offer to the Commis- sioners is open to the serious objection that certain people might insinuate that, by doing so, was endeavouring to unduly influence the Com- missioners in regard to any charges concern ing my own conduct or that of ray firm." We wonder it has not occurred to Mr. Roberts that the publication of his first letter to the Mayor is open to a somewhat similar objection for, sur44y, it is calculated to affect the decision of the Commissioners in regard to a ques- tion at issue—that of reporting—and it is undesir- able that any outside influence should be brought to bear on these gentlemen. 'What they have te do is to decide among themselves—and decide quickly—what shall be done in order that the inquiry may proceed at DM° on thorough and satisfactory lines.

We are at last in complete agreement with Captain Crosfield--on one.point ! He concludes a latter, which we publish elsewhere, by asking " Whether, with a view to strengthening the navy, we shall not do better by spending four millions annually in training up a sound hoale defence army, than by spending an equivalent amount in building battleships ? " Certainly, gr. Crosfield ! Four millions will not go far in tile, production of battleships, whereas a great deal may be done with such a sum towards the trai,lll" ing up of the home defence army. \Ye should be very pleased to see such an additional sum voted annually for such a purpose. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
OCTOBER 31st 1903.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S CCM- "JOE ' structive ability has often THE CONJURER. been questioned; but after the Liverpool speeches there can be no doubt of his capacity to invent a per- fect maze of arithmetical puzzles. The Liverpool working men followed him with interest. They would have followed a conjurer with much the , same feeling. We all know that the conjurer does net produce rabbits out of the hat, but the illu- sion is none the less entertaining. When Mr. CHAMBERLAIN :tells us one day that the foreign manufactured goods we import are the products of sweated labour, and the next day that the foreign workmen are on the whole rather better eff than our own, he is even more bewildering than the conjurer. We are left wondering whether the rabbits come out of the hat or the hat out of the rabbits. The Britisa workman has not had any reason hitherto for envying the fortune of the German workman. He knows that his wages are better than are paid elsewhere, save in the United States, and that money goes further in purchasing power for him than any other country. It is true Mr. CHAMBERLAIN tells him that he has not enough empleyment,and that he will have more under a Protectionist system. But that is most problematical, whereas the consequeat in- crease in the cost of living, disguise it as Mr. CHAMBERLAIN may, is certain. All the elaborate calculations to show that taxation on corn does not increase the price in proportion to the duty cannot hide this plain fact. The automatic opera- tion of import duties is to raise prices all round,and the onlyiassurance the workman has that he will not be worse off than ever is Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S personal pledge. We do not doubt the sincerity of that pledge for a moment. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has hypnotised himself. The conjurer really believes that the rabbits come out of the hat. But it is curious that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN should be SO oonfident of improving the household budget of the poorest families by his re-adjustment of taxa- tion, and yet he leaves maize and bacon out of the scheme. No explanation of this has been given except the suggestion that bacon: is an im- portant article of diet for the humblest toilers. Does not this reservation excite a little suspicion in the workman's mind? Why does Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN shrink from experiment on bacon? If he fears that it would upset the household budget, what ground is there for his confidence that his manipulation of duties on bread and meat will not have the same disastrous effect? There is a superficial attraction, of course,in the appeal to the workman, "How long are you going to take it lying down 9" Is it not in human nature to suppose that foreign competition is benevolently designed to improve our trade. Some people try to persuade themselves that ';in allf the transactions of international commerce there must be exactly the same advantages for everybody con- cerned. This is not the case; but the workman who is tempted to think that, in his particular trade, retaliation would be gratifying must count the cost. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN treats it as a mere bagatelle. We have his personal pledge that it will be really of no consequence. Moreover, he throws out the most delightful assurance of all— that if we should adopt his plan, and find it delusive, we can drop it it without concern and return to Free Trade. "Suppose I am wrong, suppose that in common with ninety- nine out of a hundred of the whole civilised world I am wrong, and the pure Free Traders or free importers are right—well, any way it is perfectly evident that the adoption of these proposals will not do you much harm, because the ninety-nine out of the hundred—these other countries, our German competitors, our French competitors, our Italian competitors, our Russian competitors, our Swedish competitors—are all doing very well." We are not to be afraid of try- eing Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S prescription, becausa, if it should happen to disagree with us entirely, we shall have the satisfaction of assuming that it agrees perfectly with the constitutions of other people. What would a patient say to a doctor who reasoned in this style: "My dear sir, I think this prescription will cure you ; but, if it should not, pray read .these testimonials from other patients, and thank Heaven that it has cured them, or at any rate they think so ! " Would such a physician inspire unfailing confidence? "After all," says Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, "my prescription only involves, if it involves anything, this small transference of taxation and this small protection against foreign manufactured goods." We can 1 re-transfer the taxation and abolish the protection, and everything will go on as before. Does not Mr. CHAMBERLAIN know perfectly well that by the experience of the foreign countries that he is and of citing the first step in Protection is ;never retraoed, and that when it has failed there has always arisen the cry, "Oh, it is not enough ; we must take a longer stride" ! Nothing could be more futile, and more instinct with a dangerous levity, than to tell us that we can dislocate our 1 entire trade, and be none the worse off if the experiment is a failure. The Liverpool speeche

argument we will allow him to assume this much, Particularly as a letter in yesterday's "Manchester 'Guardian " from the chairman of the executive 'Committee of the Navy League demonstrates very forcibly that our naval preparedness is very ,far from being what it should be. This brings us back to the point we have emphasized all along— that the need for the maintenance of the navy at a standard of the highest possible efficiency is far morti urgent than any drastic transformation of military policy, and espocially on lines so objec- tionable to this freedom-loving people ,as the supporters of the National Service League advo- cate. We feel bound to assert our ever-strength• nning conviction that Captain Crosfield has no •case. Conditions will have to change enormously before the need for any form of conscription in the British Isles can arise. So far Captain Oros- field has failed to show any change in the status ,quo ante bellum which justifies any serious con- sideration of his extreme proposals.

The gift of books to form the nucleus of a library at the Liberal Club is another evidence of the interest of the Crosfield family in the welfare of the institution. The Liberal Club has had few •tvarmer friends than those bearing the honoured name of Crosfield, and it is refreshing to find that :their interest in it has not abated. The annual -report which was presented at the meeting on 'Tuesday evening, shows that the club, like many other institutions, has suffered from the period of trade depression through which we are passing. -A feature of the evening's proceedings was the excellent address on current political topics by Mr. A. H. Crosfield. He is a sound Free -Trader and has no sympathy whatever with Mr. Chamberlain's" raging and tearing propaganda.' • Trade Unionists will read with pleasure Mr. Cros- • field's remarks on the attack which is being made on their trade organisations. He shows that by recent judicial decisions the workman has been 'deprived of valued rights and privileges, which up to a year ago everybody .hought were his by de finite Act of Parliament. Mr. Crosfield urges that early steps should be taken to re-define the position of the workman with respect to organisa- tion. Comparisons, it is said, are odious, but we think workingmen might very profitably compare the attitude of Mr. Pierpoint with that of Mr. Crosfield on this important question.

The Warrington magistrates have again marked their determination to check the street betting !mil as much as lies in their power. The only fear •is that the smart fines inflicted will not have the • salutary effect desired, as it has come to the knowledge of the Bench that the money is speedily forthcoming from the coff9rs of a syndicate which exists for the protection of the bookmakers in their nefarious calling. The crusade of the police is being extended in a new direction, and aiders and abetters—in other words ..outs—will have to be upon their mettle lf they are to escape tha penalty for their s hare in the system which all who have the bes G interests of the community at heart will wish to see stamped out. We have it on the authority of the Chief Constable that the difficulties of the Police are enchanced a hundred-fold by these men and the sooner some of them are brought to book the better for good government and public morality.

The riegotiationewitn reference to the Ship Canal Company's proposals at Warrington have broken down. At a conference between represen- tatives of the Corporation and local traders and manufacturers, and directors and engineer of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, the proceedings came to an abrupt termination owing to a proposal of the company, which could not be accepted,that the, judgment in the action, against which they have appealed, should be set aside and dismissed. We do not suppose that many tears will be shed over this contretemps. The benefits which 'Warrington was to receive from the scheme were never of a character to was enthusiastic over, and the latest proposal of 'the Ship Canal Company with reference to the decision in the High Court of Justice seems to give colour to the idea that the Company had as their first consideration, the weakening of the Corporation's position with regard to the presery t- tion of a dredged river at Warrington. The decision is now to be carried to the Court of Appeal, but we fail to see on what reasonable grounds the Ship Canal Company can hope to get any assistance from His Majesty's judges of appeal in another attempt to shelve their obligations to Warrington.

div.head: Marriage of Miss Agnes Knowles.
div.p: Marriage of Miss Agnes Knowles.

An interesting marriage took place at Cairo-street Unitarian Chapel on Saturday. The contracting parties were Mr. Harold Alcock, of Doseley, Salop youngest son of the late Mr. S. H. Alcock, of Bury, and Miss Agnes Knowles, younger daughter of Mr. J. H. Knowles, of Lovely-lane, Warrington. The marriage service, which was held at 11 o'clock in the morning, was conducted by the Rev. Charles Harvey Cook, the newly-appointed pastor. Miss Emily Pemberton was bridesmaid, and Mr. Fred Wenham had the honour to fulfil the office of best man. Mr. J. M. Muir, A.R.C.0., presided at the organ, and rendered an admirable selection of music. After the ceremony the bride and bridegroom, accompanied by the guests, adjourned to the n...‘w school buildings, where the breakfast was held. Very many valuable presents have been given to the happy couple.

div.head: Compensation to Publicans.
div.p: Compensation to Publicans.

At-a meeting of the Latchford Baptist Literary and Debating Society on Monday night a paper was given by Mr. E. Wynne Jones on Compensation to Publi- cans." He endeavoured to show that England was being "pressed down almost to ruin with this cursed. drink." He was minute in his plea for urging tem- perance reform. The trade principally existed in localities where the will power of men and women was weakened. He suggested as a way out of the difficulty, that the trade form themselves into a com- pensation insurance company, the trade contributing alone, each paying a premium, so that if a house lost its licence the others would be the ones to compen- sate. A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Jones for his able paper. The following members took part in the debate :—Messrs. J. Albinson, P. Cliffe, A. Albinson' R. P. Williams, S. Albinson, J. Adams, and W. W. Drewett.
A GOOD REsourrioN.—Wear ALF TAYLOR'S

Wonderful Boots.—Advt. British Women's Temperance Association. The opening meeting of the British Women's Temperance Association was held on Tuesday in the Church Parlour, Bold-street, when Mrs. Garnett pre- sided. After the opening exercises, in which Mrs. Carnson engaged in praver,and the communicationsand papers had been read by the secretary Mrs Garnett and Mrs Simpson gave interesting accounts of their visit to the Convention held in Geneva. As our meetings are held on the last Tuesday in each month, writes Mrs. Simpson, the hon. secretary, we hope the ladies will attend and help us in this branch of Temperance work. We may not seem to do great things as a band of workers, but by meeting together we are inspired individually to go and do what we can to stem the evil that is in our midst. We read of active work being done in other towns. May we not fall short, but go ahead with our duty and the needs that are around us. At our next meeting we will discuss, "How to work and win the people for the Temperance cause." FIRE GRATES Of every description.—J. S. GAR- LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warringion.—Aclvt. Marriage at the Parish Church. _

The marriage took place at the Parish Church, on Tuesday, of Sergeant John Sykes, of the 4th Northum- berland Fusiliers, Dublin, to Isabella, fourth daughter of Mr. William Woods, of Church-street. The Rev. A. & Cameron was the officiating clergyman. The bride, who was given away by her father was hand- somely attired in a dress of French grey voile, trimmed with lace and chiffon, and white felt hat, trimmed with feathers. She carried a beautiful shower bouquet of white flowers. The bridesmaids were Miss Millie and Miss Ada Woods, sisters of the bride, and they wore dresses of pink voile, with black picture hats. Their bouquets were composed of marguerites, and were the gifts of the bridegroom. The duties of hest man were dischargeel!by Mr. Thomas Turner. A recep- tion was afterwards held in St. Clement's schoolroom, and subsequently the bride and bridegroom left for St. Annes-on-the-Sea for the lionesmoon. They will afterwards reside in Dublin. They were the recipients of numerous presents. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the ICING OF TONICS.---63, SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. The Attendances of Members of the Council. A return has been issued of the attendances of members of the Town Council from 9th November, 1902, to 26th October, 1903. It appears that the total number of meetings of the Council and committees I and sub-committees was 467. Alderman Smethurst heads the list with 191 attendances, and the Mayor is a very good second with 183. Councillor James Evans has the best record of the Councillors, his attendances numbering 168. Councillor John Evans runs him close with 166. Alderman Fairclough comes next in order with 152. Other members who have made over 100 attendances are Alderman Hutchinson 145, Councillor Wilkinson 141, Councillor John Roberts T 33, Councillor Rogers 129, Councillor T. Burton 123, Councillor Ellison 117, Alderman Bolton 111, Alderman Bennett 109, Councillor Duncan 107, Alderman Sutton 105 and Councillor Barton 105.

The Recent Opera.—The Proceeds.

When the curtain was rung down for the last time on the performance of "The Yeomen of the Guard" at the Parr Hall on Saturday evening, it was admitted on all hands that the members of the Warrington Musical Society had scored a great triumph in its first attempt at presenting light opera in Warrington The dosing performance was witnessed by a crowded house, and rarely has "The Yeomen of the Guard" been more capably produced. If anything, Saturday's doting performance excelled all previous ones, and the audi- ence showed their appreciation by demanding frequent encores. Jack Point was especially seen at his best and Mr. Gough has reason to be well satisfied with a most successful debut. At the. close the -principal artistes appeared before the curtain and secured hearty encomiums. The conductor (Mr. F. H. Crossley) and Mr. E. Thornley Dodge (stage manager) also received ovations. The principal ladies were made the recipients of choice bouquets, two falling to the lot of Mrs. Arthur Booth. One of the bouquets was presented by the members of the Warrington Cycling Club"in recog- Rition of her fine rendering- of her important part in the opera, and as the wife of a prominent club mem- ber." When the hall was cleared, there was also anl interesting ceremony behind the scenes. Silver cigar cases were presented to Mr. Thornley-Dodge and Mr. Crossley as souvenirs of the occasion. Mr. Thornley- Dodge commented upon the admirable performances which had been given and paid a high tribute to the musical and dramatic talent possessed by the mem- bers of the Musical Society. Mr. Crossley observed that lie had had to deal with such a willing band of artistes that his work had been pleasant in many ways. They had all been repaid by the great success which had attended their efforts. He hoped this first venture in light opera would not be the last. He did net see why they should not perform another opera about that time next year. (Hear, hear.) Cheers having been raised for Mr. Thornley-Dodge and Mr. Crossley, the members :joined hands on the stage and sang " Auld lung syne." The financial result of the opera is alSo very satisfactory. The accounts are not yet complete, but it may be safely stated that there will be a balance in hand, after meeting expenses, of well over £lOO.

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday October 31, 1903. THE FISCAL PROBLEM.

Coming Events. ) Madame Ella Russell and a first-class concert party will appear at the Parr Hall on Tuesday evening next. , For particulars see advertisement. lilutsford Division Liberal Association: public meeting in Providence schoolroom, Chapel-lans, • Stockton Heath, on Tuesday evening. Warrington Women's Liberal Association: Annual tea meeting at Liberal Club, Bewsey-street, on Wed- nesday evening, Address by Mrs. Ellen Robinson, of Liverpool. • Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay; "Sunny South" bazaar in schools, Thewlis-street, on Thursday, Fri- • day and Saturday next. Full particulars in our ad-• I vertising columns. The Macedonian Crisis; town's meeting in the Parr Hall on Thursday evening. Address by a deputation , from the Balkan Committee of London. Warrington Musical Society ; first subscription con- cert of the season in the Parr Hall, on Wednesday, November 18th. Baptist Church, Golborne-Street, to-morrow (Sun- day) missionary anniversary. Morning, Councillor Brough ; evening, Rev. A. Wells (of China). University Extension Lecture on Dante,Wednesday, November 11th, and not on November 18th as pre- viously advertised. Emmanuel Church special Protestant sermons to-morrow (Sunday) by the Rev. , G. Attwood, of London. A Widow's Death. On Sunday afternoon, Louisa Harrison, 50, widow, who resided at 138, Liverpool-road, was found dead in bed. GIVE THEM A TRIAL.—ALF. TA.YLOR'S wonder- ful boots for everybody. Police Charity Sports. We are informed that the amount realised at the annual police sports, held on the 27th August last was .£32. Of this sum Safi has been devoted to the funds of the Warrington Infirmary, and .£8 handed over to the Nursing Association, while the remain- ing £8 goes to the Police Athletic Club funds. Though the amount is much less than that of last year it is very satifactory considering that the sports had first to be posponed on accounit of the weather and finally- held under extremely unfavour- able climatic conditions- H. M. ASHTON'S LIFE TONIC is the KING OF TONICS.-63, SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. St. John's Literary Society. The members of this society held their usual fort- nightly meeting in St. John's Church schoolroom on Tuesday evening last, Mr. D. R. Hodge, vice-president, .being in the chair. The evening was devoted to impromptu discussions, among the subjects put forward for consideration being the following, viz. "Are the passive resisters acting in accordance with bible teaching?" "Is the influence of christianity declining?" Should we support Mr. Chamberlain's fiscal proposals?" "Should military service be made compulsory ?'". Should bicycles be taxed ?" &c., &c. There was a good attendance of members and the questions were freely discussed. St. John Ambulance Brigade. The annual distribution of prizes and certificates in connection with the local corps of this brigade took place at the Gymnasium last evening. Mr. R. Pierpoint, M.P„ presided and said the members of the corps had done very great service not only in the town but services never to be forgotten in South Africa. He expressed regret that Captain Waring was unable to be present. —Mrs. Pierpoint distributed the prizes and certificates as follows :-- Attendance Prizes: Sergeants W. D. Fell and W. A Banning, Privates A. Sinclair and J. H. Sayer. Footballground prizes: Sergt W. Newns, Privates J. Lee and B. Green. Certificates : Messrs. Gilks, Tanner, Perry, Bonnell, Hawthorne, Rigby, Garnett, Robinson, King, Lund, Marley, Knox, Savory, Brown, Wake, Jefferson, Holden, Smithson, Spann, and H. James. A Wife's Sad Death. A sensation was created in Warrington on Tuesday when it became known that Alfred Putnam, a handy- man employed at Mr, E. Connors' posting establish- ment, and lodging at 23, Erwood street, off Tanner's lane, had been arrested on suspicion of having caused the death of his wife •Elizabeth. At 8.30 in the morn- ing the woman was found lying dead on the kitchen floor with a wound on the side of her head. It ap- peared that she had quarrelled .vitli her husband on Monday night and blows were exchanged. Putnam was taken to the Police station by P. C. Lewis and the woman's body was conveyed to the mortuary I where a post-mortem examination was made— . Happily this disclosed the fact that she had not died from violence but from natural causes, the bursting 1 lof one or more blood vessels having caused pressure , 'on the brain. Consequently "Death a verdict of Death Ifrom natural causes was returned at the inquest and I on Thursday morning Pqtnam was discharged. BEST BOOTS FOR £LL.—UNDER theCLOCK.—Advt.

Mr. Edwin Woods and the "Manchester Guardian." A Fallacy Exposed. A letter from Mr. Edwin Woods, embodying the facts and figures published in his contribution to our columns last week, appeared in the "Manchester Guardian" on Wednesday, and gave rise to the following editorial comment in that paper: "A Warrington correspondent's letter which we print to-day puts the root-fallacy of the Pro- tectionist in a nutshell so neatly as to repay notice. He takes the amount of iron and steel imported from foreign countries into Great Britain in 1902, and shows the amount of raw material—coal, ore and lime- stone—whose production is involved in the production of the ironand steel. He then turns to the imports of machinery in another year and those of all manufactured articles in 1902 and comments on the amount of pro- duction represented likewise by these. If this produc- tion had been carried on in England, how much capital, how much labour would have found employment! The total imports of all manufactures for 1902 was 140 millions, andas it is admitted that one-half of the value represents wages, we have here a clear loss of seventy millions last year which would have been earned in weekly wages by the working classes of this country. Now, if the average wage per week which in this way was not earned last year be a trifle under £2, there will be required to earn the seventy millions a body of 700,000 wage-earning workers. Does our correspondent suppose that 700,000 wage-earning workers exist in this country in a state of total unemployment or that an amount of unremunemtively invested capital exists by the use of which the 700,000 could do the work? It is surely clear that neitherthe men nor the capital could be obtained except by withdrawing them from other in- dustries and occupations. And why are they engaged in these other industries and occupations? Because—we tremble at suggesting it to one whose views "have been formed in the practical school of blisiners life"—they pay better. When a cobbler buys his hatsand his butter and his butter-dish instead of making these articles he does on a small scale what England does on a larger one; he makes what he can make most profitably and buys his other requisities with the proceeds. How does our correspondent suppose that we can buy our imports unless, indirectly, we work for them? Any.theory that we buy them by "living on capital "—that is, selling off foreign investments—is awkwardly cornered by the fact that our foreign investments are steadily increasing in amount."\ Mr. C. E. Parker Replies to Mr. Edwin Woods. Sir,—Mr. Woods tells us that he is nut in favour of taxing "raw material." It would be interesting if Mr Woods would define what he means by raw material.. He tells us that in 1902 we imported 140 millions of manufactures. Of these Warrington took a fair share, but to our manufacturers they come as raw material. This amount includes pig iron for the iron works, cod oil for the tanneries, tallow and grease for the soap works and manures for the farmers. I could go on until I had enumerated almost all the industries in Warring- ton which depend for their raw material on goods in- cluded in the 140 millions as "manufactures." ,`A glance at the list of such goods in the Board of Trade returns will show Mr. Woods how erroneous it is t suppose that such goods should be made here. Some doubtless could, but at a greater cost. The manufac- turers buy foreign prodeets,not becanse theyare foreign but because they are better value than can be got at home. Any tariff barrier raised against such goods wil increase their cost to our manufacturers, but it will also raise the price of any home product which competes with the foreign import. The user therefore will have to pay the extra price for both the home manufacture and the imported. It comes therefore to this, that the advantage gained by the protected industry is gained at the expense of the manufacturers or users who buy the product. Where then is the advantage? It merely enriches one class at the expense of another. It is a mistake to think of the nation as being divided into consumers and producers. We are all in some form consumers, and all producers, (I mean all who do any ' honest work at all). The direct manufacturers,who are ' generally i spoken of as ,producers, are con- sumers n a double sense, they are consumers of the products used in manufacture and con- sumers in their private capacity, and I think those manufacturers who are clamouring for Protection scarcely realize what the effect of Protection would be upon the materials, which are raw goods to them but may be finished articles of some other industry. Take for example the industry in which I am engaged, that of tanning, which is one of the elementary class. We use hides and tanning extract to convert the hides into leather. 'lf the farmer in consequence of Protection has to pay more for all he consumes, in justice his pro- duct has a right to be protected,and he has every right, if other industries get Protection, to claim Protection for his hides as well as his corn. The extract manufac- turer is in the same position, and in justice he also has a right to claim Protection against foreign tanning extracts. You cannot have partial Protection without injustice to the unprotected industries. *1 But let us follow the operations of Mr. Chamberlain's plan further in respect to the leather industry. The leather is produced by the tanner ; and goes to the con- sumer, the boot manufacturer, currier, belt maker, &c., and is their raw material. If we understand Mr. Cham- berlain aright there is to be a graduated tax which is to average 10 per cent on imported manufacture. If we start with a duty on hides and tanning extract of 6 per cent, on leather of 10 per cent and on boots of 15 per cent, taking into account the quantities there will be a yield roughly of 10 per cent all round. The advantage to the fanner and extract man will be out- weighed by having to pay more for all he uses. The advantage to the tanner will be discounted by the extra price of his raw goods, and the increased cost of all the accessories to his manufacture, while the hoot manufacturer having to pay 10 par cent extra for his leather will be worse off unless he can get all the extra cost back from the consumer. The 20 per cent on boots will be no compensation to him, for the boots coming into this country are largely specialities, and on the whole do not constitute one fiftieth of the production. There are just enough boots coming into this country to give the stimulus which is so beneficial in keeping manufacturers up to the mark. Presuming the boot manufacturer is no .worse off in our home markets in consequence of dear leather, because he is able to get the whole back in the increased price of boots,then the final effect will be to reduce the purchasing power of every buyer and wearer of boots. If for example by the general rise in prices of all products of our manu- facture through Protection, the man earning 20s. per week finds that he can only buy with it as much as formerly he bought with 17s. Gd. something must be cut off, and where there is little to earn and many to I keep, the cutting down is terribly serious matter. But the shrinkage of the value of the weekly wage to I the earner is only one aspect of the question. The limitation of the spending power means less demand for articles, lessened demand means lessened call for labour to manufacture these articles, which in its turn means more out of work, and increased power to the influences which depress wages. I should like to ex- amine the question from the export point of view say of boots and shoes, but this can keep for the present. t We might merely ask ourselves the question, is an increase to the cost of production likely to help us in exporting? A correspondent who signs himself" An Accountant" asks me to carry my argument against Protection further and apply it to secret processes which indi- viduals or firms may possess. Mr. Woods says in regard to the wisdom of buying anything we can get cheap from the foreigner, "for the sake of reasoning carry this further and say, let us stop all works, and not manufacture anything, and purchase all our goods from the foreigner." Again in regard to my words about safeguarding our mineral resources "as far as wise and practicable," Mr. Woods contends that if I carried this point to its logical conclusion, we should not want any of our ore. coal and limestone, and that our men would starve. Now this style of argument carries little weight. It would be as sensible to say that if I set out to walk to Liverpool, because the road led through Liverpool to the river, that I was logically bbund to follow and walk into the Mersey. I deny that the logical conclusion of any of these arguments leads to the absurd conclusions named above. My argument about the purchase of foreign commodi- ties leads in exactly the opposite direction to the one suggested by Mr. Woods. Instead of stopping our works, and not manufacturing anything, it is to our interest to manufacture all we can to facilitate the exchange of commodities which cannot Possibly be one- sided as suggested by Mr. Woods. You cannot pur- chase if you have no goods to purchase with. I must again bring Mr. Woods backto the point which T clearly stated in my former letter # and which Mr. Woods avoids altogether—unless indeed his last sentenee is meant as a reference to it wherein he says that "his views may not accord with the theories of political economists, but they have been formed in the practical school of business life." I was struck by the following words of a Canadian newspaper commenting on this fiscal enquiry in Great Britain. "There is no possible method of arriving at the results of a proposed fiscal charge in Great Britain or any other country except by the deductive logic which modern economists affect to despise, but which they have neither refuted nor improved upon. British politicians must reason from the known laws of human conduct in commerce and industry for these form the only reliable guidance they can possibly obtain." The question upon which I sought the opinion of Mr. Woods and those who think with him, was, that imports could only be paid for by export of goods or by, service rendered. In a word that imports involved exports. That the one depends unon the other, and the other depends on the one. This is no mere theory.' It is a principle inherent in the conditions of exchange. But if I am wrong in this surely Mr. Woods can put me right. If, however, I ant right, then the contention in his first letter, repeated in another form in a second letter, that imports involve a loss of wages equivalent to the labour spent on the imported article falls to the ground like a palace of cards. If every import involves

n equal value of export the question to consider is whether the labour saved by importing is balanced by the labour spent on the exported goods. Until Mr. Woods addresses himself to this point and we come to an agreement on it, further correspondence will be futile. CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketh, October 28th, 1903.

div.head: INQUIRY.
div.p: THE INQUIRY.
MR. H. ROBERTS J.P. OFFERS £250. Correspondence with the Mayor.

Mr. H. Roberts J. P. has issued a poster, in which he calls attention to a proposal that he has made in regard to theexpenses of the inquiry, in a letter which he has addressed to his Worship the Mayor. The letter re- ferred to reads as follows : Kingsley, Hill Cliffe, Warrington October 27th 1903

, To His Worship, the Mayor of Warringto'n, Dear Mr. Mayor,—lt is very desirable that there should be no further delay in investigating the serious charges which have been so freely made against so many of our public men by the leaders of the Non-trading agitation. I therefore beg to place at your disposal the sum. of £.250 for which I now enclose my cheque, on condition that any of the leaders of the Non-Traders will deposit a similar amount with you. The £5OO thus provided, to be used to defray the expense incurred in retaining the services for the pur- poses of the " Enquiry" of an expert shorthand writer and for transcribing his notesand printing same. If my offer is agreed to, the ratepayers will be relieved of the charges which would otherwise be incurred in this con- nection, and they will also have an opportunity of ascer- taining how far the serious allegations which have been made, are true or false. I am, dear Ma Mayor,faithfully H. ROBERTS.
We have since received the following corres- pondence:—

Town Clerk's Office, Warrington. 30th October, 1903. Sir,—l am directed by the Mayor to state that Mr. H. Roberts's letter to him has been published without his cognizance and to send a copy of his Worship's reply for favour of publication in your issue of to-morrow. The dates speak for thenagelves.—Yours truly. The Editor, "Examiner." J. LYON WHITTLE

Town Hall, Warrington. October 27th, 1903. Dear Mr. Roberts.—in reply to your letter of this day's date I feel that I cannot take the responsibility of accepting your cheque for £250 on the terms you mention. The matter of the enquiry has been left in the hands of the six Commissioners and the Council declines to interfere, and leaves the question of report- ing to their discretion. I therefore return your cheque herewith and would suggest your communicating with the Commissioners direct on the subject.—l am, yours faithfully, J. CHARLTON PARR, (Mayor.)
October 30th, 1903,

Sir,—l am informed by the Town Clerk that the Mayor is sending for publication to-morrow, his reply to my letter of the 27th inst., in connection with the "Enquiry." I haye written to the Mayer a further reply, a copy of which I enclose herewith, and which I will thank you to attach to the clrrespondenle in 0.183.- tion in order that the whole of such correspondence may be before your readers in to-morrow's paper.---- Thanking you in anticipation, yours faithfully._ The Editor, "Examiner." H. ROBERTS'.

Kingsley, Hill Cliffe, Warrington, October 30th, 1907. Dear Mr. Mayor,—Your letter is duly to hand and in reply I can only urge as my reason foraddressing my proposal to the Mayor of Warrington that i , as the ques- tion s one which affects the Government of the town. felt it was my duty to make my proposal to the Chief Citizen of the Borough. I hoped that you would read my letter at the Coun- cil Meeting on Tuesday last in which case, it would not have been necessary for me to have made my proposal public by any other means. Your suggestion that I should forward my offer to the Commissioners is open to the serious objection that certain people might insinuate that, bv doing so, I was endeavouring to unduly influence the Commissioners in regard toany charges concerning my own conduct or that of my firm. lam still prepared to carry out my proposal either through yourself or your successor in office. _ --
Believe me, Dear Mr. Mayor, Faithfully. H. ROBERTS.

div.head: Quoth the Raven, Never more!"
div.p: Quoth the Raven, Never more!"

SiT,—By an act of very great condescension Mr. E. Woods has paid a passing notice to the letters of myself and those whp think with me that his letter in your issue of the 10th was the sorriest exhibition of ignorant imbecility which has appeared in the flood of ignorant imbecility which has deluged the press on the subject of Fiscal Reform. He does me the honour of singling me out for special reference for which lam intensely gratefuland which I assure him is appreciated by me at its true value, but he indicates that he cannot so favour me again unless I will sign my name to my letters. lam sorry that modesty should be such an effectual bar to pleasing Mr. Woods, butl fear I cannot even purchase his favour by doing that. I have never schooled myself to think that "Tis something sure to have one's name in print, i A book's a book although there's nothing n't." However, I may be wrong and this may be only one of Mr. Woods' adroit methods of evading a difficulty, for I asked him "If the foreigners were so generous as to make him a free gift of the 1,000 tons of wire rods about which he complained or whether they were paid for and if so,how?" If he could have correctlyanswered my question and have done so, he would thereby have justified the claim which his letter tacitly set up, of being a, teacher of the people, but inasmuch as he did not do this,l must assume that they were not given and had to be paid for. But how? Now I won't say it is known to Mr. Woods, but it is very generally known to those who have given any serious thought to the sub- ject, that money does not possess a universal function, but that its chief function is merely local and, is con- fined to the country in which it circulates, that it has no inheront value,that it is simply a medium of exchange and that it has no value as moneyin any other country than the one in which it circulates. If then money has no yalue in another country, one country could not c- cept payment in money from another country to which it has supplied goods, no matter whether they be wire rods or anything else. If these goods were not paid for by money, how was payment made? Most likely by other goods or by services or by previous accommoda- tions. For the:sake of my argument I will assume the 1000 tons of rods which Mr. Woods cites are paid for by other goods. If so, how are these other goods obtained? Do they fall down from heaven like the, gentle dew, upon the railway trucks heneath or in the shipholds ? Well, even Mr. Woods will hardly assert that. Their they must be worked or laboured for and if goods of equivalent value to 1,000 tons of wire rods have to be prodticed,it follows that a corresponding amount of labour must be expend- ed, so that the purchase of 1,000 tons of foreign wire rods does not entail the loss on the country that Mr. Woods tries to make out. But suppose it does. Sup- pose we take on credit all that Mr. Woodsasserts,where does he stand? The principal objections raised against a Free-Trader are, that he is a Little Englander, that he favours every country before his own, that he will serve his own self-interest whatever becomes of his fellow-countrymen, and that he has no patriotism. But Mr. Woods stands k condemned on his own confession, that in order that the Longford Wire Co. miy have its di vi's more assured, he buys rods Made abroad and thus as he believes, or does not believe, deprives his fellow coun- trymen of the labour and therefore of the rewards of that labour, of handling and producing 6,500 tons of material. Does this constitute a Big Englander? Is this serving his own country before any other? Is this considering the general interests of his country before his own? Is this that bastard thing called patriotism? If so, I'll have none of it, and I readily plead guilty to all the charges that are urged against those who are not of Mr. Woods' way of thinking. Perhaps I am altogether wrong. An act of this sort performed by me or anyone of my way of thinking may be vice, but be transformed into a virtue when performed by men of Mr. Woods' i lk. It is surprising how Aiese men were indignant at the foreigner being allowed to send goods here that can be sold cheaper than the same class of goods made in this country, and then seize upon every possible advantage of saving a copper or two in the purchase of these self- same goods, the starving workman notwithstanding Yours etc., BASSANI°. .

div.head: MAYOR
div.p: THE MAYOR
THANKED BV THE COUNGIL.
MR. PARR's TWO YEARS'_ SERVICE.

On Tuesday, at the close of the Council meeting, Alderman Surros moved :—" That the best thanks of this Council be presented to Joseph Charlton Parr, Esq.' D.L.,J.P., C.A., for the satisfactory manner in which he has discharged the responsible duties devolving upon him as Mayor and Chief Magistrate of the Borough dur- ing this his second year of office, and for the unvarying courtesy and impartiality displayed by him when pre- siding over the deliberations of the Council. and in his intercourse with its members." He said: lam quite sure that every member of this Council will give his heartiest support to this resolution which I have the honour to propose, because never in my opinion has this Corporation had a Mayor who has been more earnest in his endeavours to fulfil the duties of the office with strict impartiality or more honest in his desire to benefit the borough. When Mr. Parr was approached two years ago by a committee presented by this Coun- cil to request his acceptance of the office he only con- sented to do so because it was represented by the depu- tation that it was the unanimous wish of the Council and the assurance that byaccepting it he would be con- ferring a great benefit on the town. It would be remem- bered that the Mayor on his appointment expressed his regret and the fear he felt that as he had no previous experience in the Corporation work he would not be able to acquit himself so satisfactorily as might be expected, but that, trusting to the generosity of its members and officials to make allowance for any shortcomings in that respect and relying on the promise that every member would do his best to make his year of office as easy and as pleasant as possible, he would do his best to give satisfaction. Now we all know with what zeal and determination the Mayor at once entered upon his duties, and how quickly he made himself thoroughly acquainted with the Cor- poration bylaws and the duties and proceedings of almost every committee. He attended almost every committee and Council meeting throughout the year, and it appeared almost marvellous how he in so short a time acquired more knowledge of the work of the com- mittees collectively than any other member of the Council. (Hear, hear.) To giau idea of the amount of time he deyoted in the inter ‘ts of the public I may just state that the number of his attendances at meet- ings during the first year of his office was 217: (Ap- plause.) During this second year of his office the Mayor has been no less attentive to his duties, his total attendances having reached no less a figure than 183—the average attendance of the members being 98. (Applause). So that with the experience and knowledge he had acquired he has on many occasions been able to give valuable advice to the Council on many important matters affecting the welfare of the borough. And if any Mayor ever deserved the thanks of the ratepayers our present Mayor is certainly entitled to the best thanks We can give him, and I only regret that we cannot induce him to retain the position for another year, if only to give as an opportunity of endeavouring to make his itext year of office pleasanter than the past. (Hear, hear.) In proposing this vote of thanks I would at the same time like to incluiclq in it the Mayoress, who has always done her best to assist the Mayor to make everybody comfortable and happy in connection with the various functions and entertainments they have generously given during his mayoralty. Councillor TINNION seconded the resolution most cordially, and said he endorsed all Alderman Sutton had said. The ratepayers of Warrington, as well as the members of the Town Council, would, he was sure, join in that expression of opinion that during the two years Mr. Parr had occupied the mayoralty his work had redounded to the'credit of himself and the honour of the town. His experiencewas that all who had come into contact with the Mayor had been always treated as gentlemen, and it had always been a pleasure to meet him, and receive advice from him. They were indebted to Kr. and Mrs. Parr, for the many services they had rendered to the borough. (Applause.) The resolution was carried nath enthusiasm, and the MIYOR, in reply, said: I thank you most cordially and from my heart, for the kind words you have given , vent to this evening, especially as they affect the Mayoress, who,l feel, is much more worthy of this vote than I could be, and who, I assure you, will very math appreciate it. I thank you also for the cordial support and kindness I have received at the hands of the Council and especially the respect and deference which have been shown to the chair. We have tried to carry out our duties carefully, judiciously, impartially and efficiently, anandl hope we have maintained the propriety and dignity which a Council of this kind naturally should enjoy. (Hear, hear.) We have had differences, and where is there a council that has not lhad these differences ? ; in fact, we ought to have them; but where there has been any word used, in the heat of debate which in m opinion ought not to have been used, it has been ' unhesi- tatingly and loyally withdrawn, which I have always appreciated. I should like to thank the gentlemen who have proposed and seconded this vote of thanks, and also the permanent officials of the Corporation,who have so loyally assisted me in all the work I have been called upon to fulfil,from the Town Clerk,Deputy Town Clerk,to the Borough Treasurer and Borough Surveyor in fact. I hardly know where to end, as I have re- ceived the greatest courtesy and the kindest sympathy from every officer of the Corporation. I thank all,from the very to to the very youngesto'fice boy. The past two years have been most responsible as they have also been pleasant; and if I can only hope, that they have been useful. I shall feel that I have been amply repaid and know that when I retire into private life, as I shall now do,that I may take with me the friendship of many Heave behind. Although, for practical purposes,l may be removed fromthe sphere of NVarringtnn's action, you may be quite sure that my interest will not flag, and that I shall do ray best and take the greatest interest ill tile good old town of Warrington. (Applause.)

div.head: MAYORAL "AT HOME."
div.p: MAYORAL "AT HOME."
Bust of the King Unveiled.

There was a certain amount of appropriateness in the Mayor and Mayoress Pin awl Mrs. J. Charlton Parr) being "At Home " at the Parr Hall. The spacious hall which bears their name perhaps never looked better than it did on Thursday evening, when 800 guests assembled to pay their respects to the Mayor and Mayoress at this the last social function of their Mayoralty. The guests were received in the body of the hall and as they assembled from 8 o'clock until 9.30, a programme of musical items was sub- mitted. Mrs. W. B.Roberts' Ladies Orchestra played selections of sweet music and there were perform- ances on the piano by Affss Parr and Miss M. Parr, and Mrs. Jackson Holmes. The vocal items included a duet " The Song of the Sirens," by Mrs. W. Peter Rylands and Miss Bleckly, and solos by Mrs. W. E. Atkin, Mr. W. H. Ireland, and Mr. James Monro. Mr. W. H. Payton, Afus. Bac., played the pianoforte accompaniments. At 9.30 the Mayoress performed the ceremony of unveiling the bust of the King which has been kindly presented to the town by the Mayor. The bust is of white marble, and the King is represented in his Coronatfon. robes. The sculptor is Mr. Alfred Drury, and the bust is considered to be a fine work of art. It has been seen and approved by the King. The Mayoress graciously unveiled the bust amid cheers. Alderman SUTTON, on behalf of the Corporation and inhabitants of the Borough, accepted the gift and asked the guests to express their thanks by raising three hearty cheers for the Mayor and Mayoress. This was done with enthusiasm. The MAYOR, in responding, said although that was the last time he had the pleasure of meeting so many friends- in his official capacity he could assure them that if they would not forget him he would not for- get them. (Applause.) During the evening, the Mayor was the recipient of a unique walking-stick, the gift of Mr. Bancroft, It was composed of thousands of used postage stamps which had been compressed compactly together and then turned and polished. A similar stick was pre- sented to and accepted by theaing. The Mayor re- ceived the gift very graciously and was greatly pleased with it. Dancing was afterwards engaged in to the strains of Mr. Alfred Starkey's efficient orchestra. Refresh- ments were provided in the crush room, and the catering was satisfactorily undertaken by Mc. and Mrs. Powys. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
SAD RESULT OF EXCESSIVE DRINKING.

At the Police Court, on Saturday, Peter Taylor, junior, who resides in Water-street, was charged on a warrant with assaulting Kate Chorley. The complain- ant said she was getting dinner ready on October 16th, when Taylor, who is a neighbour, came in drunk and struck her in the face. He would not have struck her if he had not been drunk.—The Chief Constable said that in the interests of the prisoner something ought to be done. He was a respectable man when sober, and was most respectably connected. He had been inter- mittently under medical treatment for twelve months for chronic alcoholism, and the doctor had told him (Mr. Talbot) that it would be a mercy to give prisoner the full extent of imprisonment. His will power had been absolutely destroyed by drink, and he would either commit murder or suicide if he remained outside. Mr. Birchall, the presiding magistrate, said that in prisoner's own interests they would send him to prism for two months.

div.head: BRUTAL HUSBAND'S SMART SENTENCE.
div.p: A BRUTAL HUSBAND'S SMART SENTENCE.

A brutal wife assault was brought before the notice of the magistrates at the Police Court on Tuesday William Cotton, Welsh's yard, being charged with as- saulting his wife on October 24th.—Mrs. Cotton said that on Saturday night her husband was drunk. He assaulted her violently, striking her on the face and head. She had to be treated at the Infirmary. She appeared in the witness box with her head still in ban- dages, and her face was badly swollen and discoloured. —The Chief Constable said the prisoner's domestic record was absolutely ghastly. In June he had three months for drunkenness, assaulting the police, and common assault, and previously he had six months for neglecting his children several times. He had been convicted of assaults on his wife ; assaults on the police and many other offences. He was a lucky Man not to have been brought up on a charge of murder or manslaughter. It had been a mere chance.—Alderman Sutton said the Bench considered it a very bi-utal assault, and prisoner would go to goal for six months with hard labour.
A HUSBAND'S HEARTLESS CONDUCT.--LENIENT SENTENCE":

laillAt the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, John Barry, Halifax-street, was charged with causing his child to be exposed in a manner likely to injure its health. The evidence showed that on Tuesday night, prisoner threatened his wife whilst under the influence of drink, and she left the house clad only in her night- dress and carrying her two days' old baby. The rain was falling in torrents, and the woman had to walk to her sister's house 40 or 50 yards distant.—Prisoner was sentenced to fourteen days' imprisonment.—Mr. A. Browne prosecuted on behalf of the N.S.P.C.C.

div.head: PAIMFUL ST. HELENS DIVORCE CvSE.
div.p: PAIMFUL ST. HELENS DIVORCE CvSE.

In the Divorce Court, on Thursday before Mr. Justice Bucknill, a case was heard in which Dr. Robert Jackson in practice at St. Helens,petitioned for a dissolution of his marriage with Mrs. Cherith Jackson on the ground of her adultery with Dr. Adam Brydon, who had been an assistant to the petitioner. The suit was undefended The petitioner gave evidence that he was married to the respondent on July 15, 1890, at Pimlico, and there had been four children. At one time Dr. Brydon was his assistant, and he was also apersonal friend. He had no reason to suspect anything wrong until a communi- cation was made to him by the governess into whose hands a letter from Dr. Brydon to respondent had accidentally fallen. He then instructed his solicitor to see his wife, and he received a letter from the co-re- spondent, who said he did not wish to defend either himself or Mrs. Jackson. Mr. Brewis, solicitor, stated that he saw Mrs.lJackson at the request of the petitioner and asked her for an explanation. She then admitted misconduct, and said that she had a sincere affection for Dr. Brydon, and would not give him up. Other evidence was given to prove that the respondent and co-respond- ent had stayed together at hotels at Dawlish and Teignmouth, and on this, the suit being undefended,his lordship granted petitioner a decree nisi with costs,and gave to him the custody of the children.

div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
"Y"' BRANCH OF RUNCORN WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE
Assoc I ATION.

The first meeting of the season of this Branch was held on Monday. the 26th inst., in the Greenway-road schoolroom.—Mrs. Baker (president) presided over a good attendance of members. Miss Hay, of the Heswall Branch addressed the girls on individual and united efforts in Temperance work. The musical part of the evening was contributed by the following :—The Misses Handley and Clare, Mrs. Pritchard, and Mrs. Mack. The singing of the Temperance Doxology brought the meeting to a close. DROWNING MYSTERY AT RUNCORN.

On Thursday evening, at Runcorn Police Court, Mr. R. Dobson, coroner, held an inquiry into the death of James Houghton, aged sixty-one years, of Cawley-street, whose body was taken from the Bridgewater Canal on Wednesday. In the pockets of the deceasen's clothing was a small memorandum book, and on one leaf was written :—" October 27, 1902. My dear Leonard,— Will you look after mother and Clara, and all the rest, and forgive aII.—FATHER." In reply to the Coroner, Mr. J. B. Houghton, the son, said be did not know that his father had any treuble.—Detective Mottershead pointed out that although the entry was dated 1902, it was in the middle of memoranda dated 1905. The jury considered there was a doubt as to the writing, and returned an open verdict.

div.head: DAMAGES FOR ASSAULT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: DAMAGES FOR ASSAULT AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn County Court, his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands and a jury heard an action by Julius Pick stock, joiner, of Ellesmere-street, to recover damages for assault from Harry Booth, cab proprietor, and Fred Edwards, a labourer. 'Mr. Madden. barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Mr. Burton) appeared for the plaintiff, axid Mr. Giles, of Chester, defended. It was alleged that Booth aud Edwards assulted Pi ckstock and. Booth knocked him down' andj broke hiscollar- bone and caused him other injuries. The defence was that it was a fair stand-up fight between Booth and Pickstock, and that Edwards had no part in it. In sum- ming up, the Judge described Booth as wearing the laurels on his brow and not a wound upon his body. The jury returned a verdict against Bo oth for £lO damages, and judgment was entered for that amount with costs.

Alexander Phail, an Earlestown clerk, employed at Bootle, was on Thursdayfined 20s. and costs for defraud- ing the London and North-western Railway Company, by travelling from Liverpool to Earlestown with an old ticket, the date of which had been erased. MR. SAM WOODS AND NEWTON DIVISION. _

The officials of the Miners' Federation of Great Britain have just been informed that owing to ill-health Mr. Sam Woods has definitely decided not to contest the Newton Division in ahe Labour interest at thenext Parliamentary election. Mr. Woods has been in ill- health for some time, and at the recent Trades Congress at Leicester he collapsed, and was absent for a day or two.

div.head: EARLESTOWN WAR MEMORIAL.
div.p: EARLESTOWN WAR MEMORIAL.

On Tuesday night, at the Earlestown Town Hall, a number of Lancashire lever watches were presented to the remainder of the Lancashire Hussars and Volunteers who went from Earlestown and Newton-le-Willows as Volunteers to the South African War. The reoipients were : Farrier Quartermaster-Sergeant P. Cameron (watch to be sent to Glasgow), Corporal W. Pilling, Lance-Corporal H. Hutchings, Trooper S. Pickup, Trooper J. Kynaston' Trooper H. Burgess,. Trooper W. R. M'Tighe, of the Lancashire Hussars; Corporal T, Green, Ist V.B. Prince of Wales's (South Lancashire) ; Private W. Owen, 6th V.B. King's (Liverpool Regi- ment). The watch for the late Trooper W. A. Frost (Lancashire Hussars), who died of enteric, was handed privately to the deceased's mother.—Mr. C. B. F. Borron informed the meeting that the Town's War Committee had that evening selected a design for a public memorial. Forty-six designs were sent in, and the one accepted is that of a momument. Gothic in style, with detached columns in green granite, with marble bases on red granite, surmounted by a moulded pediment on which will be the coat-of-arms of Newton-in-Makerfleld in relief, the date of erection, and the names of the troops who took part in the war from Earlestown. The cost a to be about £3OO, and the monument will be erected near the Earlestown Town Hall.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, October 31 1903
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 31 1903
MR. CHAMBERLAIN AS DICTATOR.

div.head: "LEST WE FORGET."
div.p: "LEST WE FORGET."
By RUFUS ISAACS, K.O

There never was a time in recent years when the electorate were called upon to deal with greater and more urgent national tasks. Chief among these is the work of setting the defences of the Empire on a basis efficient and permanent. The state of affairs in the department of national defence revealed by the South African War Commission Report is a condition which no self-respecting people can afford to overlook. It is impossible to calculate the harm suffered by the prestige of Great Britain in the sight of Europe owing to the amazing mismanagement which the im- partial] investigations of the War Commissioners have brought to light. A revelation so astounding cannot have failed seriously to affect our position among the Great Powers, and to diminish that respect in which England had for generations been held. Let us recall some of the facts presented to our rivals and friends among the civilised Powers, who are not usually averse to profiting by our misfortunes, particu- larly when so clearly disclosed. During the summer months of 1899 the eyes •of Europe were narrowly watching the development of that diplomacy which finally toppled us over the brink of war. Those were days of magniloquent phrases and sweeping demands. The New Diplomacy. was in full swing. The attitude of the Government in their relations with Mr. Kruger suggested that the whole of the fighting resources of the Empire were in a state of complete readiness to be used at any moment. What was the real condition of affairs? The War Report tells us that, notwithstanding the dangerous tendency of the diplomatic negotiations, despite the repeated warnings of the responsible heads of the War Office, in the face of the urgent representations of the Commander-in-Chief, the Government persisted in postponing the considera- tion of measures for the war equipment of the Army. While Mr. Chamberlain was occupied in threatening Mr. Kruger the Government, knowing the absolute un- preparedness of the fighting machine, made no attempt to put it in a state of readiness to back up in the field the demands of the council chamber. Incident after incident could be cited during the protracted negotiations to skew the incredible recklessness of the Government; but there is one fact which brings out most clearly not only the sheer indifference of Ministers in general, but of Mr. Chamberlain himself in particu- lar. On August 24th, 1899, Lord Wolseley sent another urgent minute to the Cabinet, advising the Ipostponement by diplomacy of any overt act of hostility on the part of the Transvaal. The Commander-in- Chief sought to gain time in order to make those preparations which were absolutely necessary for the successful undertaking of the rapidly approaching campaign. He saw, as he said in his evidence, that the war had become inevitable; he also knew that we were totally unprepared for hostilities, owing to the refusal of the Government to grant supplies for equipment. These facts were also known, without doubt, to the Government, including Mr. Chamberlain. But what did the missionary of Empire do? Two days after, Mr. Chamberlain went down to the famous garden-party at Highbury and talked about a squeezed sponge, and threatened Mr. Kruger that the sands in the glass were running out. Was ever bluff more glaring ? Was ever bluster more incredible? Mr. Chamberlain knew perfectly well that the military advisers of the Empire had urged the Cabinet to play a waiting game—no effective action could be taken in the then state of the fighting machine—and yet the Colonial Secretary used language gallingly I:provocative of that very condition of hostility which the Government had been urged to avoid?

Again, still keeping to the ignorance and neglect of the Government in preparing for war, Mr. Balfcur de- clared at Dewsbury, in November, 1899 (after the out- break of hostilities),that had he been asked two months before whether it was likely we should be at war with the Orange Free State he would have replied: " You might as well expect us to be at war with Switzerland !" What were the facts at that time ? The Cabinet had been repeatedly warned that the Orange Free State would join forces with the:Trans- vaal in the event of war! Letters, reports, and memoranda had been considered by the Cabinet on this very point, and no member of the Cabinet (pro- vided he was awake) could have failed to become convinced of the absolute certainty that we should find the Orange Free State against us in the field. The most charitable view to take (but none the less ruinous of Mr. Balfour's reputation as a responsible statesman) is that the First Lord of the Treasury was asleep:on several occasions when this question came before the Cabinet. Moreover, as Mr. Balfour would probably be the first to remind us, it was not in his department! This explanation being accepted (if not understood), it is perfectly clear that Mr. Balfour's notions about the condition of affairs were, as he said, those of the man in the street. Think what this means! The Leader of the House of Commons and First Lieu- tenant of the Prime Minister knew nb more about the nation's fortunes, on the eve of war, than Tom, Dick, or Harry in the street ! What, then, is the main conclusion reached on this aspect of the matter by the War Commissioners? The responsible Government of Great Britain entered upon the greatest war in which the Empire ever en- gaged without the slightest preparation for the Her- culean labour. Aware of the amassed stores of the enemy, they yet made no attempt to replenish our own resources (notwithstanding the urgent advice of the authorities concerned) ; conscious of the internal weakness of the fighting machine, they still persisted in the fighting machine, they still persisted in a course of aggressive diplomacy which could only precipitate the hostilities for which we were absolutely unready. Such was the action of a Government which taunts the Liberal party with indifference to the true interests of the Empire ! When that Empire was at its needi- est the Government culpably. neglected to strengthen its resources; and now that its weakness has been revealed the present Government, instead of straining every nerve to mend a deplorable condition of affairs, sleepily ignores the lessons of a great campaign, and is assiduously endeavouring to conceal from the electorate that Mr. Balfour and his sup- porters are being led (or driven) by Mr. Chamberlain through Retaliation to taxation of Food and Protec- tion. It is high time this crowd of muddlers and blunderers gave place to men worthy of the confid- ence of the nation, and capable of performing those great tasks which a reckless and mischievous Administration invariably bequeaths to its successors.
