div.head: Dante Lectures.
div.p: The Dante Lectures.

Mr. Philip H. Wicksteed, M.A., delivered the third of his course of lectures on " Dante" in the Co-opera- tive Hall, on Wednesday evening. He dealt with the history and politics which influenced Dante in his writings. In the course of a graphic description of Florence and its surroundings, he said there was no authentic history of this city until we. came to about the year 1115. The reason why this was such an important year was because in that year Countess Matilda, of Tuscan, died. She governed with such ability and such a firm hand that all the elements of discord and confusion which broke out after her death were restrained by her powerful hand. By close reasoning, the lecturer t xplamed the external conflicts between the citizens on the one side and the nobility on the other. In discussing the position of affairs in the 13th century, the lecturer showed how the com- mercial party in Florence tried to get the formal government of the city in their hands, and also tried to make the government of the city really effective. The trade guilds which made the "commercial party so powerful and useful in preserving order were fully described. These guilds were so highly organised that it was pretty nearly impossible for a man to defy his particular guild. All connected with a par- ticular trade were members of their own guild and it was the custom for persons of the sasne trade to live in the same street or locality. By this means, the particular guild became responsible for order in that locality and they maintained it for the prosperity of the city and the credit of their guild. Although the representatives of the different guilds met and dis- cussed the affairs of the industrial portion of the city and practically governed it, they were not recognised as governors. The recognized governor was one of the nobles, who was generally a Teuton. The feuds which took place between the two and the effect they had upon the writings of Dante were touched upon, and the lecturer concluded by giving in chronological order the course of events between the Guelfs and the Ghibellines from 1248 to 1282.

div.head: GIVE ME A MANDATE.
div.p: GIVE ME A MANDATE.
THEN YOU WILL SEE WHAT I CAN DO FOR YOU.

Food, Taxes, Trade, and Empire. THESE are the chief headings under which Mr. Chamberlain appeals to the workers to support Protection: He says our food will be cheaper, our taxes will be no greater, the foreigner will pay them, our trade will be larger and our Empire stronger. Let us consider some of these propositions.

div.head: Food.
div.p: Food.

MR. CHAMBF,ILLAIN, for the sake of Colonial growers, asks us to tax some of our foods, and he promises us in return to take part of the taxes off tea, coffee, and sugar. Then, he says, we shall make a profit out of the trans- action! Said he at Newcastle: What you lose on bread you sage on tea.
. . . lAsk you to pale 'a transfer of taxes which under no circumstances can cost you any- thing, but which will benefit you to the small extent of 2d. or 3d. per week.

But when you take the tax off tea, you take so much money out of the Exchequer. Mr. Chamberlain reckons he will take about 1:2,800,000, which he is going- to make up by taming goods, or, in other words, by increasing the cost of our boots, shoes, clothes, woollen and cotton goods. Let him argue as he may, juggle with the food taxes as he may, in the end, according to his showing, we shall have to find those millions he promises to take off.

div.head: Preference to Whom?
div.p: Preference to Whom?

WHEN Mr. Chamberlain says he will take the taxes off tea, sugar, cocoa and coffee to square the other food taxes, which will give the Colonies a preference, doe he mean all the Colonies? If so, he will h, e to let in the following goods free:
Tea from Ceylon. India, and other Colonies.
Sugar from the West Indies and other Colonies.

Coffee from India and other Colonies. Cocoa from the West Indies and other Colonies. If Canada is to get a preference on corn and New Zealand on meat, why not the other Colonies for the goods they produce ? If the above Colonies had a preference on tea, sugar, coffee, and cocoa the revenue now derived from taxes upon ;hem would soon disappear! The Colonies, by the help of a preference, would soon cut out the foreigner. Is that not what Mr. Chamberlain wants to do? Well, to do it fairly and squarely all round it would cost the Chancellor of the Exchequer some £12,000,000 of money a year!

The Foreigner Pays. AT Glasgow Mr. Chamberlain told us that it was bsurd to say a tax upon foreign goods was not paid by the foreigner. It is, apparently, one of his strongest points, to try and make people believe that you can put taxes upon foreign goods, or foreign foods, and make the foreigner pay them. There is no doubt Mr. Chamberlain has already thus deluded a few simple-minded souls. Listen to these delightfully simple remarks from Mr. E. M. Pollock, the Unionist candidate for the Spalding division Of Lincolnshire. A week or two ago this gentleman went down to tell the people all about the fiscal question. Said he:

When you talk of a Fiscal Question you are discussing the question as to how the nation's purse should be filled, and as to how the money that is in it should be spent. It is a matter of very broad politics as to whether we should collect the revenue we require to spend on the upkeep of this mifhty Empire from the foreigner at our ports, or whether we should levy it entirely on the dwellers at home.

There you have the Chamberlain theory in all its natural simplicity. Mr. Pollock ought to be Chancellor of the Exchequer in a Chamberlain Government. Then he would doubtless arrange taxes by which the foreigner would, not only pay for the entire maintenance of the Army, Navy, and Civil Service, but also wipe out the National Debt, proyide Old-Age Pensions for everybody, pay house rent and funeral expenses into the bargain! Once you can evolve a scl,eme to make the foreigner pay there is no end to it. The entire British nation could be kept in luxury and idleness while the despised foreigner works and pays. --- Trade.

Ma. CHAMBERLAIN says if we will only tax our food he thinks the Colonies would give a preference and open up to us £26,000,000 worth of trade,. and therefore our trade would be so much larger. He seems to have found it convenient to forget that £10,000,000 of that additional trade .belongs to Canada, on which we already get a preference; a prefer- ence which, in Mr. Chamberlain's own words to the Colonial Premiers, lies been very dis- appointing. Deductim,Y Canada's £10,000,000, me have £13.000,000 of Colonial trade which, under Mr. Chamberlain's scheme, we might try and catch. But does anybody imagine we should collar the lot? If they do, will they explain how it is we have not got all the Canadian trade. ? Since a preference was granted to us the increased imports into Canada have been as follows:

From France £4,200,000 „ ninny ... 4,500,000 „ Untted kingdom ... 16,200,000 „ America ... ... 64,500,000 Preference in Canada has given us next to nailing. Yet according to Mr. Chamberlain's plan, we should risk the whole of our foreign trade for the 'sake of the Colonies. Said he at Tynemouth : Eleven million colonists take from you £5 or £6 per head, while, I think, it is 270,000,000 of foreigners who only take a few shillings a head. It is much better if we can increase the number of our customers at £5 than that we should bother ourselves too much .about our Customers at five or six shillings. Mr. Chamberlain reminds one of the village grocer who boasted that he traded with all the village, while his town cousin could not trade with a quarter of London. But lot us see how much trade we get at £5 a head, and how much at ss. a head. Here are the Board of Trade figures for last year: ss. Foreigners ... £653,325,538 £5 Colonists £224,304,515 Mr. Chamberlain, we know, has peculiar ideas of business but most other people would not go out of their way to risk losing the ss. foreigners. Be Warned.

Reliable information, giving a complete reply to Mr. Chamberlain, can be had from the following books: "Through Preference to Protection," by L. G. Chiozza;Money, post free 4d. "Handbook for Speakers on the Tariff Ques-

tion," post free 7-id: Both can be had from local booksellers, or direct from the Free-Trade Union, 8, Victoria- street, S.W. Another excellent work (price is.) is pub- lished by the Unionist Free-Food League, 15, Victoria-street, S.W., the title of which is "The Case Against the Protection Taxation of Food and Raw Material."

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
ANOTHER LONG SITTING.

The closing meeting of the Town Council for the present municipal year was held on Tuesday at 6 o'clock, the Mayor, Mr. J. Charlton Parr, presiding. There were also present :—The Deputy-Mayor (Alderman J. Feirclough), Aldermen W. Bolton, R. W. Francomb, R. Heaton T. Hutchinson, J. Smethurst, T, H. Sutton; Councillors T. Barton, W. Brough, T. Burton, J. G. Craik, S. Davies, J. Dodds, James Evans, John Evans, L. Ellison, W. J. Forshaw, A. Horrocks, J. Lod, A. Peacock, J. Pemberton, J. Roberts, W. Roge:s, J. Sampson, H. Thornton, D. Tinnion, J. Wilkinson with Messrs. J. L. Whittle (town clerk), S. Wilson (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (deputy treasurer), T. Long- din (borough surveyor), W. S. Haddock (gas engineer), W. H. Grimsdale (electrical engineer), J. G. Glornall (medical officer): J. M. Murray (director of education.) INFECTIOUS DISEASES (PREVENTION) ACT. Alderman SUTTON moved: "That the Mayor, Alder- men, and burgesses of the borough of Warrington,acting by the Council as the Local Authority for the said borough, do hereby gorder that the above' Act (the Infectious Diseases (Prevention) Ac;, 1880) shall per- manently apply in the borough to the infectious disease known as measles," and "that this order shall come into operation on the Ist day of January, 1904." He explain- ed that the order could be rescinded at any time if thought advisable by the Council. Councillox JAMES EVANS seconded, and it was carried. EDUCATION COMMITTEE—TILE VACANCY.

COM:16110r DODDS submitted the usual formal resolu- tion confirming or otherwise such recommendations of the Education Committee as require the confirmadon of the Council. Councillor CRAIK seconded, and the resolution was carried. ALDERMAN SUTTON DECLINES OFFICE.

The Council proceeded to appoint a representative member of the Education Committee in the place of Mr. F. \V. Monks, resigned. Alderman SMETHURST moved that Alderman Sutton be appointed on the committee. He held no office in connection with the committee, and would be a useful member. He had had to do with schools something like 30 years to hisknowledge. Councillor ELLISON seconded. Councillor DODDS moved an amendment to the effect that the appointment be left over until after the November elections.

Alderman SUTTON said as far as he was concerned he would rather be left off the committee. His time was fully taken up with work connected with the Council and that was the reason he made a reouest that he should not be appointed a member of this committee.
The MA.YoR :—Does that mean that you actually decline?

Alderman SUTTON: I think I shall have to do. The motion falling through, Councillor Dodds's amendment was put as a substant;ve motion and carried. PADGATE-LANE TRAMS.---EXTENSION REFUSED Councillor CRAIK moved :—" That having regard to the limited time allowed by the Board of Trade for the construction of Tramway No, 7, viz., 6th August, 1904, and to the improbability of the time being further pro- loaged, instructions be given to the Electricity and Tramways Committee to proceed with the construction of that tramway from the termination of Tramway No. 6to the finger-post opposite the smithy in Padgate- lane." He thought the present time was opportune because the time limit of the Board of Trade would shortly expire, and he was told on the authority of the Town Clerk it was extremely unlikelythey would consent to a further postponement. He did not know why this particular line should hive been left in an unfinished state. All the other routes extended to the boundary. In this neighbourhood pro- peAy was being erected very fast, and there was a large population to be catered for. The route had been well patronized and it would be infinitely more so if the. cars went to the finger-post. If they decided upon the extension it would not be necessary to increase the number of cars or make any alteration in the time of f. ervice. An extensively signed petition asking the Council to make the extension was presented some twelve or fifteen months ago: The number of houses that would be affected, all of which were in the borough was 369, and the population .1,800. To provide for theselpeople and to add to the revenue from the cars demanded the favourable considaradon of the Council. Councillor THORNTON seconded.
Councillor ELLISON said the committee had bad this matter under consideration; and had postponed it for twelve months.

Alderman SurroN said it would be as well if the Council were given some information on the question of expense in making the extension, and also as to the probable income to be derived from the increased number of passengers. Councillor JOHN EVANS called "attention to certain particulars of cost and incom3. The cost per car mile was ninepence. The earnings since the commencement of the sch3me had been 9.498 d. In the last fortnight the Cemetery route had earned £124 12s. 2d., and the Sankey route (a non-paying route) £11.2 17s. id. Sankey route had earned 7d. and Cemetery route 10d. They might safely say that the cost 02 the extra line would cripple the Cemetery route in the same manner that the Sankey route was crippled and reduce the 9.498 d. t 3 something below the actual working cost. He would oppose the resolution by voting against it. Alderman BOLTON, as a member of the Tramways Committee, said they wouldnot recommend the Council to carry this work out. If the Council cared to take' the responsibility upon themselves they could do so. It would not be a paying concern. Alderman SMETHURST said he would vote against the proposal. Councillor Evans had given the figures they h&c' all had, and he did not know how Councillor Craik dared to get up in the Council and propose such an ex- tension after an electioneering speech in the way of retrenchment and reform. (Laughter.) If they passed this resolution it would be one of the greatest blunder:, they had ever committed. rhe Sankey and Longford routes were not paying. Were they going to have a third extension ,suprorted out of the rates ? It was monstrous to p-opose it. Tn the Lovely-lane district there were thousands of houses to the hundreds in the other district, and irste'id of ex- tending the tramways to tbe boundary there it would be far better to go round from the Cemetery and along Orford-lane. The cost of the proposed extemion would be £6,000 or £7,000 and twice the present number of passengers to make it pay. The older members of the Council had been charged with spending money and yet they hada gaitleman who had not been in the Council twelve months preposingo spend £6,000 on this exten- sion. He was a good Councillor. (Laughter.) Had Mr. Craik put his wonderful scheme before the rate- payers be would not have been Councillor Craik to-day. (Laughter.) Councillor TINNION raid in his opinion it was incum • bent upon Councillor Craik to prove that this exten- sion would not be a charge upon the rates. There was no harm done in bringing the matter forward, but he suggested that Councillor Craik should withdraw the motmn until he could bring forward some additional proof. Councillor CR 4 TIC said he was not at all particular about the matter being deferred. He did not know that he could bring forward more in t' -e shape of fresh fa rrts, and be did not see why the proposal should not go for- ward that night. The Corporatiornad been spending money outside the borough at Stockton Heat:), and he did not know why the tramway should not be extended at the Cemetery end of the town. With regard to the twaddle—(laughter) of Alderman Smeihurst about retrenchment and reform and the thousands of houses about Lovely-lane and Orford-lane, he thought it would puzzle Alderman Smethurst to find anything in his address aboutretrenchment and reform. He sa;cl that if elected he would advocate the extension of the tramways in the Ward. (Hear, hoer.) That he was now trying to carry out. If therouncil wished tie resolution to be deferred for a short time he was willing. He should certainly not defer it for twelve months. How were they fixed with regard to the Board of Trade?
The TOwN CLERK : The time :Allowed will -expire on the 6th of August next. Councillor THORNTON consenting, it was agreed to defer the question for a few months.
THE COUNTY AND BOROUGH FINANCIAL ADJUSTMENT.
HONORARIUM FOR THE BOROUGH TREASURER.

The DEPUTY-MAYOR movefl the confirmation of the Finarce Committee's minutes which stated that the Borough Treasurer laid before the committee the order of the Local Government Boardadjusting the firarcial relation between the County and the Borough. It was resolved that the committee desire to record their appreciation of the able services rendered by the Borough Treasurer in connection with the satisfactory settlement of the claims of the County and the Bo:ough and thatan honorarium of fifty guineas be voted to him for such services.

The DEPUTY-MAYOR read the following statement in regard to the firancial adjustment, I feel that some reference should be made, to the two resolutions. The Memorial to the Local Government Board to constitute the borough into a county borough, was presented in November 1899; the inquiry was held on the 15th February 1900, and the Order granted on the 9th May. 1900. Prior to the inquiry the County of Lancaster sent in their claim for £47,797 for compensation for Iseverance under the Local Government Act of 1888. IDuring the past three years many intcrviews have taken place between the Financial Officer of Vie county and our Borough T.:3asurer with the rewlt that the county claim was reduced to £7,177; our claim against the county eventually reduced this amount to £24,000, which was finally agreed upol, and which the Finance Committee believe to bea vary $ )t:sfactory settlement.. (Hear,hear.) The position in shc:t is as follomn :—For thethree years prior to our becoming a county borough we paid to the county a sum equal to a rate of 41d. in the 2 ; we are now able to me 3t all the expenditure formerly paid by the county, r,nd to repay by instalment the £24,000 agreed to be paid without calling upon the rates for more than 4d. in the 2. (Hear, hear.) The grant to us from the county for technical instruction under the Local Taxation Act.

1900, averaged for the last three years as a Non-County Borough £590. We now receive the contribution direct from the Government, and for the year endin-r 31st March, 19G3, it amounted to £1,005. There is nodoubt that the fact of ourbecorning aCounty Borough will be 'of great financial benefit to the town, and we have moreover, got rid of the control bythe County Council inall matters of Technical instruction, and it will pre- vent also the overlapping, which would occur in the administration of the new Education Act. From these remarks, it will be seen that the adjustment has been in hand forsome considerable period during which time the Borough Treasurer his devoted himself to the matter with such assiduity aud skill that the Committee felt it only due to him that such services shaald be recognised in the way proposed by the resolutions. (Hear, hear). Councillor PEMBERTON: I move that the money be paid to the staff. The DEPUTY-MAYOR: Certainly not. Mr.Fairhurst did the work. To my knowledge he saved the town 24,000. Councillor PEMBERTON: He is paid for it. Councillor W. ACINSON: He is not. I know he has been busy many and many a night, and has slept on that work. (Hc .r, hear.) Councillor DODDS: I should like to endorse what hos been said ab: ,t the Borough Treasurer. (Hear, hear.) I should a'L like the Council and the public to know that I myself proposed this honorarium of £5O. I know what the work has been, and what pains Mr. Fairhurst has : ike„-. The town has gained by what he has done, and rather tha i he should not be recompensed I am prepared to pay one-filth of the amount myself, if the motion is defeated, (Applause). The minutes were then carried unanimously. THE "OLD CROW."

Alderman SUTTON said, the purchase was for the widen- ing of Market-gate. It was decided that there should be a larger circle, and this was one of the buildings they would have to pull (1(3%1. Councillor PEACOCK asked how far the "Old Crow" was back from Bridge-street. The TOWN CLERK said the committee had already purchased Messrs. Holmes and Booth's shop, and this property was immediately behind. If they wanted to rebuild they must buy the land behind. Alderman SMETHURST supported the minutes and emphasized the necessity of securing" back land." The minutes were then passed. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

Tii-e-Min-u-tes were confirmed. THE INFIRMARY.

Alderman Bolton proposed the adoption of the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committees minutes which stated that a deputation consisting of Messrs. F. Monks, Charles White, and Dr. Fox attended to ascertain whether the committee would grant the trustees of the Infirmary an additional piece of land for extensions. In was pointed out by the commibtee that any exten- siors on the gardens would necessitate the removal of the new greenhouses, and they regretted that they were unable to recommend the Council to grant the site. Aldertran SmErHußsr seconded and the minutes were approved. RIVERS COMMITTEE—THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME.

Alderman BOLTON proposed the minutes of the Rivers Committee, including the report of Sir John Wolfe Barry and J‘the resolutions of the committee on that report, both of which appeared in the" Examiner" last Sai,urday. 'lite scheme would give them a ;letter river, more dock- age, and 8 feet of water at all times. Councillor TINNION secondr d. Councillor LORD asked a question with regard to the raising of the water L'me 2/ feet. How would that effect Vote navigation under Warrington bridge? Alderman BOLTON, in replying, said the raising of the waLer was only at low water. DuLton-street would never be flooded again, owing to the drainage of the Ship Canal. Mr. Norbury Williams had said that the whole matter depended on the con-

structionlo be placed on the words "the prod - iings:' He would like to point out that the original draft of the committee's report presented to the Town Clerk containedlthe stipulation that a full report of "all the proceedings" was to be taken. He was not going to say that the committee intended that a full report should be transcribed and printed, but it was their intention that a shorthand note should be taken of the whole of the proceedings. The Town Clerk, in recast; ing the committee's report had left out the word "all.- He suggested that the matter should be referred back again to the Council for further instructiong,. The TOWN tLERK said it was quite true that he did alter the form of the words as stated by Councillor Tinnion. He left out the word "all," but he failed to see any distinction between the words. div.head: WARRINGTON BETTING CASES.
div.p: WARRINGTON BETTING CASES.
Bookmaker and Tout Fined.
WHAT THE POLICE‘INTEND TO DO.

Thomas Travis, who resides at 5, Stoney-yard, ap- Peared at the Warrington Police Court on Monday in opswer to a summons charging him -with frequenting tlrrPley-walk, Stanley-street, Shuttle-street, and Friars' een for the purposes of betting on October 16th and zast. Mr. Steel represented the defendant who pleaded gililty to the second charge, but denied the offence alleged to have been committed on the 16th. The Chief Constable stated that- on October 21st, the 2ecasion of the Gatwick and Newcastle meetings, de- lft:dant was seen to take seven slips and sums of money lo Stanley-street and three slips in Friars' Green. A 3r°lliig man named Miller, who would give evidence, was seen to make a bet with him. Constables Whittaker and Clough were watching defendant and ulti- ately followed him into the "Star and uarter" beerhouse where he went along with a Ilian named Dempsey. Defendant went to the olice Station with the officers and on the way handed c'ver a number of betting slips and Bs. in cash. He admitted that he was betting and made a state- Ment to the effect that he was doing so on his own oecount. in regard to the other charge the officers saw def at Indent receive slips and what appeared to be money the end of Arpley walk. He received four slips in rluttle.etreet and a large number of people followed A__lll,_ down Arpley Walk and returned immediately. 6141rr Miller made a bet on the 16th and saw other People bet. P. C. Clough was called and gave evidence as to the betting Attie 16th October. Arthur Miller, wire worker.4,Hart's Place,said he made o, bet with the defendant on behalf of another person. Mr. Steele contended that the police had not made out their case. The magistrates must have it on sworn facts that defendant was using the ktreets for betting .4nlrPoses. The only evidence was that the officers, stand- -100 yards away, had seen defendant receive slip& 4-11ey could not swear that money was passed. „„ Chairman (Mr. F. Monks) said the magistrates ;Lem quite satisfied that the defendant was guilty and `44e3' would inflict the full penalty of £5 and costs in 'each case. John Dempsey, 5, Twiss yard, who was also repre- zented by Mr. Steel, was then charged with aiding and abetting Travis on October 21st. The Bench, on the advice of the cl erk, over-piled a Preliminary objection by Mr. Steel that a pershn could Oot be:summoned for aiding and abetting inn breach of bye-law. The bye-laws said Mr. Steel were made for the goodlgovernment of the town, andwere not on the Statute Book. The Chief Constable said street betting was a crimi- offence, and it was possible to aid and abet any criminal offence. The Chairman: I think Mr. Steel's logic is at fault. The Chief Constable said it was alleged that the defendant was standing at the corner of Friars' Green, Which, as a strategic position was a masterpiece, for it commanded every approach to Friars' Green—and their /lame was legion. Persons went to him and had con- .versations with him and he pointed with his stick towards where Travis was standing. These people were th,„eil seen to go to Travis and hand him money and 'llPa. When a policeman in uniform appeared in the neighbourhood, .Dempsey "heliographed" with his stick ,to Travis who immediately disappeared until the danger mid blown over—or walked away. (Laughter). . _

The witness Miller then deposed Lo being directed to Travis by the defendant. Mr. Steel said he felt the Bench would be istraining the law very much indeed in allowing a conviction for aiding and abetting book-making. Defendant was not a tout or runner for book-makers. He was ,b,..ern on Friars' Green and had lived there all his life. tie was a cripple and unable to follow any regular em- ployment and he therefore did work for people living in Stanley-street. He stood at the corner of the street in order to be within easy call of the people. Before the magistrates could convict there must be proof that the defendant was in the employ of a book-maker and was kept there regularly for the purpose of directing people to the bookmaker. No such evidence had been offered.

The Chairman said he was very sorry Mr. Steel had made these remarks. They implied that the magistrates were acting unjustly and unfairly. That was entirely foreign to their intention. There might at times be a miscarriage of justice through a pure technicality but Mr. Steel was at perfect liberty to appeal against judg- ment they gave. He thought in common fairness Mr. Steel migh accept their judgment as being an honest 'one and Intended to comply with the Act of Parlia- ment.

Mt--; Steel said he did not suggest that the magis- trates were uujust—far from it. It rested With Mr. White-to interpret the law. He (Mr. Steel) thought it 'was straining the law to summon people for aiding and abetting an offence under a bye-law. The Chairman: We exercise our judgment within the limit of our discretion. I don't think it is a fair remark for you to say we are straining the law. We take into account the •circumstances surrounding the case and the evidence given. If you want to go further into the easel should say "You prove what the object of these men is in assembling like this in a public street, signalling to one another as soon as a policeman aPPears, and getting away as soon as possible." What Possible object can they have if they are not betting? Mr. Steel pointed out that it was not inonmbent aPon him to prove that. The Chief Constable said he laid more stress on the Present prosecution than on the other. The difficulties °f the police were enhanced a hundred-fold by conduct $.311011 as they alleged in this case. He might say for the !nformation of people who aided and abetted bookmakers, 1214 the crusade of the police would be extended much '4°re strongly against them than against the book- -the Chairman said with regard to the plea that defen- z‘,rit Was a poor 'man, it was within the knowledge of "le Bench that all the fines inflicted were paid by a 4Yndicate. Mr. Steel: I don't know that. Defendant was fined £5 and costs.
LOCAL IMPROVEMENTS.
WARRINGTON'S "TERRIBLE LEGACY."
More Expenditure on Street Works.

At the Warrington Town Hall on Tuesday, Mr. H. Ross Hooper' M.A., A.M.1.C.E., conducted an inquiry on hehalf of the Local Government Board into the application of the Corporation for sanction to borrow £lO,OOO for works carried out under the Private Street Works Act, 1892 1£18,315 foripurposes of public street improvements, and £1,750 for the purposes of Sankey Recreation Ground. The loan for private street works is necessitated by the decision of the Council to ex- tend the time for the repaymont of private street accounts to seven years. The public street improve- ments are in Bridge-street and other parts of the town. With reference to the Sankey Recreation Ground, Lord Lilford has given two of the four acres acquired for this purpose.—Major C. E. Norton should have con- ducted the inquiry but was indisposed. The TOWN CLERK explained that the population of the borough was estimated at 66,000, and the annual assessable value was £223,113. The outstanding loans under the Sanitary Act amounted to £227,568 and £8,432 was sanctioned but not yet borrowed. The INSPECTOR: Your liability will really be £236,000? The TOWN CLERK replied in the affirmative. The BOROUGH TREASURER: We have in sinking fund against that £5,775. The TOWN CLERK said the rates at the present time were 7s. 4d. in the £ which included 9d. for educational purposes. A penny rate would produce £930. The INSPECTOR asked if there was any opposition to the applications, but none was forthcoming. STREET IMPROVEMENTS.

The TOWN CLERK pointed out that with regard to the application for permission to borrow £lO,OOO for private street works, most of that sum was required for works already carried out under the Private Streets Works Act 1892.

The INSPECTOR said he should require full details in regard to. the expenditure on each street. He asked what period the Corporation applied for for the repay- ment of the loan. The TOWN CLERK :, Ten years. _

The INSPECTOR: 1 don't think you will get it. The BOROUGH TREASURER said they were constantly lapportioning the expenditure on the streets so that while they were paying off one loan they were piling up another. They were constantly borrowing. He was going to suggest that they should have a kind of float- ing borrowing power, not to exceed £lO,OOO, and the amount that was received from the owners would be paid directly into that account. The INSPECTOR: That is a matter which we are not. considering. The time you will be allowed for repay- ment will probably have some connection with when the work was completed and many other questions. The TOWN CLERK said about 100 streets were con- cerned in the application. The INSPECTOR I said the Local Government Board had no information as to how the money had been expended except the statement from the Town Clerk that it was for private street works. Each point must be taken in detail in order that he could be quite satis- fied that the conditions imposed by the Act had been fulfilled. The TOWN CLERK agreed to forward certain inform- ation in regard to the dates on which the money was spent and the amounts which have been repaid, to the Local Government Board. The -amount already spent, he said, was £8,700. _ .
The INSPEC TO it then proceeded to consider the applica- tion for sanction to the borrowing of .C 18,315 for public street works.

The TowN CLERK said that all the purchases of property had been agreed to by the Council. The INSPECTOR pointed out that there was no resolution of the Council in regard to the cost of road-making Sze. The TOWN CLERK said he would get a resolution formally passed if the Inspector desired it. The INSPECTOR : I should like that to be done. The TOWN CLERK said the period asked for repay- • ment was fifty years. The BOROUGH TREASURER saidithe Board had pre- viously granted the Corporation permission to borrow money to be repaid in that period. The INSPECTOR asked what necessitated the improve- ments. The TOWN CLERK said the Council had passed a resolu tion that all the main thoroughfares should be at least 60 feet in width. For what were termed secondary streets they had prescribed a width of 50 feet, and for other streets as required by the bye-laws a width of 40 feet. In 1896 the Board gave the ,Corporation an order under which they had power to' prescribe a building line wherethe streets were narrow and inconvenient. They had taken advantage of the Act to prescribe a building line throughout all the streets and it was in a great measure in consequence of that that the application was made. They had gone through all the streets of the borough and prescribed lines according to the resolution of the Council. The Corporation had purchased five out of the fourteen lots of property by public auction. Some of the property bought would not be re- quired for the improvements and there would be land for re-sale. The TOWN CLERIZ and other officials then proceeded to give full details of the whole of the improvements. At a later stage the TOWN CLERK informed the in- spector that since theapplication was sent to the Board the Corporation had agreed to purchase two other blocks of property. He asked if it was the desire of the Board that the Council should apply for the sanc- tion of the Board to the borrowing of money for small purchases. The INSPECTOR said he could riot answer in regard to that policy. The Town Clerk had better write the Secretary of the Board.

div.head: WARRINGTON'S TERRIBLE LEGACY.
div.p: WARRINGTON'S TERRIBLE LEGACY.

The INSPECTOR asked if anyestimate had been formed of the cost of the improvements to the Borough. The TOWN CLERK said £270,000 had already been spent and it was estimated that a further expenditure of £200,000 would be incurred. The INSPECTOR: Has all the money expended been borrowed from the Board? The TOWN CLERK : Most of it. It is a terrible legacy to have to spend all this money on unproductive work. We could not have tramways for many years owing to the narrow streets. The INSPECTOR: How long will it be before the widening of the streets is completed? The TOWN CLERK : lam afraid it would have to be a guess. lam afraid even to guess. The INSPECTOR : Have you gone in for any com- pulsory powers? TheTow's CLERK: We are carrying out compulsory powers in regard to Bridge-street. The INSPECTOR: There are no compulsory powers in regard to the streets before me this morning? The TOWN CLERK replied in the negative. "I am hoping " he continued "to survive long enough to see some of the improvements carried out, but Tam getting a little bit doubtful. I have had some of them in hand myself for over twenty yes. THE PROPOSED RECREATION GROUND AT

div.head: SANKEY.
div.p: SANKEY.

The application to borrow £1,750 to providea recrea- tion ground at Sankey was then dealt with. The Town Clerk said the period asked for repayment was fifty years. The Corporation undertook when Little Sankey was included in the borough to provide the recreation land. They had acquired four acres of land, two being presented by Lord Lilford; and the remainder would be purchased at a cost of £875. The district was very thickly populated and the ground was much needed. The land was free hold and there were no restrictions except as to fencing. The inquiry then concluded.

div.head: SIR JOHN BRUNNER ON TRADE AND EDUCATION.
div.p: SIR JOHN BRUNNER ON TRADE AND EDUCATION.

Sir John Brunner, M.P. addressed a demonstration of railway workers at Northwich on Sunday afternoon. England would never progress, he said, until education was made cheaper, more valuable, and more available to the masses. The best way to improve our trade was to raise the purchasing power of the people. The ex- ploded notions of Protection and Retaliation were not the methods by which level-headed mel ought te work to mend affairs. If the distribution of voting power in Germany was fair, if every vote had an equal value, there would to-day be a Free trade majority, in the Reichstag. To allow the manufacturers to dictate the price of their wares was the worst thing which workers could do. French and German wages were low, because the workers had no chance to getmore. English wages were maintained by freedom. In alluding to the need for social legislation,Sir John,declared that rates and taxes sbauld be imposed upon the real and not upon the fancy value of land.

"Thomas Longshaw, clerk in the Water Department states :—.on Saturday, the 26th, September last, I gave the letters to Mr. Dens, who sat down at his desk and immediately called 'Tom.' I went to him, and he said Look what I have done. What do you think we had better do with it' (producing the envelope)? I said Endorse it and leave it as it is,' but he said 'You had better take it to Messrs Evans and explain.' I accord- ingly went straight away to Foundry-street and asked for Mr. London but he was not in. I saw his chief clerk and told him my business, and gave him the tender, which he put in a drawer and locked. I promised to callivain, which I did, and saw Mr. London about 1.45. The tender was then taken from the drawer and given to him in my presence. He tore the remain- ing portion of the envelope open and went up to his private office with the tender in his hand. When he came down from his office he offered the tender re- addressed but I said he had better have it delivered at our office. I can positively say that Mr. Deas did not take the tender but of the enve- lope or see it in any way. Mr. Gray atm prove that it would have been impossible to have taken the tender out as the envelope was not opened sufficiently. We could only guess that it came from Messrs R. Evans and Co., by the post mark being on the envelope. There was no name on the envelope." "James Gray, assistant waterlengineer.states:—l was presantlwhen the envelope containing the tender of Messrs. R. Evans and Co., was brought out of the Water Engineer's office by the witness Longsliaw. I examined the envelope, which had been partially opened. The tender could not be taken out without the envelope being still further opened. It was impossible for Mr. Dens or anyone else in the department to have seen the tender. Councillor DODDS asked for the date of the tender.

Alderman FRANCOMB said the first tender was delivered on the 26th September, and the meeting was on the 28th. Continuing, he said he wished to go into the matter thoroughly. (Hear, hear.) Mr. London's name had been brought into the matter. That gentleman had been 40 years with Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., and for 20 or 21 years he had been the manager of the Foundry-street office and yard. He (the alderman) asked for his version of the matter, and it was given as follows :—"44, Foundry-street, Warrington, October 26th, 1903. Dear Sir,—ln reply to your favour of the 25th current, re opened envelope. This was seen by our tw. clerks before being handed to me, and mu.- book- keeper remembers distinctly the, appearance of the envelope. We enclose one to give some idea of the condition in which it was received by us from the Water Office. We took the letter out of the envelope , to put it into a new one, but did not read the cvntents, when the clerk who brought it suggested that we had better leave the tender in the torn envelope and enclose the whole in a new one, which we did. If the letter had not been opened, we think it would not have been sent us to seal afresh. We did not tear theenvelope thel slightest bit, and our book-keeper can confirm what we say.—Yours faithfully, Richard Evans and Co., Ltd. (Edward London), It. NV. Francomb,Esq., Wilderspool." , Now added Alderman Francomb, he would refer to the tenders. He noticed that they advertised for washed slack, and when the tenders came before the committee on the 28th they did not know they had been opened accidentally, wilfully, or in any other way. The com- mittee thought that all was straight and above board. Richard Silk sent in a tender which was not for wa,shed slack, and the committee decided not to take iv4ice of ' it. The Wigan Coal and Iron Cempany sent in for washed slack, but did not send the sample which was asked for in the newspaper advertisement, anl the 4om- mittee said they would keep strictly to the letter and ' CEslovamacnkpsab anunyt d Woodcod. that they must go out. Messrs. Richard Evans and yi t notsolau slack and s.teon send in sayin fitnahiartn et sfhsoorto v v oiNwolde sa s shpreisdt slack gave every . ,idthPe satisfaction during the last contract they had,had with the Committee. He was sorry to find that the word " washed " slack was put in. Messrs. J. Pendlebury and Co.. put in for washed slack, and sent a sample. The Slate Company put in for washed slack, and sent a sample. He asked Mr. Dees to have the samples there, so that the members could inspect them, but they had not been brought. The assistant, however, had gone for them. Messrs. Pendlebury and Co.'s samples were what were called washed peas —about as big as the top of a pencil. The quality might have been good, and he was not going to say a word against that. The Slack Company sent in a much larger sample, ranging from the size of Pendlebury's up to a walnut. The committee thought the sample was very much better. Besides, Messrs. Pendlebury's price was 9s. 4d. for the washed slack, and the Slate Company 9s. Therefore the Slate Company got the order. As a committee," said Alderman Fran- comb, "we are exceedingly sorry these things are happening, and I must say that if I were outside the Council I should have serious thoughts about things going on in a very irregular fashion. lam thproughly disgusted with it and I should like to see the whole of the Water Committee, with myself, clear out, and others put in our places." Councillor LORD: Are we in order in discussing the question? The MAYOR: lam told you are not in order.

Alderman PRINCOMB then moved the adoption of the Water Committee's minutes.—A meeting was held on October 23rd, having been specially convened for the purpose of hearing the explanations to be given by the Water Engineer in reply to the questions put on the agenda for the next meeting of the Council by Mr. Councillor Lord with reference to the tender of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. Ltd.,having been opened previous to being submitted to this committee. The Engineer submitted a written explanation that he had inadvert- ently partially opened. the envelope, but had not taken the tender out, and immediately on finding out his mistake had sent one of his clerks to the local agent of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., explaining the circum- stances, and requesting that it should be put into another envelope and returned to his office. Mr. Dens also tendered two witnesses to corroborate his state- ment, and after considering the matter it was resolved, that while the committee are satisfied that Mr. Dees had opened the envelope inadvertently, they are of opinion that he was guilty of carelessness and expressed strong disapproval of his action in the matter. The Engineer was then requested to retire from the room, whereupon a discussion took place with regard to the unsatisfactory manner in which he had performed his

Alderman SUTTON said he didinot intend for one moment to support the action of Mr. Dens in this matter; but, at the same time, he did not ithink that we ought to act rashly towards him in any way. Con- tinuing Alderman Sutton said: I thinklit is veryprobable indeed that he may have endeavoured to open this letter inadvertently, and that he found out his mistake before he had opened it entirely. We can all understand that it places the Water Committee in a very difficult posi- tion, because, after all that has transpired on another occasion, it would look as though they were giving Mr. Dens sanction to do things which were altogether im- proper. But, as I have said, he may have done this thing inadvertently, and finding out his mistake, instead of going to the Chairman of the Committee, he goes to try and put it right by induceing Messrs. Evans aud Co. to put it .in another envelope in order that it might appear in a proper manner before the committee. Now, we must not forget that Mr. Dens has had a considerable amount of work to do during the last year or two. This may have affected his health and his nerves to such an extent that he was, scarcely responsible during the last few months for his own actions. On that account I should say we should deal justly with him. (Hear, hear.) It is only recently that many members of this Council have shouted for justice in relation to other servants of the Corporation, and there has been an endeavour to grant that justice; and therefore, why should we not, under these circum- stances, be lenient in a case of this kind, and believe the statement of Mr. Dees that he had no evil or cor- rupt intention whatever in regard to his action inopen- ing this letter. I should suggest that instead of dealing with him in the way the amend- ment proposes, that he should be satisfied by the resola- tion-that has already been passed by the committee. I say: Give him a chance, that chance Avhich so many of you have been asking for, for other servants of th e Corporation; and let us deal out the same justice to one as you would have dealt in all cases. (Hear' hear.) can feel for Mr. Dens, and if it is through illness brought on by excess of work I think we ought to con- sider his case in a fair and reasonable way,, and if he does not conduct himself during the next three months to the satisfaction of the committee then I say let the notice be put in force and carried out. (Hear, hear.) Councillor JOHN ROBERTS thought the resolution o f the committee would meet the case. He did not think for a moment that it was Mr. Deas's intention to open the envelope, and considering the state of his health some consideration should be shown towards him. _ _
Councillor PEMBERTON asked what--Was—t-Ee—cia-e upon which the Warrington Slate Company's tender was received.

Councillor TIN-mos: And the data upon which Messrs. Evans's tender was received and opened. Alderman FRAxcomß stated that the tender of Messrs. Evans and Company was received en the Saturday morn- ing and the tender of the Slate Companyon the Monday morning following. Councillor PEMBERTON said then he had great pleasure in supporting the amendment moved by Coun- cillor Dodds. In dealing with this question they had not to look simply at that individual case, but at the unsatisfactory state of. the proceedings of the Water Committee for some time past. He vas a member of the committee, and he had not been satisfied with the way its business was managed. What they had to look at was the way Mr. Deas had been setting the com- mittee at defiance on other occasions. The Chairman of the Water Committee had in that Council on several occasions said that he could not support the action of that official. If the business of the Corporation was going to be carried on as it ought to be carried on they must exact that service from their officials that was necessary for a public body of that description. This committee had met once a fortnight—the average time being thirty minutes once a fortnight—twelve hours a year. That only showed the tremendous amount of responsibility and trust that was placed on their officials, and the need for their marked action if any official violated that trust in any way. He contended that the business did not receive sufficient supervision from the officials, but when he had brought the matter forward in committee he had been insulted. Everything ought to be carried on fair and square and above hoard, and the officials ought to obey the dictates of the committee This gentleman (Mr. Deas) seemed to have been his own master and the master of the committee, and in his own opinion there was no other way to deal with the question than by carrying Councillor's Dodd's amendment. Against the evidence of the two clerks as to the letter they had Mr. London's letter. (Hear, hear.) He did not want to say too much about Corporation clerks, for they were in a very awkward and unfortunate position—a position with which he sympathised, and a position in which they ought not to be placed. (Hear, I hear.) Tt was a difficult thing when the head of a de- partment called one into his room and said "Did I do ! this or that ?" If the clerks were put in that position they as a Council ought not to allow it—(hear, hear)— unless they appointed a committee to guarantee their protection. The Council should set its face once and for ever against the practice of the head of a depart- ment getting letters from subordinates in support, of ! his actions. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Sutton had imide a great deal of the extra work Mr.Deas had done,but the Corporation had employed two highly qualified gentle- men to assist Mr. Deas in all the work that had been ! carried on in the way of water extension all the time it had been going on. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Loft!) said he would like to know what was the last date for receiving tenders. A VorcE : The 28th September._ -
Councillor LORD, continuing, said a lot had leen said

div.head: Examiner, Saturday October 31, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday October 31, 1903.

duties during the past few months, whereupon it was resolved "That an intimation be conveyed to Mr. Deas that unless he paid greater attention to the duties of his office and carried out his work during the next three months to the entire satisfaction of the committee he would be called upon to retire from the position of Water Engineer; and that the Town Clerk be instructed to obtain from Mr. Deas a written acceptance of these terms, failing which a legal notice terminating Mr.l. Deas's services in three months be given to him." Alderman HUTCANSON seconded.

Councillor DODDS moved as an amendment " That the minutes of the Water Committee of October 23rd. be referred back, and that the conimittee be instructed to forthwith give the necessary three months' legal notice to terminate Mr. Deas's services." He said that after the serious irregularities which had come before them month after month, and now that the worst case of all had arisen, it was necessary that the Council should deal in a drastic way with Mr. Deas. He was very sorry for him personally but as a public body it would be disgraceful on their part to allow him to go on longer and continue to bring them into such messes. The town was seething with suspicion in regard to this and similar matters, and unless they took up the present case in the way he proposed, he was quite sure that the Council would be blamed. He (Councillor Dodds) had opened hundreds of letters every day for 25 years,but helthought he had never .opened a letter belonging to his chairman.lf he had done so did they thinkhe would he have gone to the one who had sent the letter and asked him to put it in another envelope? Would he not rather have gone to his chairman? He did'nt want to be suspicious and suspect Mr. Deas, but he could not accept the explanation that because a little bit of the envelope was opened and the enclosure could not be reached it was desirable that he should go back to the parties and get them to put the tender into another envelope. Mr. Deas's diity was to have gone to his chairman and he(the speaker)was sure the chairman would have accepted the explanation if the letter was in such a state that the contents of the envelope could not be got at. He (Councillor Dodds) proposed the amendment without any hesitation whatever and he appealed to the members on all sides to support him. He was against many of them in some matters, but he hoped he had friends here. He believed the majority of the mem- bers wished to do what was right and best for the town, and he asked them to join with him in passing the amendment and let the town see that they were deter- mined to set their faces against the conduct to which he had referred, and that as far as they were concerned it should be stopped at once. Councillor JAMES EVANS seconded the amendment. If Mr. Deas had wished to clear himself in the eyes of the committee he should have taken the course suggested by Councillor Dodds. Painful as it might be to him, he (the speaker) felt constrained to second the amendment. Councillor JOHN EVANS said that after what had occurred he was sure the Chairman of the commit- tee would accept the amendment. He strongly sup- ported it. Councillor TINNION said an insinuation appeared to have been thrown out with reference to the accept- ance of the lowest tender. He should like to know the dates upon which the tenders of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., and the Slate Company were received. It was only fair to the Council that they should have that in- formation. He was not present to apologize for Mr. Dens; he only wanted the matter considered in a calm and dispassionate spirit. He hardly thought the action of Mr. Deas,which he was not going to defend for one moment, had for its object the giving of informa- tion to other people. They should call a spade a spade, and if a man had done wrong they should charge him with it, and there should be no insinuations or inuendoes about something he had not done. (Hear, hear.) He had come to the conclu- sion that what Mr. Dens had done was nothing more or less than gross carelessness in opening the tender. He did not think that he or anyone in the office saw the tender. It was an unfortunate thing for Mr. Dens that he had made this mistake. It was a gross hlunder,and the punishment would be very severe, probably more than most of them would care to inflict upon one of their own officials. He thought the matter might be referred back without the express instruction to dis- miss Mr. Dens. If the Council desired that Mr. Deas should be dismissed they should take the responsibility for such a course andnot refer the question to the com- mittee. It was not right to ask the committee to deal with the matter with their hands tied.

about Mr. Deas's condition. It might, therefore, be , interesting to know what Mr. Deas was really suffering 1 from. There seemed to be a misconception in the town as to what it was. They might also be told what holi- I days he had taken to recruit his health during the past I two years.

Cotincillor THom.--roN commented upon the difference —which amounted to a contradiction—between the letters of Mr.Deas's assistants and. Mr. London's letter. Was nothing to be done in the shape of an examination of the two clerks?

Alderman HUTCHINSON, referring to what Alderman Sutton had said with reference to giving Mr. Deas another three months' trial, remarked that they had had Mr. Dens a good many years as water engineer. The duties had been very heavy for the last few years, and considering the time he had been with them he thought it would be reasonable to give him another three months' chance rather than take such a drastic course as to give him notice. If the amendment was carried his hopes would be blighted for ever almost. The committee had decided to give him three months' trial, and if that did not prove satisfactory he must leave. That, he thought, was only reasonable, and he would support the committee. Councillor Pemberton rather under-rated the time the Water Committee spent on business in twelve months. Councillor Pemberton had, he noticed, attended 20 out of the 30 meetings, and that was a fair average, but still he might have attended more. The committee met at three o'clock and the Markets Committee came on at 20 minutes to four if they had finished by that time. That put the time of meeting at 40 minutes, and the meetings sometimes lasted longer. That would bring their work up to much more than 12 hours inl2 months. He wished to put Councilor Pemberton straight on the matter. He thought he might speak the truth. Councillor PEMBERTON took exception to the re- mark, and observed that there were times when the Water Committee had not sat 15 minutes. Councillor WILKINSON said that if Mr. Deas had been guilty of the action insinuated that night, instant dis- missal was what he deserved, but it had not been proved to them that he did open the letter wilfully, and they ought as men to believe that he had done it inadvert- ently. Whatever the cause of Mr. Deas's illness was he did not defend his conduct at all, but they ought not to stamp him guilty straightway. Mr. Dees opened the letter, and when he found that he had done so, he sent it to Messrs. Evans and Company, and the fact of his doing that showed to his (Councillor Wilkinson's) mind his innocence in the matter. If he had wanted to "cook" the thing he would have gone to the Chairman of the committee and told him thathe had unfortunately partly opened the letter and asked him to take the matter in hand. He (the speaker) was sorry he could not vote for the drastic measure proposed by Councillor Dodds. They had already taken from Mr. Deas the management of the sanitary works, and that meant a loss of £2OO a year to him. He had therefore not so much money to spend, and to use an old saying, be would be "able to stand his corn."

Alderman BOLTON thought they might give Mr. Deas the benefit of the doubt. The letter in question was not sealed with wax, and if it had been it could not have been mistaken for an ordinary letter. The fact of its being opened by a knife showed that it was not intended to be opened for a wrong purpose, as in that case it might have been steamed or something of that kind. He thought it could be left as the committee suggested, because if he was found not capable of doing his business properly, Mr. Dens could be discharged. Councillor DODDS : I don't know whether I wave a right to reply to the discussion or not- The MAYOR: lam instructed that you have not. _
Councillor DODDS : When referring-to the matter, I included irregularities which had gone before and which, backed up by this, make it impossible to draw back.

Alderman SMETHURST said he was much grieved when the matter was brought up. He could tell Councillor Pemberton that he had himself attended 191 meetings last year, or 40 more than the highest member except the Mayor (Hear, hear). He did not like Coun- cillor Pembertonsaying thatithey did not attend to their business.

Councillor TINNION remarked that this was either a slight fault on the part of Mr. Deas or a very gross misdemeanour. If Councillor Dodds did not think this was an accident his inpendment did not meet the case. If he believed that what had been done had been done with an intention, and that intention was not honest he ought -to say that Mr. Dens should be in- stantly dismissed. Councillor DODDS: I made no suggestion of that kind. Igo on the facts. Councillor TINNION : It is insinuated by those who sit around you, by the sniggling and giggling that has been going on, that there is something behind that has. not come out.
Councillor JAMES EVANS : No such thing was in my mind.
Councillor TINNION : I did not say in anyone's mind. It was in several minds.

Councillor JAMES EVANS : I object to an inference of the kind. I have a right to second an amendment without being suspected of improper motives, and if Councillor Tinnion will keep within the limits of the debate Ifiave no objection._ -

div.head: SLACK CONTRACT.
div.p: THE SLACK CONTRACT.
THE WATER ENGINEER'S POSITION.
" Guilty of Carelessness."

Councillor LORD had again several pertinent ques- tions to ask of the Chairman of the Water Committee with reference to the slack contract, at the meeting of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening. His questions were as follow :- 1. Is it not a fact that Messrs. R. Evans and Co.'s tender was opened two or three days prior to the time fixed for the Water Committee to open and con- sider tenders for slack for Wiuwick and Delph-lane for a period of six months from October to March next?
2. Is it not a fact that the tender was addressed to the Chairman of the Water Committee and endorsed "Tender for slack?"

3. Who opened the tender, and what authority had he for so doing? 4. Is it not a fact that the tender was returned to Messrs. R. Evans and Co.'s local office with the original envelope cut open with a request to re- envelope and re-address? 5. Who returned this open tender to Messrs. R. Evans and [Co's local office, and by whose authority was it returned? •

6. Was the chairman made acquainted with the fact that this irregularity had taken place, an,d was it mentioned to the committee when the tenders were opened and considered? 7. What were the prices contained in Messrs. R. Evans and Co.'s tender, and the accepted tender of the Warrington Slate Co., Limited? Alderman FRINCOMB answered the questions as follow :—No. 1, Yes. No. 2, Yes. No. 3. Mr. Dens opened the tender and he had no authority to do so, and he says he did it inadvertently. 4, Yes. Mr. Deas says the envelope was only slightly cut, and that it was so small that no one could possibly take from the envelope the letter it contained. 5. Mr. Deas returned the open tender to Messrs Evans's local office by one of his clerks. He had no authority from anyone to do so. 6. To that I say " No.' The chairman knew nothing about the matter until some days after the contract was settled,and the information came from Mr George,:the Secretary of Messrs. Evans andCo.'s Haydock Collieries.Thave no recollection of it being mentioned when the tenders were opened. 7. Messrs. Richard Evans' price was 9s. id. per ton, and the Slate Company 9s. per ton. eAlderm.anrrancomb!added that Mr. Deas's explanation was as follows :—" The tender of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., was addressed to the Chairman of the Water Committee and properly endorsed, and was received by the Water Engineer with other letters on the Saturday morning previous to the meeting of the Committee on the Monday. The envelope containing the tender was partially opened by the Engineer inadvertently, but not opened sufficiently for the tender to be taken out. The mistake was at once found out, and as a matter of fact the tender was not taken out of the envelope, or seen by the Engineer or anyone else. The Engineer immedi- ately sent one of his clerks to Messrs. R. Evans and Company's local agent explaining the circumstances and requesting that it should be put in another envelope and returned, which was done accordingly. The Engineer did not think it necessary to bring the matter specially under the notice of the chairman or Committee." He had (continued Alderman Francomb) a letter from one of Mr. Deas's clerks, who declared that he saw the envelope only just slightly open. He had another letter from another clerk corroborating that. Several MEMBERS: Read them.
Alderman FRANCOMB read the two letters as follow :

Councillor TINNION said he would try to do so. If this was a gross misdemeanour on the part of the Water Engineer three months' notice was not what he de- served. He should be instantly dismissed, but if he had simply made a mistake, to give him three months' notice was more than the fault deserved. Mr. Deas had done efficient service for the committee, and if during the next three months he proved himself efficient he should still remain in the service of the Corporation. He (Councillor Tinnion) would never be a party to ruining any man. Let them give Mr. Deas an oppor- tunity of retrieving his character. (Hear, hear.) Alderman FRANCOMB skid the two assistants were brought before the committee and examined and it was decided "That while the committee are satisfied that Mr. Deas had opened the envelope inadvertently, they are of opinion that he was guilty of carelessness and expressed strong disapproval of his action in the matter." Mr. Deas was then asked to retire from the room, and after a discussion they came to the further decision that appeared in the supplemental agenda intimating to Mr. Deas unless he carried out his duties during the next three months to the entire satisfaction of the committee he would be called upon to retire from the position of water engineer. The voting then took place on Councillor Dodds' amendment, and resulted as follows :
FOR THE AMENDMENT. AGAINST. Councillor Davies Alderman Sutton
