div.head: 'NE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: 'NE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
NEXT MONDAY'S CONTESTS.

Monday next will witness contests for seats on the Town Council in six of the nine Wards of the borough. Messrs. Charles Roddy and Samuel Gough, who were nominated for Howley and Whitecross Wards respec- tively, sent in notices of withdrawal on Monday, leav- ing the following candidates in the field : Wards. Candidates. TowN Ham, Councillor Lord, WHITECROSS Councillor Barton, BEWSEX Councillor 'NV. Pierpoint, { Councillor Peacock, Mr. F. Stott, Mr. W. J. Shaw, f Mr. John Ashley, IMr. John Maginn. f Councillor Hulse, I Mr. J. Povey. f Councillor John Evans, 1 Mr. W. Benson. f Mr. James Critchley, 1 Mr. T. H. Ashcroft. • f Mr. NV. J. Wilson, IMr. S. B. Stringer.
ORFORD
ST. JOHN'S
FAIRFIELD
ROWLEY
ST. AU ST IN'S
LA.TCIIFORD

The only addition to the list published last week is the name of Mr. W. .T. Shaw who is one of the three candidates in Orford Ward and has the support of the Non-Trading Committee. Mr. Arthur Peacock, the re- tiring represcatative, is busily prosecuting his cam- palgn and has issued an illustrated circular explaining his scheme far the provision of a recreation ground be- tween Orford-lane and Winwick-road. )Jr. F. Stott is making a hi& for the seat in the interests of labour and the contest is arousing much interest. The paing stations are as follows:— Orford 'Ward: Silver-street School. St. John's Ward: The clubroom, Jdhn-street. Fairfield Ward: Fairfield Infant's School, off Man- chester-road. Howley Ward: National School, Church-street. St. Austin's Ward: Calro,street Infants' Solaeol, and Thewlis-street Infants' School. Latchford Ward: St. James's School, Old-road, and Christ Church School, Wash-lane. NON-TRADERS' MEETING.

Spetches in Parr Hall Last Evening. Parr Hall was again crowded last evening when a meeting was held under the auspices of the Municipal Non-Trading Association. Mr. James Dodds presided and he was accompanied on the platform by Mr. Norbury 'Williams, Mr. Conecillor Pemberton, Messrs. Hulme, Kenyon, Benson and Ashley. THE CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH. Mr. Dorms, who was cordially received, said:— Ladies and Gentlemen, At Tuesday's Council meeting, a letter was read from ex-Alderman Monks, in which, ml there and then stated, that gentlemanraade an ungener- aius and an uncalled-for attack upon your four or five representatives, his clear purpose being to discredit them and to insult you, the great majority of the rate- payers, who -elected and sent them to the Council to do -the very- things the'ex-Alderman condemns. I told the Council I should direct your attention to the unworthy attack of this gentleman, 'alto, although a member of the Council for 13 years, never once faced a contest for his seat, never once made a single protest against the immoral and illegal doings which we have already exposed, and has never once had the fairness or the courtesy or the justice to acknowledge the invaluable services rendered to the cause of publiapurity arid probity everywhere by you the ratepayers of Warrington. For the work of purify- ing yourCenncil has been your own. You elected the Non-Trading members, you sent me by the largest majority of all, although there is not a single elector that can say that I ever asked him for his vote. Let me therefore remind Mr. F. W. Monks that when he attacks me, he attacks the people of Warrington who are behind me, and who sent me and others to the Council to help to bring to an end the reign of Tammany against whose encroachments he never even lifted a hand. (Applause). 'Well, he has gone, like many others of the trading stalwarts and their slavish satellites, he has passed away. Our little-systems have their day, Thar have their day and cease to be, and although some of these men have ren- dered in some respects, some service they will ever carry the consciousness and the shame of having been the opponents, instead of the friends of the best work ever done for Warrington in the regeneration of its public life. But gentlemen, we had yesterday a sensational event, a deposit of £250 with the Mayor by one bearing a well-known name, to be:used as a contribution, provided a similar contribu- tion of £2lO be made by a Non-Trader or the Non- Traders, for the purpose of defraying the expense of the inquiry. Has it struck you that this is a -rather singular proposal to come from one whose brother, a lawyer, threatened the Non-Trading members with criminal proceedings if they voted in the Council. for the. inquiry. (Hear, hear.) am. myself, a com- paratively poor man, but the fight against immoral trading,, and to secure an inquiry, has already cost me snore than the sum named, and on the best authority I am told that -an inquiry on the lines laid down. by Messrs. L. Greening and A. J. Jolley would cost from £54300 to £B,OOO. Hence if ourgenerous friend had sent £2,500 to the Mayor it would, as I am advised, have been a more rearenable.antount. On this very subject, I have this morikng received a question, among others, anti under registered cover, from a Mr. Warren, aid in further reply to him I think I can submit a pro- posal which ought to commend . itself, and will commend itself to all !honest men. My pro- posal is this, that every gentleman who has been a member of the Council' between April Ist, 1896 and March 31st, 1903 (the period of the inquiry) shall execute a guarantee under which he shall be liable to pay at the conclusion of the inquiry, so much of the total cost of the inquiry, as shall bear the same propor- tion to-such whole cost, as the amount of his trading, through private firras or Limited Companies, direct or indirect, bear to the total value, of all such trading. Untlerthis proposal, if it came out that the total cost of the inquiry was £6,000, the total of all trading done was £lOO,OOO and my own or any firm's share of that total•tradina was £50,000, then I would have to pay 22,.1C1D towards the cost of the inquiry. I and my -colleagues are quite prepared to execute such an under- taking and to.abide by it; if Mr. Henry Roberts and his friends -will do the same the question is solved. (Applause.) If he or his firm has done no crarling he will have nothing to pay, If 116 or his firm have done any trading he will pay on his proportion of the total trading done over the 7 years. We shall now see whether this chal- lenger really means business. But, gentlemen, we, who have fought for two years for this inquiry, intend to have it, but we are not going to put you to expenses which are altogether unnecessary, as was so clearly shown at our last meeting, when you unanimously ap- proved the action of oar Commissioners. Talking of inquiries what think you of the revelations brought cut at Tuesday's meeting of the Council? When I got private information some three weeks ago, and put the matter of the latest slack tender scandal into the bands of Councillor Lord, I little thought the nesult would be so damning as the details were brought out-on Tuesday night. T was shocked, it made my blood boil to think that so soon after the re- cent Contract Scandals and notwithstanding that the town has been shocked thereby, and was seething with suspicion, occurrences such as those brought out by Mr. Lord's questions should be possible. (Applause.) Mr. Lord will deal with this matter later, I will only ex- press my deep regret that my amendment was defeated by two votes. You will notice that on that matter, as on the new street question, your elected representa- tives were defeated by those miserable aldermen who voted solidly against us although they represent only the discredited party compact. We thought the com- pact was dead. Ah ! we were wrong. Do you not see the trail of the serpent in every contested Ward, and especially in Howley Ward where the Liberal party leaders have passed a resolution not to oppose the Tory brewer and publican candidate? Your few members in the Council, sadly too few; have been struggling in your sole interests throughout the past municipal year, against these very men—thatis the remnant of the compact party led by Alderman Sutton and Francomb on the Tory side, and by Councillor Tinniim on the Liberal side backed outside by such men as Mr. W. Furness, the treasurer of the Liberal Association, constituting the most insidious and least scrupulous of all the 'opponents of the Non-Trading cause. I see the last named party has been giving his blessing to Mr. John Maginn, who is still determined to carry on his campaign byl characteristic and wanton unscrupulousness. A few days ago in regard to myself, be so misquoted my words as to entirely misrepresent my meaning Those of _you who heard me at our last meeting here know that I never called down the vengeance of God

upon voters Ivhc: did not vote as I thought. Nothing o the kind. I indicated that the vote was a sacred trust for which we were responsible to God, and that to use it improperly would be highly wrong. I also said, but in a separate sentence, that to vote for a man for no .other reason than that he had subscribed to children's I vicnies, or to um institution in which you are interested, I would be positive corruption, and I should think . •se. (Applause.) At the declaration of the St. John's Poll a few months ago Mr. iVlaginn , in my hearing ta.nce insulted the ratepayers of that Ward by saying be had been defeated by I wealth, prejudice and ignorance. If he meant any. I thing, he meant that wealth had been used against him, a shameful insinuation against the electors—and in using the word ignorance be cannot.now—struggle as he may—wriggle out of the only possible 9onstruction it carries namely a gratuitous and gross insult to the intelligence of the people of St. John's Ward. (Hear, I hear.) I .G.lnnot nor will I believe that after the way in which -Mr. Maginn was defeated last July any event I that has happened in the interval can have so influenced the free, independent and self-respecting electors of St. John's as tG endanger the purity cause in that great and important murd.—And so in relation to all the otb,er mrds we slat ask you to vote Conservative,

Liberal or Labour. We don't want to create a new and separate party; we want to so mould, guide and lead men of all parties in regard to our own vital question. which is that no man, whatever his political or other views' shall seek, gain or utilise a public position for personal gain or personal ends. I ask you to do what ' you can by working, by canvassing, and by voting to leave no stone unturned from to-night until next Mon- day night at 8 o'clock in your efforts to secure the return only of those candidates who may be safely relied upon to work and vote to secure and to maintain the pure and honestfadministration of the public busi- nessof-Warington. (Applause). THE CHAIRMAN ANSWERS A QUESTION.

The CHAIRMA.N, in replying to a question by Mr. A. Warren, 10, King-street, as to why he opposed the in- crease of £5O a year to Mr. Madeley and on the other hand was in favour ofi a donation being given to the Borough Treasurer of 50 guineas, said he opposed the 450 to Mr. M.adeley because the duties for which he received it were beiag done by another man who was receiving a larger salary for doing it. He also objected to it because it was being paid in an irregalar way—it was done in an underhand, surrep- titious way. With regard to the honorarium to Mr. Fairhurst, he (the Chairman) believed the Borough Treasurer thoroughly deserved it. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Fairharst had done an enormous amount of work and after the Corporatien had promised to pay a certain sum to the county, Mr. Fairhurst stuck to his points and reduced that sum by thousands of pounds. He assured them that if the ratepayers of Town Hall Ward objected to that vote he was prepared to resign his seat. (Applause.)

div.head: MR. HULME'S CRITICISM.
div.p: MR. HULME'S CRITICISM.

Mr. HULME criticised Mr. Maginn's statement that a member of the Town Council was entitled to his fair share of trading, and said he would like to know who would be called. upon to decide what was a fair share of the trading. (Laughter and 'applause.) Referring to the offer of Mr. Roberts, he said if a Non-Traderhad had as much trade with the Corporation as hadthe com- pany with which Mr. Roberts was connected, it was quite possible that he would be able to put down the other £250 that was required. (Hear hear.) If the people of Warrington wanted an inquiry—and he believed they did—they were independent enough to pay for it —(applause)—so long as it was conducted on reasonable lines. (Hear, hear.) He thought Mr. Roberts had strangely misunderstood the spirit and feeling QR the people of Warrington. (Hear, hear.)
• Mr.. KENvON £h3n addressed the meeting. COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON AND CORPORATION OFFICIALS.

Councillor PEMBERTON reviewing the rules which were drafted for the guidance of the Inquiry Com- missioners, said they were very careful not to embark on any wasteful expenditure. There was no necessity, he said, for a shorthand report of the preliminary investi- gations,but they were determined to have one, when the witnesses were called and the inquiry really com- menced. It would cost, he said, £lOO a week to report and .print the preliminary investigations and they might as well throw their,mon.ey down the gutter as spend it in that way. Dealing with the proposed new street, Councillor Pemberton said if the land had belonged to a workingman they would never have heard of the new street. (Hear, hear). He had given notice to rescind the resolution passed at the last meeting. In defending the conduct of tram conductor Spencer in having a bottle of beer in his possession, Councillor Pemberton askedamid a great outburst of cheering whether they ever saw any of the heads of the Corporation departments going into the Lion hotel during working hours? In conclusion, Councillor Pemberton said it was not only trading, di- rect and indirect, that they had to stop but also one of the greatest curses—the commission business,condemned by the Lord Chief Justice (Hear, hear).

div.head: SPEECH BY MR. NORBURY WILLIAMS.
div.p: SPEECH BY MR. NORBURY WILLIAMS.

Mr. NORBITar WILLIAMS referring to the arrange- ment inWarrington of appointing committees, said it wasas old as the hills. It was absurd to have one man on eight committees and another on two and it could only be done in Warrington and a few other places he knew of. There ought to be a distinct understanding,as in Manchester, that members were placed on a certain number of oommittees whether they were Aldermen or Councillors. (Hear, hear.) Alluding to the record number of meetings in Warrington on this question,Mr. Williams said no town could hold the candle to it for continued enthusiasm in a great cause. (Applause.) One fact or in the present situation,l he said, was that three Non-traders had gone in unopposed: and another factor was that the three Roberts's had gone and so far as !the Town Council was concerned—gone for ever. (Applause.) So far as he was concerned—and so far as every member of the committee was concerned— they had not the slightest animosity against Mr. Roberts or anybody else. (Hear, hear.) When the , Non-traders spoke severely of the action of traders they were only referring to theirpublic conduct. (Hear hear).Speaking of Mr.Maginn's candidature,Mr. Norbury Williams said that Mr. Maginn had given utterance to certain things about him (Mr. Williams) which to put it mildly were not quite accurate. Amongst other things he had said that he (Mr. Williams) had attacked Mr. Parr and called him anything but a gentleman. That was entirely incorrect. He had never entertained anything but the kindest sentiments towards Mr. Parr. He had gone so far as to say that they were under a great obligation to him for undertaking the Mayoralty. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Parr might have made mistakes but he had stepped into the breach in the most kindly and public-spirited way. He (Mr. Williams) did not want the people of Warrington and particularly the Mayor in his last days Of office to think that he had said anything which could be con- strued into .anything like unkindness to Mr. Parr as Mayor. '(Applause.) Alluding to Mr. Maginn's offer of £3OO towards the expenses of the inquiry, pro- vided a Non-Trader made a similar offer, Mr. Williams said they did not want John Maginn's money for either a picnic or an inquiry. (Laughter.) What was more they would not have it. (Applauee). Mr. Maginn knew little of public life, or he would not insult the people of Warrington by making these ridiculous offers. They were going to have an inquiry. (Hear. hear.) Let that be understood in Warrington. (Applause). He had the kindliest feelings towards the three gentlemen appointed by the Corpora- tion to make the inquiry, but in a public sense Ihe believed they had no public sentiment behind them, and were not entitled to involve the ratepayers into a large expenditure for & shorthand note. He characterised the.offer of Mr. Roberts as an outrage. The paltry sum of £230 would be swallowed up in ten days whereas the investigations might last six, eight or ten months. In a closing word, Mr,Williams appealed to the electors to support the Non-tradinr, candidates The meeting terminated with a vote of thanks to Mr. Williams on the proposition of Mr. Ashley.

div.head: MR. MAGINN AND THE "NON-TRADERS' INCONSISTENCY."
div.p: MR. MAGINN AND THE "NON-TRADERS' INCONSISTENCY."

Last evening Mr. John Magian addressed a meeting of electors of St. John's Ward iu Brick-street Mission. Mr. S. Wright, J.P., presided, and contended that the Non-Traders were not acting as friends of the working- men in opposing the candidature of Mr. Fred Stott in Orford Ward. He attributed the Non-Trading agitation to personal differences between "Dodds and Co." and members of the Council, and expressed the opinionthat if an inquiry were held the town would come out of it with credit.

Mr. MA.ortol said he had been threatened with legal proceedings for a statement which Re made on Monday night. In order that the other side might have a good case he would repeat it. He went on to state that Mr. Henry Thornton was a shareholder in a company which did business with the Corporation and gave particulars of a recent con- tract. He also criticised Councillor Pemberton's connec- tion with Messrs. Artingstall and Co., Limited and contended that these;were evidences of the inconsistency of the Non-Traders. Mr. Norbary Williams was referred to as the "Manchester basoon ' and Mr. IVfaginn said that Warrington ought to be able to work out its own salvation without the assistance of Manchester. Speak- ing of the needs of the Ward he strongly advocated a recreation ground, a branch library, and a pnblic hall. On the motion of Mr. Kilduff, seconded by Mr. Forster, and seconded by Mr. Delaney a resolution in support of Mr. Maginn's candidature was passed. MR. F. STOTT'S CAMPAIGN.

An enthusiastic meeting in support of the oandidaL ture of Mr. Fred Stott of Orford Ward washeld in the Co-operative Hall, Winwicit-street, last evening, under the presidency of Councillor Upson. Addresses were delivered by the candidate, Mr.J. Bruce Glasier, I.L.P. organizer, Councillor Short, of Bootle and others.

div.head: WARRINGTON MALE VOICE CHOIR. Annual Concert.
div.p: WARRINGTON MALE VOICE CHOIR. Annual Concert.

From the musical point of view the third annual concert promoted by the Warrington Male Voice Choir and held in the Parr Hall on Monday evening was a distinct success. The only cause for regret was that the attendance was not nearly so large as the excellent entertainment merited. The numerous powerful attractions in the way of entertainments which have been provided of late were doubtless in a great measure responsible for the disappointing attendance. The members of the choir are to be congratulated upon the progress which has been made. Their singing, on the whole, did them great credit and was cordially appreciated, by the audience. The part songs were rendered with taste and expression, one of the best efforts being "The Britons" (D. Protheroe). The solo was admirably sung by Mr. Corrin. Mr. S. Hassan wielded the baton with ability. The vocalists were Mies Annie Nelson (soprano), Madame Alice Berten- shaw (contralto), and Mr. Cuthbert Allan (tenor) 111 of whom found great favour with the audience. The humorous element was entrusted to Mr. Ernest Hastings who was eminently successful in his efforts to create hilarity. His account of the Irish walking contest in which "no one walked at all" was particu- larly good. The duties of accompanists were efficiently discharued by Mr. J. Tinkler and Mr. J. Atkinson and Mr. Tinkler's piano solos contributed in no small measure to the evening's enjoyment.

MR. PARR AND FAIR TRADE.

There is another interesting letter which has been published in the Warrington" Observer." It is a letter written by our respected friend the Mayor in, I believe, 1887 on this very question of Fair Trade, and it is very significant. Mr. Parr writes : " At the same time I think that Fair Trade to be fair must embrace all trades and industries alike and that to give protection to the artisan and manufacturer while you deny it to the agricul- turist would be manifestly Unfair. The effect on the farmer would be to enhance the cost of all he has to buy, but without giving him any compensating advantages for what he has to sell. Thus our great agricultural community would be pro taut° placed in a worse position than at present. Therefore until the Fair Trade (which I suppose means modified pro- tection) can be evenly distributed among all classes I cannot think it would be fair or advantageous to

it unciaubtedly certainamount of risk. But in regard to the benefits that all of them derived from Free Trade he felt there was no doubt whatever. He felt that on this question—whatever they thought of others— they were standing on a sound and solid rock. (Applause). He trusted that they would remove pro- tection out of the way and that the matters referred to by Mr. Crosfield, which unfortunately had been thrust aside by this policy, would be pressed forward. He hoped Mr. Crosfield would have health and strength of mind and body to lead them in the fight that they hoped to make in maintaining Liberal principals in Warring- ton. (Applause.) Mr. GEORGE WALLINGTON seconded the vote of thanks and said he felt very strongly on this Free Trade question. Ths fiscal proposals reminded him of the epitaph :—" I was well.; I would be better ; here I am.' (Laughter.) It seemed to him that Mr. Chambe- rlain's proposals afforded nothing in the way of im- provement. He had better leave well alone. (Hear, hear.) As a family man *he (Mr. Wallington) had studied what the effect of the proposed fiscal changes would be on tlie household expenditure and he found that the increased cost would be at least eightpence or tenpence a week, independent of the taxes on foreign meat. The moment they started this system of tariffs no one could tell where it would end. He was pre- pared to bear the ills we had rather than fly to that which they knew not of. Mr. Chamberlain had made many egregious blunders, as for instance his under- estimation of the cost and duration of the South African war. Mr. Chamberlain prophesied before he knew and therefore made great blunders. He (Mr. Wallington) could not see the wisdom of making it dearer to buy things when we were manufacturing for the world (Hear, hear). It was absurd to talk of the foreigner paying the tax. The consumer had to pay the extra cost and also the cost of collection and every thing else: (Hear hear). It was a false policy altogether and was calculated to make our last position worse than the present one. (Hear hear). The vote was carried unanimously. The chairman responded, and then proposed a vote of thanks to the secretary a proposition which was carried unanimously. Mr. PE mEER,TON, in acknowledging the compliment, said that was the 17th time he had introduced the annual balance sheet. They had gone through dark days in the past and at one time the debt was £552. He was pleased t.) say they were on the right side to-day. ( (Hear, hear). I The proceedings then terminated.

the country generally to introduce it, in a partial, an uneven, and unequal form." Well that is a straightforward, and from Mr. Parr's point of view a forcible statement of the case—a statement which with a million menemployed in agri- culture would have very considerable weight at election time, in country constituencies. Mr. Chamberlain says his policy is quite simple. Ali, well, we know that simple policy which comes from Birmingham. (Laughter) We remember it in '9swhen Old age Pensions were trotted out and dangled year after year before the constituencies (Hear hear). But Mr. Parr's proposition for a mild dose of Protection all round—it is always a mild dose to start with—is perfectly intelligible and its consequences were per- fectly simple. It just means dear food and dear goods, and a general increase in the cost of living. (Cheers). And what becomes then of Mr. Balfour's half way house? It is neither wind! nor weather proof (Hear hear). Founded on the sands of philosophic doubt (laughter) it is bound to be swept away by the tor- rents of Mr. Chamberlain's eloquence. (Cheers).

MR. CHAMBERLAIN HAS CAPTURED THE TORY PARTY for protection, and a very serious fact that is. (Hear, hear.) And if he had his way one very simple and also very serious consequence would follow. The purchas- ing power of the whole nation would be reduced. You would then be able to buy less with a sovereign than you can now buy with 17s. 6d. (Hear,hear.) And then follows a question which to fe plain man seems to go to the very root of the controversy. If the purchasing power of the sovereign is reduced all over the country then your whole consumption is reduced in the home market which, mark you, is five times greater than the export trade. • That means less manufacture, less trade and less demand for labour. (Hear, hear.) Does that point to a rise in wages? (No.) Mr. Chamberlain began in his earlier speeches promising a rise in wages: but I suppose that would not do for employers of labour, and so now he is promising more work instead. I think if you are prudent you will accept these pro- anises and statements with a large grain of salt. (Hear, hear.) Well, if this revolution in our fiscal system is rotten economically, it is just as unsound from an Imperial point of view. (Hear, hear.) Lord Rosebery has pointed out with almost impassioned eloquence the folly of sowing the seeds of jealousy and discord by introducing these financial differences into the Imperial household, and as he scornfully asks, "How can you build up the Empire upon a schedule of restricted indus- tries?" It has been suggested that some people have thought this "raging and tearing propaganda." was going to be a sort of sponge to wipe out the whole records of the Government. (Hear,hear.) Well we are not going to have those records sponged out. (Hear, hear.) Let me very briefly touch upon a few questions which con- cern us all, and which most vitally concern the members of a club like this, which is composed of 90 or 95 per cent of working men.

div.head: ANNUAL MEETING. Speeches by Mr. A. H. Croslield and
div.p: ANNUAL MEETING. Speeches by Mr. A. H. Croslield and
Mr. C. E. Parker.

Mr. John Wormll presided at the annual meeting of the Warrington Liberal Club, held on Tuesday evening. Unfortunately, the prolonged meeting of the Town Council kept the Liberal Councillors away. There was however, a good attendance and amongst those ' present were: Messrs. A. H. Crosfleld, C. E. Parker, S. J. Beaman, W. Ford, J. G. Chappell, C. H. Hibbert, G. Beard, E. A. Sanders, G. F. Freeman, G. Wallington, John Harrison, T. Locker, S. W. Jeffery, A. H. Sanders, 3. Russell, J. Birkhead, G. H. Shaw, John Davies, T. Pemberton (hon. secretary), and G. H. Lamb (manager).

div.head: GIFTS TO THE CLUB.
div.p: GIFTS TO THE CLUB.
The CHAIRMAN apologised for the absence of Coun- cillor Tinnion and Councillor Wilkinson, who were engaged at the Council meeting. Mr. Thomas Pember- ton had received the following letter:—
Bryn Elthin, Colwyn Bay, Sunday.

Dear Mr. Pemberton, My brother Arthur and I were talking about the Club, and wondering whether the members would care to have some novels in the reading room? My brother has some three dozen books of varying worth, which he would be only too pleased to send to the Club should you approve this suggestion. These would form a nucleus, and I have several duplicates I would bring from here; the words "Liberal Club" could be written on the flyleaf of each, and I think personally there might be many members who would care to read them through in about three evenings' attendance, even though they could not take them home. Should you agree, I should be so pleased to furnish a small bookcase for them to stand in the reading room, and will procure one if you will kindly send me a note by return saying if the club consents to the idea. Apologising , for troubling you, believe me. Yours Faithfully, TRUDA H. CROSFIELD. The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Pemberton had acknow- ledged the letter with very great thanks indeed. (Hear, hear.) One of their vice-presidents had offered to supplement the gift by other books for use in the read- ing room. In referring to Mr. Arthur Crosfield, the Chairman said the gift. of books was another of the little acts of kindness which the club had received from the Crosfield family. (Hear, hear.) REPORT AND ELECTfON OF' OF'F[CERS. Mr. PEMBERTON submitted his annual report and balance sheet. Having regard to the bad state of trade during the year, the club receipts were satisfactory. Mr. E. A. SANDERS proposed the adoption of the report and Mr. J. WOOD seconded. The CHAIRMAN said they had not had ideal bowling weather and that had interfered with the club's receipts. The electiontf officers was then proceeded with and resulted as follows :—President and hon, treasurer, Mr. A. H. Crosfield; vice-presidents, Councillors W. Pier- point, D. Tinnion and J. Wilkinson; hon. secretary, Mr. Thomas Pemberton; auditors, Messrs. John Harrison and William Ford: committee, Messrs. S. J. Beaman, W. Bibby, John G. Chappell, John Davies, George H. Shaw, E. V. Walker, John Worrell, J. Birkhead, J. Russell, and A. H. Sanders. SPEEC3H BY MR. A. H. CLWVIELD. THE NON-TRADING CO VIVIETTEE. Mr. A. FL CROiFEELD who was heartily received on rising to speak said : Oar good friend Mr. Pemberton wrote M 3 the other day and said he thought it might not be out of place if I said a fey words to-night, and candidly lam rather glad of the opportunity. (Hear, hear.) Before referring to politiceat all I should like to say a word or two on a noa-pelitical question in per- fect good humour and good temper. There was a remark made in the Parr Hall the other day which I don't think I can very well pass over in silence because it might lead to rather serious misapprehension amongst some of our friends. It was stated that this time twelve months ago, whea the municipal elections came on, that amongst others, I took up a partisan atti- tude in regard to this great non-trading question. I just want to tell you that that is a =stake. I have never taken up any partisan attitude on the non-trading question. (Hear, near.) The President of our Liberal Association, which, as you know' is distinct altogether from the management of this Club, and the members of the Executive and myself ware entirely in agreement that this Liberal Association as such, should not be used as an organisation for or against the Non-Trading Asso-i ciation. (Hear, hear.) The best illustration of that I think, is the very cordial support that, for instance, was given by the President. myself Und others to our good friends Mr. Upson and Mr. Brophy. I will say further that I had no motive whatever to lead me to take up an antagonistic attitude to the Non-traders in the town as such, because no more than our President and no more than any other gentleman of our Executive have I any wish to encourage wholesale trading in the Corporation. l(Flear, hear.) It is perfectly true that I did write to Mr. Dodds, who had shortly before joined our Association, and suggested that it was a pity that stalwart and valued Liberals of great service to the town and of great service to our party like Councillor Tinnion and Coun- cillor Evans should be opposed. (Cheers). I don't say that Mr. Dodds wished them to be opposed; very likely not. As to what mayhave been his own preciseattitude on the matter I say nothing, but the fact remains that unfortunately Mr. Tinnion was opposed, and it was only at the eleventh hour our good friend Councillor Evans found that he was going to have a walk over, and I think chiefly because he was too strong a candidate in the Whitecross Ward to tackle. (Laughter.) I hope this makes it quite clear to von all that it is not the fact as ' stated inithe Parr Hall that I was against the non-traders; that on the contrary, like our President, I took up an attitude of strictimpartiality. Some rather sarcastic remarks have been made though about im- partiality, so let me take this opportunity to say that at the present juncture, I think it would be much better if there was more impartiality on this question shown in certain quarters. (Cheers.) I am not alluding to any fellow townsman of ours, but I do think there is very great justification for the remarks which were made in a letter published in last Saturday's papers by a man who is not only honoured in this club, but who will alwaysbe honoured I believe, quite irrespective of party inWarrington, that is our good friend Mr. Thomas Birchall. (Applause.) MR. PARKER'S CORRESPONDBNCE. There is another letter in last Saturday's papers and lam going to read an extract from it. You know it is said "All roads lead to Rome.," and nobody can get on his legs nowadays without showing symptoms of the complaint which they call `fisc.alitis." (Laughter and applause). "Mr. Chamberlain says," observes the writer, "no doubt jocularly, 'how I wish that I could deal with economio facts:* There are a great many of his country men who wish so too,and what strikes us in Mr. Chamberlain's speeches is that when- ever he leaves generalities and perorations about Empire, and comes downto figures, he invariably mis- uses them, and manifests an unfortunate facility for inaccuracy in his efforts to compel economic facts to adjust themselves to his political aspirations." I dare say a good many of you will recognise that quotation from a letter by our President—a very strong letter too. (Hear, hear.) Well very likely at this moment Mr. Chamberlain is either entertaining his audience in Liverpool or making their blood run cold —(laughter)—by terrible prophecies based on fantastic figures which are in very striking contrast to any of the statistics which you and I have had to study of late. (Hear, hear.) But instead of going through a number of these figures, which I am sure are very familiar to you already, it occurred, to me this morning that I would reada letter that I have heard my father read many years ago. So I telegraphed to Mrs. Crosfield to ask her if she would let me have it to-night and it reached me shortly before I came here. it is A LETTER FROM MR. MCMINNIF.S to my father in the early seventies, and whether it has any bearing on certain doleful prophecies we have heard of late Twill leave you to judge when I have finished it. "County Hotel, Carlisle, Tuesday. My Dear John,— I am on my way to the funeral of an old relative of mine, and I shall not be in Warrington this week excepting perhaps for a few hours on Thursday night. asked Mr.Reaney to give us an article this week, but he has not time,and I am afraid we must ask you again to perform this task." [I may mention, Gentle- men, that in those days Mr. Reaney and my father frequenly wrote leading articles in the "Examiner, when it was giving a whole-hearted backing to Liberalism all through, as it does now.] "There can only be one subject this week: The Member and his meeting, and as I hope the paper will be taken up with a good report of the meeting, the article need not be a long one. My business to- morrow almost out-faces me. First a journey on a mourning coach for three hours and a half over the moors of the Western Highlands, then a Scotch burial service in an old kirk-yard, where there has not been a church for over a century; with the day as cold and , wet, and the parson as cold and dry—(loud laughter) —as Scotch days at this time of the year and Scotch parsons at all times are. (Renewed laughter.) Andl know that that parson will have neither compunction nor compassion. (Laughter). No matter how bleak and cold and wet it may be on that hill-side, he will read a long chapter, make a longer prayer and deliver a still longer exhortation on the uncertainty and brevity of human life—(My relative was 93.) (Laugh- ter.) Also, Tam to-night sleeping at an out-of-the-way inn at New Cumnock. You never heard of it before and will never hear of it again. (Laughter.) lam quite sure I shall be put into a damp bed. I feel so sure that I am going to my death that I would nob mind changing places with any soldier who has to join in the next sortie out of Paris, (laughter) and I am equally sure that my end will be cold and damp. I suppose from the name there must bean Old Cum.

div.head: TIIE ATTACK ON TRA.DES UNIONS.
div.p: TIIE ATTACK ON TRA.DES UNIONS.

There have been in recent years decisions by the judges which, I am sure, Trade Unions inWarrington have watched with serious alarm and apprehension an 4 which have entirelyaltered the status of trades unions all through the country. It happens that some time since I had written a letter on this very subject for the press. I did not quite complete it because with this epidemic of flscalitis raging through the country, it seemed best to 'concentrate one's energies in resisting that attack, for I can call it nothing else than anattack upon the welfare of the nation at large. (Hear, hear.) But .I do intend to take an early opportunity to com- plete and publish that letter in which I shall deal with the question at more length than is possible to-night. On this occasion I will only briefly point out that the legal position of Trades Unions has been enormously weakened .by recent decisions of the judges, of which the Taff Vale judgment was perhaps the most important example. The workman has been deprived of valued rightoand privileges, which up to a year ago everybody thought were his by deffniteAct of Parliament.—(hear, hear) —rights which it is beyond question the legislation of the early seventies meant to confer upon him. In the interests not only of the workman, but as history has taughtuslequally of the!social well-being and the contentment of the community I submit that it is im- perative that his position should be re-defined. (Loud cheers.) That would have been done if the Government had been willing to accept what was I think a very temperate measure introduced last session by Mr. Shackleton. (Hear, hear.) Not only is that Bill resisted andconsequently rejected but the whole matter referred to a Royal Commission upon which Labour h as not a single representative, though care was taken to place upon it an exeeptionally able representative of capital. (Hear, hear.) This is a good illustration of what workingmen have to expect from the present re- actionary and effete administration.

div.head: SOUTH AFRICAN MUDDLE.
div.p: THE SOUTH AFRICAN MUDDLE.

Then there is the report of the South African War Commission. The Government appear before a tribunal of their own choosing and the verdict is clear and emphatic—guilty. This great Imperial Government which talks sol,much of the Empire and does so much to expose it to needless and terrible risks, is found guilty of muddle, mess, miscalculation, m.akebelieve. (Cheers). They were unprepared for the very war which they always assured us was "inevitable." They gambled with the safety of the Empire by bluffing, on the chance that the Boers would, climb down. They neglected the clear and emphatic warnings of the soldiers whoadvised them. They went into war with a lack of stores and a defection of equipment that enormously increased the cost of the war both in life and material. (Hear, hear). This is no partisan account of the findings of the Commission. I defy you to read the War report and not discover that this Tory Government of ours is short weight. (Laughter).

div.head: 11DITC A.T lON.
div.p: 11DITC A.T lON.

Then there is the great question of Education. In a Parliament elected ostensibly to wind up affairs after a war they told us was finished,and for no other special purpose, the Government have forced through Acts in defiance of a clearly hostile public opinion which in the first place destroy every popularly elected School Board in Englandand Wales; in the second place allow religious tests to,be kept for teachers paid for entirely out of public money; and in the third place, they have . placed denominational schools upon the rates whilst , leaving them under denominational management. This it a sorry record and little wonder that great masses of the most law abiding of our fellow countrymen should find themselves compelled to resist payiag for what they in their consciences disapprove. (Applause.) We i want the religious question got out of the way by a ' settlement which will outrage the feelings 'of none, and then, but then only, will the way be clear for the pro- gress which shall result in our educational equipment being levelled up to the standard of Germany and the • United States. (Applause.) THE HOUSING OF THE PEOPLE. Another question which is of supreme importance to the people of thif4countrylas we all know is,that of housing ;Hear, hear.) Now some of us have been hammering at this for a long time, and it has been constantly asked how such a question can ever be solved on effective , lines until you properly and justly deal with the taxa- tion of site values and ground rents. (Hear, hear.) I • believe it is impossible to exaggerate the immense im- portance of that reform—the taxation of site values and g round rents—and the housing question is inextricably bound up with it. I repeat it is impossible to exagger- ate the far reaching effect of it, and the God-send it will be to the people and the splendid effect it is bound •to have on the physique of the country. (Hear, hear.) Not only did Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman deal with the'subject in his powerful speech at Bolton but Mr. Asquith and other leading Liberals on our side are now • putting this question of land reform right in the front of the party's programme. (Applause.) What I have mentioned constitutes work of enormous importance and I don't understand how anybody can say with work like that ahead of us that the difference between Con- servative and Liberal, or Radical and Tory is only a difference in name. (Hear, hear and applause.) It is a very great deal more. (Hear, hear.) Well the great political battle which is to be fought out in this country cannot be long deferred now. I think we have a very strong case to call upon all thoughtful citizens to put in office a more capable set'of men—(applause)--to elect ,a Government which will combine reasonable economy , with efficiency and which will enforce well-considered reform and put into practical effect some of the work that is to improve the social fabric of this nation. , (Loud applause.) MR. PARKER AND THE FISCAL PROBLEM. Mr. C. E. PARKF:n said he simply rose to ask them to • accord to the chairman a vote of thanks for taking the *place of Counc.Allor Tinnion and discharging the duties so well. If he began, he said, to speak about the fiscal policy he hardly knew where to stop. it was said of Lord Beaconsfield—he did not know with what truth— that'somebody approached him and said he had a friend who'wanted to bring before him a paper he had written on protection. Lord Beaconsfield said to him "Tell

div.head: DEATH OF MR. J. SHUN GREEN.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. J. SHUN GREEN.
A USEFUL CAREER.

It is with deep regret we record the delth of Mr. J. Shaw Green, who, until recently, played a prominent part in the public life of the town. 111-health caused the deceased gentleman to sever his long and honour- able connection with the Town Council in April last, and since that time the ex-Alderman has been an invalid. It was in the hope of recruiting his health that he removed to , Latchford in May last. He suffered from pernicious • anwmia, and despite the assiduous attentions of Dr. Hopper of Liverpool and Dr. James Bennett of Padgate, he gradually lost strength. On Sunday there was a marked turn for the worse, and early on Thursday morning he peacefully passel to his rest. On the news becoming known in Warrington, the flag at the Town Hall was hoisted half-mast and regret was generally expressed at the loss of so useful and con- scientious a citizen. He was 55 years of age, having been born on the 28th of May, 1848. The deceased gentleman was the son of the late Mr. John Green, of this town,who carried on business as an estate agent for many years in Sankey-street.The late Alderman commenced his business career at the offices of Messrs. Marsh and Barrett, an old firm of solicitors in Warrington, whose offices were in Winwick-street. Subsequently, he took up the position of chief managing clerk of the probate department of Messrs Robert Davies and Company, Ararket Place. He eventually commenced business for himself as an accountant and quickly established a good connection. In 1885 he was elected a fellow of the Society of Accountants and Auditors and the members of this association showed their appreciation of his worth by electing him to the presidential chair. At the time of his death he was a member of the general council of the society and occupied a seat on the disciplinary and finance com- mittee'. Locally, he became auditor for many in- stitutions, including the Co-operative society, the Warrington Borough. Building society, and local com- panies like the Firth Company and the Zillah Shipping Company. His connection with the Town Council brought him prominently before the public, and he soon became one of its most valued members. He was first returned to the Town Council by the electors of the North-West Ward in Jubilee year (1887), and on the redistribution of the town into nine wards, he became the representa- tive of Bewsey Ward. It speaks well for his popularity that on these two occasions he was returned without a contest. Subsequently • he had to fight for his seat, but he succeeded in holding it without a break. In October, 1900, he was elected an Alderman, from which position he retired in April last. One of Mr. Shaw Green's earliest and most useful works as a member of the Council was the part he took in the acquirement of and transfer to the Cor- poration of the Waterworks undertaking. This monopoly had long been in the hands of a private company and its management gave cause for loud coraplaints. It was felt by many leading citizens that the time had arrived when the Corporation should have the control of the water supply in its own hands. &poll of the inhabi- tants was taken, and a decision being given in favour of the transfer, the Corporation decided to take the step. Mr. Green's knowledge as an accountant enabled him to give valuable assistance in the negotiations which led to the acquirement of the undertaking and the subsequent promotion of the Cor- poration Water Bill in Parliament, when he gave evidence before the Committee of the House of Commons. As Chairman of the Finance Committee, Mr. Green did much useful work. His yearly budgets were looked forward to with interest and he always succeeded in presenting a lucia statement of the financial affairs of the Borough. The two extensions of the Borough which took place during his connection ' with the Council gave him much werkof an intricate character, and'another subject which claimed his attention was the financial adjustment between the County and the Borough, on 'Warrington becoming a County Borough. For many years Mr. 'Green was the representative of the Corporation on the County Rate Joint Committee. Apart from finan- cial matters, Mr. Green was deeply interested in educa- tion and was one of the first representatives of the Council appointed on the new Education Committee. For many years he was chairman of the School Attendance Committee, chairman of the Library Sub-Committee, and a valuable member of the now defunct Technical Instruction Sub-Committee The Town Council showed their appreciation of his services by passing a special resolution thanking him for them. The thanks of the Couneil were recorded on an illuminated card which was presented to him,and he esteemed this as one of the most honourable trophies of his public life. It will be seen that Corporation , work filled up a large portion of his time; in fact he was so conscientious in the discharge of his public duties that he did a great deal of the work at home, of which fact only a few were aware. He allowed him- self little recreation. He took an interest in the Field Club and enjoyed the rambles and the intellectual enjoyment which the club afforded. In 1887 he was I appointed a justice of the peace for the Borough by the Chancellor of the Duchy. In politics he was a Liberal, but was never a promin- ent politician. He took a deep interest in all matters affecting the Wesleyan Church, with Nitich he was prominently identified. He attended Bewsey- road Wesleyan Chutch and had acted as class leader and circuit steward. He had filled almost all the offices , open to him in the Warrington circuit and discharged the duties with credit to himself and to the religious denomination of which he was so distinguished a lay- man. He is survived by a widow and two daughters— the younger of whom is wife of Mr. J. W. Duprb, of Southampton. The funeral takes place this afternoon and will be a public one. The cortege will leave the house at 12-30 and a service will be held in Bewsey-road Chapel at 1.15. The service will conclude at two o'clock and the interment will take place at 2.30 in the Cemetery. The Mayor has invited the members of the Council to attend the funeral and thus pay a fitting tribute of respect to the memory of the deceased gentleman.

div.head: OTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. By " Ovalist."
div.p: OTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. By " Ovalist."

The unexpected happened at several football grounds last Saturday, but, fortunately not at Warrington, where the Blues were easily vanquished by ten p3ints to three, a score which does not indicate Warrington's superiority. Though there have been so many changes in the ranks of late, Swinton were not badly repre- sented, and they played a game which suggested that they ought not to have lost six matches out of eight. They have, however, struck a had patch, and the effect on the men was noticeable. There was none of the fire and energy usually associated with the play of the Lions.

Warrington, for once in a way were at their full strength, both Harris and Dickenson re-appearing after injuries. The former received a warm welcome from the crowd on his first turn out with the premier team this season. Right from the commencement of hostilities Warrington took up an attacking position, and the Swinton line only escaped on two occasions through the selfishness of Dickenson in sticking to the ball too long. Numerous opportunities went begging, and the crowd was beginning to feel exasperated, when Harris fielded at the quarter line, and punted cleverly behind the posts, where Morrison won the race for possession and scored. Fish landed a goal. Then came Swinton's turn. With one of those unex- pected efforts which seem to be their forte,they rubbed off three of the points. Hampson got possession as the result of bad play by Davies, and after a clever run from half-way, assisted by Tayloi, he scored far out. Dickenson broke clean through for Warrington, but was brought down by the full back, and at half- time the homesters were only 5-3.t0 the good.

It was generally expected that points would accumulate rapidly On resumption, but they failed to materialise for some time. Davies got clear away on two occasions and nothing came of it, while the centres both dropped passes at critical moments. It was only a question of time however, and at last Isherwood got a grand try after combination with Davies, Bate and Dickenson. Swinton made a couple of unproductive raids on the home line, and just be- fore the dose Dickenson raised the home total to ten points by a fine goal from an oblique angle.

The game was by no means a poor one, though the way Warrington missed chances was aggravating to the home crowd. If anything like a good proportion of opportunities had been turned to good account. Warrington must have won by 20 points. They had four-fifths of the play and repeatedly seemed certain to score, only to fail through their own want to finish. The home backs were by no means seen at their best, and nothing proves this more conclusively than the fact that, though the team got possession oftener than not,lsherwood and Fish never made a single com- bined effort. The passing generally broke down at the centres, both of whom were guilty of mistakes and yet did grand work for their side. Isherwood was a constant thorn:in the side of the Lions, and he well- deserved the try he eventually got. Dickenson had an even better chance, but he hesitated and succumbed to the full back. His worst fault was,however, in not serving his wing properly. Harris, though out of training, must have scored twice if his partner had played the game.

Harris has not got anything like his speed back,but I believe he is training hard. Nevertheless one had more confidence in him than in Forster,and his cross kick was worthy of Fish. The same tactics might be employed at Hull to-day, if other means of scoring fail. Fish got his side a couple of tries on Wednes- day in the County match with judicious kicking. Reverting to Saturday's game,praise must be given to the home forwards, and to Thomas in particular. He was here, there, and everywhere. Hallam was also at his best, while Bate and Davies made the most successful pair at half-back Warrington have tried so far. On the Swinton side, only Hampson, and Dixon the reserve full back, did anything of note. The latter was particularly smart and reliable. He astoniiied even his friends.

Salford met their masters on Saturday, when the y succumbed to Oldham on their own ground. The committee seem greatly' to blame for playing Lomas and Bedford while totally unfit. Kingston Rovers won at Leigh and now tie with the Reds for first place. Warrington have risen to third, while Hunslet have deteriorated owing to a bad fall at Keighley• The latter, with Widnes and Wigan, recorded their first victory of the season.
The league table up-to-date is as follows For. Against. _ _ _

Lancashire easily overcame the depleted forces of Cheshire at Broughton on Wednesday, and the spectators were treated, to a very fast open, and scientific game. Opinion among the crowd was generally in favour of the 12 aside game, which was certainly attractive to a degree. The only regrettable feature was Cheshire's weakness, but they had more of the ;play than a score of 1 goal 8 tries (26 points)to 1 goal 1 try (5 points) represents. They might have scored again if Molyneux 'and Richardson had not been such sinners in the way of neglecting their wing men. They kicked splendidly, but this was of little use in a twelve-aside contest. Butterworth played a great game, and praise is also due to the Runcorn "A." teamer, Harrison for the way he filled Houghton's place at full back.

Fish was in very flail form, scoring a try in the first three runs, another at the close, and practically giving Wilson and Baxter one each. He made a number of brilliant runs down touch which delighted the crowd. Lomas was badly missed, for W. James made none of the headway one relies upon from the famous Salfordian. Baxter was, in my opinion, the best half on the field. In addition to fast passing and running by the backs, there was some fine dribbling, which showed. that there is plenty of scope for clever forward play in the new game. The Lancashire tries were scored by Wilson three, Fish and Hogg two each, and Baxter one, while Davies registered Cheshire's solitary point. The impression given of Lancashire's form was that the County Palatine could lick anything at 12 aside. Beware, Yorkshire!

Warrington, to-day, have a very stiff engagement with Hull Kingston Rovers, at Hull, and will be represented by last Saturday's fifteen. I cannot think very highly of their chances, but the Rovers have vet to prove themselves the superior side. Should War- rington win, they will be casting their eye on the Championship Cup, and it is time they did.

Cycling Club "Smoker." One of the most successful " smokers " ever held in connection with the Warrington Cycle Club took place at the Patten Arms Hotel on Thursday evening. About 100 members and friends assembled and had the pleasure of listening to a highly enjoyable programme. The genial "Pa" Davies was, as usual, voted to the chair and at the outset read a letter from Mrs. Arthur Booth thanking the members for the beautiful bouquet presented to her at the close of Saturday evening's performance of" The Yeomen of the Guard." Two gentlemen who figured very successfully- in the opera—Mr. J. Rabbitt and Mr. A. Fieldhouse contributed to the programme and had a oordia 1 reception. The artistes, one and fall acquitted them- selves with the greatest credit. There were songs by Messrs. L. Aukland, J. Rabbitt and A. Fieldhouse, banjo solos by Mr. G. Kendrick, humorous songs by Mr. Walter Dowling (Liverpool), and a humorous recital by Mr. E. A.. Sanders. Encores were freely accorded and the proceedings throughout passed off with a sociabil- ity and enthusiasm which augur well for a suceessful winter season. Mr. F. Booth was an efficient accompan- ist. The artistes were heartily thanked on the proposi- tion of Mr. W. Taylor (captain of the club), seconded by Mr. E. Pickavance, jun, (hon. secretary), and the function was brought to a close with the singing of the National anthem.

div.p: "The Yeomen of the Guard."

Sir,—May I ask you to let me express through the medium of your paper, my thanks, my very grateful thanks, to those ladies and gentlemen of the Warrington Musical Society, who presented me with the very- handsome cigar-case, at.the conclusion of last Sat--- urdays performance of "The Yeomen of the Guard:' I can assure them it is very keenly appreciated, and will always be a souvenir of one of the happiest times I've ever spent.—Believe me sincerely yours E. THORNLEV DODGE.

div.head: 17, January street, Manchester, Oct. 27th, 1903. _ Turkish Mis-rule and Atrocities in Macedonia.
div.p: 17, January street, Manchester, Oct. 27th, 1903. _ Turkish Mis-rule and Atrocities in Macedonia.
Sir,—Will you permit me to direct the very special attention of your readers to the Town's Meeting to 1:200 held at the call of the Mayor next Thursday night ul the Parr Hall.

Attractions and engagements are so many, thati fear this meeting may get hidden away. But it is of great importance that it should be both influential in its character, and as large in its number as possible. ?in is encouraging to know that public feeling is being very strongly awakened and expressed throughout the country, and also that the King's Government is bringin,g some measure of pressure to bear upon the Sultan of Turkey. No one can read the terrible doings of the Turkish soldiery against not only the men, but the women and children, of Macedonia, without feelings of the deepest horror and indignation. And every one, of whatever creed in religion or politics must be intensely desirous that such ghastly and revolt- ing inhumanities should be stopped, and rendered for ever henceforth impossible. No country has greater responsibility in this matter than our own, and no European Power could exert greater influence. It is earnestly tp be hoped that people of all sections in this town will crowd Parr Hall next Thursday night.-- Yours faithfully,
JOHN YONGE.
19 Wilson Patten-street, October 30th, 1903.

National Service League. Sir,—lt is very satisfactory, that the first_part of this argument has been settled. In stating that I have mad out an excellent case for increasing the Navy vote, you have admitted that we are not as secure as we ought to - be. This point being settled, we can confine our atten- tion to the next, i.e. the best remedy for this insecurity. In view of the opinions you have put forward, I find it convenient to divide the discussion of the remedy aS follows:
(1) Are we to trust to the Navy and to the Navy only without a second line of defence for the protection of these shores?
(2) If not, how can we best obtain this second line of defence?

It is obviously'no goodidiscussing N 0.2 before we have settled No. 1, so let us leave the former entirely on one side for the present. It is so nice to stick to the point, is it not? Now you ask me a plain question which is what I like, and which I will reciprocate. You say "presume that this barrier" (the sea strengthened by our ships of war) "is broken down by an enemy; of what use would our compulsorily trained men be, except to make things awkward ?" I admit at once that if our fleet was completely smashed up we are done for, and I am only too glad that you recognise the necessity of having a really strong navy. But there are a great many contingencies besides that of the complete ruin of our fleet, which might happen, and where a second line of defence would be indispensable. Suppose- that our fleet is decoyed by a ruse, as in 1805, and the channel is in consequence insufficiently protected for 24 hours, what is to prevent an enemy from landing 100,000 men during that period unless there is a home defence army guarding these shores ? Or, again, suppose that our fleet is put out of action for the time being, if you can keep the enemy from landing while the ships are being repaired welrand good, if not all is over. Is not your second line of defence indis- pensable in such a case? Then surely, if the Navy feels that there is no backbone behind it, if it feelS that it can never leave these shores unprotected while- it concentrates ready to strike with all its force on the weak spots of the enemy, is not its fighting value being terribly weakened? In 1805 our Navy was superior to all the other fleets put together. To make our Navt comparatively as strong to-day as it was then would cot 3 120 millions aiuntally! Yet even in 1805 we saw the need of a second line of defence. These considerations lead me to ask you whether,with a view to strengthening the Navy, we shall not do by spending four millions annually in training uP a sound home defence army, than by spending an equiv 64- lent amount in battleships.—l am, sir, your obedienv servant, better

TO THE ELECTORS OF IMF. HOWLEY WARD LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— It is now over 9 years since you first elected me as one of your representatives in the Town Councihand as my term of office will soon expire, I have been requested to again allow myself to be nominated as a candidate at the forthcoming election on the 2nd November. After careful consideration I have decided to accede to that request, and now beg to offer myself for election again on INDEPENDENT LINES. During my connectioa with the Council, I have served on the following committees :—Sanitary Works, Gas, Weter, Electricity. Tramways. Rivers, Cemetery, Gymnasium and General Purposes, and have acted as Deputy-Chairman for 6 years and Chairman for two Years of the Sanitary Works Com- mittee. Deputy Chairman for 3 years of the Water Committee, !tor' Deputy-Chairman for 5 years and Chairman for 3 years of the Cemetery Committee During this period these Committees have met on 1.227 occasions, on which I have been present 1,124. The Council has also, in the same period, held 135 meetings. I have attended 129. In addition I have attended numerous sub-committee meetings,of which no record has been kept. These figures should afford a sufficient guarantee that I have not neglected .my duties as one of your representatives, and may fairly claim to have some knowledge of requirements of the town in ganeral and of the Howley Ward in particular. If it should be your pleasure to again elect me, I shall continue to discharge my duties as ties iduously as in the past. I beg to remain, Yours faithfully, JOHN EVANS. Church-street.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, My term of Office expires this month and having been requested by influential members of both Political Parties to offer my services again, I have consented to do so. During the six years I have been your represen- tative I have (amongst many other progressive re- forms) been the means of removing the NUISANCE AT TOWN'S END, and the STREET-MAKING in Orford/ Ward has had the best attention in the Towu and that, notwithstanding I bad personally to pay over V.OO TOWARDS same—chewing self-inter- est was sacrificed in your welfare. The back passages have been lighted up in the Ward since I was appointed, but the most important reform whioh I have bad in hand is the open space between Orford Lane and Winwick Road, and after a lot of opposition I have only last month arranged for estimates to be obtained to lay out n RECREA- TION GROUND for Bowling Green. Quoiting Ground and, the most Important—swings ..tc. for children. This I can promise you will be completed if I am again honoured with your confidence. Many residents have male suggestions and com- plaints, bet in every instance I have attended to the same to their satisfaction, and the experience gained In Municipal life enables me to more successfully deal with all matters submitted to me. I aiw tys ineist upon Trade Unionism being upheld in all Corporation work. Being my own master I can devote the whole of my tinte if necessary in your interest. I have been pressing for half-penny stages on the Tramway route to and from the Jockey, owing to the shortness of that route, as the only way of mak- ing that section pay. TII4PHCTING THE " MUCH-TALKED OF EN- QUIRY " allow me to claim the credit of being the first member who proposed that the Enquiry should he held, end it was carried. and you the rate- payers • hoold demand that the same should be PUBLIC and the press admitted, which would dispense wi, h th. vexed question of cost. I am, however, not. on offi^ial Non-Trader. although I am in aYmnath9 with the principle. and I decline to be tied down by any party or clique, knowing that hstter results PAR be obtained by using your own judgment in all matters, and, as in the part. I pre- fer and will always remain an Englishman, not fear- ing to express my honest opinion on any matters brought forward but prejudice and petty jealousy I will not give quarter to. I pay rates on an AS9ES9MENT OF OVIIIR £4Ol AND PAY WEIGHS 24,030 PER Y 114.11 IN THE WARD, so that your interests are mine. Efficiency with Economy has always eon my motto, and if my humble efforts have met'with yoor approval, I solicit your votes on Monday neat, November 2nd, Yours Faithfnlly, ARTHUR PEACOCK.
